stem:
A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 33 weeks and 2 days gestation attends day assessment with a two-day history of new frontal headache and intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort that has worsened over the last 24 hours. She denies visual disturbance, scotomata, abdominal pain in other regions, vaginal bleeding or reduced fetal movements. Her booking blood pressure at 12 weeks was 108/64 mmHg and all booking bloods (including renal, hepatic and platelet counts) were normal.

Her dating ultrasound was reassuring and there is no personal or family history of hypertensive disease. On three repeated measurements 15 minutes apart today her blood pressure is 152/98 mmHg, 154/96 mmHg and 150/99 mmHg in the seated position with an appropriately sized cuff. A spot urinary protein/creatinine ratio is 18 mg/mmol, below the SOMANZ significant proteinuria threshold of 30 mg/mmol, and she has only trace blood on dipstick.

The midwife notes hyperreflexia without clonus and asks the obstetric registrar whether the patient meets the diagnostic criteria for pre-eclampsia in the absence of significant proteinuria, given the bedside biochemistry shown below.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/98 mmHg (confirmed on three readings), HR 84 bpm, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Hyperreflexia bilaterally without clonus. Mild RUQ tenderness. Uterus soft, fundus appropriate for dates.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L, platelets 92 x10^9/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, ALT 78 U/L (ULN 35), AST 65 U/L (ULN 35), urate 0.38 mmol/L, urine PCR 18 mg/mmol. CTG normal.

lead_in: Which feature in this presentation independently satisfies the SOMANZ diagnostic criteria for pre-eclampsia in the absence of significant proteinuria?

options.text: Serum urate above the trimester-specific reference range value in isolation alone here
Hyperreflexia on clinical examination without any ankle clonus present on today's review
Platelet count 92 x10^9/L with transaminases above twice the upper limit of normal
New right upper quadrant pain in clinical isolation without any other PET features
Urine protein/creatinine ratio of 18 mg/mmol on a spot midstream sample today

subtopic_detail: Pre-eclampsia diagnosis without proteinuria

stem:
A 31-year-old G3P2 woman at 35 weeks and 2 days gestation presents with three days of progressively worsening right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and increasing fatigue. Her two previous pregnancies were uncomplicated and she has no personal or family history of thrombotic microangiopathy, autoimmune disease or liver disease. Her blood pressure on three readings is 146-150 / 90-94 mmHg, she has 1+ proteinuria with a urine PCR of 42 mg/mmol, and the fetal CTG is reactive with normal growth on a scan one week ago.

She has had no recent gastroenteritis, no bloody diarrhoea and no recent E. coli O157:H7 or shigatoxin-producing organism exposure. Bedside bloods show haemoglobin 96 g/L (anaemia with reticulocytosis), platelets 68 x10^9/L, ALT 285 U/L, AST 312 U/L, total bilirubin 38 micromol/L (predominantly indirect), LDH 850 U/L, fibrinogen 3.2 g/L (preserved), INR 1.1, creatinine 84 micromol/L (normal for pregnancy), glucose 5.2 mmol/L, and ammonia within the normal range. A peripheral blood film shows schistocytes, polychromasia and absent platelet clumps. ADAMTS13 activity measured urgently is 65% (well above the 10% threshold for TTP).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, T 36.9 degC.
data_table.Examination: Mild scleral icterus, RUQ tenderness. Uterus appropriate for dates, soft.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, platelets 68 x10^9/L, schistocytes on film, LDH 850 U/L, bilirubin 38 micromol/L (mostly indirect), ALT 285 U/L, AST 312 U/L, INR 1.1, fibrinogen 3.2 g/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, ammonia normal, ADAMTS13 65%.

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this clinical and biochemical picture?

options.text: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets)
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy with hepatic dysfunction
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with neurological features
Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome with complement-mediated injury
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy with raised bile acids

subtopic_detail: HELLP vs AFLP vs TTP vs HUS in pregnancy

stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 with booking BMI 27, no diabetes history, no PCOS, no previous GDM has a 75 g OGTT at 27 weeks: fasting 5.3, 1 h 8.4, 2 h 7.1 mmol/L. The midwife asks whether this meets Australian (ADIPS) criteria for gestational diabetes, and if so, what the immediate next step is. The woman has no symptoms and her fetus is growing on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
data_table.Examination: BMI 28. Uterus appropriate for dates.
data_table.Investigations: Awaiting OGTT result.

lead_in: Which interpretation and next step are correct?

options.text: GDM diagnosed on the fasting >=5.1 mmol/L cut-off; commence dietitian and diabetes educator referral, capillary glucose monitoring 4 times daily, and review at the joint diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic within 1 week
Not GDM; only the fasting result is borderline; repeat OGTT in 4 weeks
GDM only if fasting >=5.5 mmol/L; her result is below threshold
Type 2 diabetes diagnosed (fasting >=7.0); commence insulin today
Borderline only; reassure with healthy-eating advice and re-test at 32 weeks

subtopic_detail: Gestational diabetes - ADIPS 75 g OGTT thresholds

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 woman at 30 weeks and 2 days gestation was diagnosed with GDM at 26 weeks (fasting 5.4 mmol/L, 2 h 9.1 mmol/L on 75 g OGTT). She has been on structured dietary modification with a credentialled dietitian and 30 minutes of daily walking for four weeks. Her four-times-daily capillary glucose diary now shows fasting values consistently 5.6-6.2 mmol/L (ADIPS target <5.1 mmol/L) and 2-hour postprandial values 5.8-6.8 mmol/L (target <6.7 mmol/L) after all three meals.

There is no overnight hypoglycaemia, no symptomatic hypoglycaemiabedside testing. Fetal ultrasound at 30 weeks shows estimated fetal weight on the 78th centile with appropriate liquor and normal umbilical and middle cerebral artery Dopplers. Her booking BMI was 31 and she has gained 6 kg in pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 82 bpm.
data_table.Examination: BMI 31. Fundal height appropriate.
data_table.Investigations: BSL diary: fasting 5.6-6.2; postprandial within target after all meals. HbA1c 5.6%. Renal function normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Commence basal-bolus insulin with rapid-acting analogue at meals plus bedtime NPH
Commence rapid-acting prandial insulin (aspart or lispro) before each meal only, no basal
Continue lifestyle measures only and review fasting glucose again in four weeks
Commence empagliflozin 10 mg orally daily as monotherapy in pregnancy
Commence isophane (NPH) insulin at bedtime, titrated to fasting capillary glucose target

subtopic_detail: GDM - insulin titration after lifestyle failure

stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 at 28 weeks with gestational hypertension (persistent BP 144/92 over a fortnight; no proteinuria; bloods normal; normal fetal growth and Dopplers) is asymptomatic. She has well-controlled severe asthma on inhaled budesonide/formoterol with two emergency presentations in the past year requiring oral prednisolone. She has no other medical conditions, no allergies, normal renal and liver function. The consultant is choosing the first-line oral antihypertensive.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 144/90 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Uncomplicated. No oedema. Fundus appropriate for dates.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, ALT 22 U/L, urine PCR <30 mg/mmol.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line oral antihypertensive?

options.text: Labetalol 100 mg orally twice daily titrated to target
Slow-release nifedipine 20 mg orally twice daily titrated to target
Enalapril 5 mg orally once daily titrated to target
Methyldopa 250 mg orally three times daily titrated to target
Oral hydralazine 25 mg three times daily titrated to target

subtopic_detail: Hypertension in pregnancy - first-line antihypertensive

stem:
A 27-year-old G1P0 woman at 11 weeks and 2 days gestation has a routine booking infection screen which shows Toxoplasma gondii IgM positive and IgG positive with low avidity, a pattern strongly suggesting recent primary infection within the last 12-16 weeks. She has had a new indoor kitten at home since six weeks before conception and recalls cleaning the litter tray on multiple occasions without gloves.

She also recalls eating undercooked lamb skewers at a barbecue 10 weeks ago. She is asymptomatic, has no lymphadenopathy on examination and her partner is well with no symptoms. Toxoplasma PCR on maternal blood is positive. Her booking ultrasound today shows a viable singleton with normal anatomy for gestation and no calcifications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/68 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Well. No lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Toxoplasma IgM positive, IgG positive low avidity, maternal blood PCR positive. Booking ultrasound: viable singleton at 11 weeks, normal anatomy for gestation.

lead_in: Which initial pharmacological strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Spiramycin 1 g TDS, switching to sulfadiazine-pyrimethamine-folinic acid only if amniocentesis confirms fetal infection
Sulfadiazine plus pyrimethamine plus folinic acid commenced immediately for all women regardless of fetal status
Co-trimoxazole oral monotherapy without folinic acid or any fetal assessment as the definitive treatment
Azithromycin 500 mg orally daily as definitive monotherapy without spiramycin, folinic acid or referral
Termination of pregnancy without treatment given certain severe congenital toxoplasmosis at this gestation

subtopic_detail: Toxoplasmosis - first trimester management

stem:
A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 14 weeks and 1 day gestation works as a long-day-care educator caring for children aged 12-24 months and presents to her GP with a fortnight of mild fatigue, low-grade fever, headache, mild cervical lymphadenopathy and arthralgia. She has no rash, no respiratory symptoms and no jaundice. Routine TORCH testing shows CMV IgM positive, CMV IgG positive with low avidity (consistent with infection within the past three months).

Critically, her booking CMV IgG four weeks earlier was negative, providing serological evidence of seroconversion in early pregnancy. A maternal blood CMV PCR is positive at a moderate viral load. She has no prior infectious diseases history, no immunosuppression, and her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated with a healthy term infant. She asks the maternal-fetal medicine consultant about the difference between primary and non-primary (reactivation or reinfection) maternal CMV infection in pregnancy, the next investigation step including fetal surveillance and timing of any amniocentesis, and the role and evidence base for any antiviral therapy in pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 degC, BP 110/72 mmHg, HR 84 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy; otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: CMV IgG positive low avidity, IgM positive, blood PCR positive. Booking CMV IgG (4 weeks prior): negative. LFTs mildly raised (ALT 65). Hb 122 g/L.

lead_in: Which statement most accurately describes the current Australian approach to maternal CMV infection in this case?

options.text: Non-primary CMV infection carries a higher vertical transmission rate than primary infection, so reassurance is appropriate here
Maternal intravenous ganciclovir is the established standard of care to prevent fetal CMV infection in primary seroconversion
Spiramycin reduces vertical transmission of CMV in the same way that it does for Toxoplasma gondii
CMV is a rare cause of congenital infection and routine fetal surveillance is unnecessary after maternal seroconversion
Serial fetal ultrasound, amniocentesis for CMV PCR after 21 weeks and 6 weeks post-seroconversion, and high-dose valaciclovir following MFM discussion

subtopic_detail: CMV in pregnancy - primary vs non-primary infection

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 24 weeks and 2 days gestation with a background of mild persistent asthma on budesonide-formoterol maintenance (one inhalation twice daily as preventer plus reliever) presents to the emergency department with 12 hours of progressive wheeze, dyspnoea and chest tightness after a viral upper respiratory infection. She is too breathless to speak in full sentences. Her best personal PEFR is 420 L/min; in ED it is measured at 210 L/min (50% of personal best).

SpO2 is 93% on room air. Auscultation reveals widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally and no focal crackles or signs of consolidation. She is afebrile at 37.1 degC, has no calf swelling, no chest pain, the fetus is moving normally and the CTG is reactive with a baseline of 140 bpm. She has stopped her preventer inhaler for the past four days because she was worried about possible effects on the baby and asks whether she should continue inhaled corticosteroids and whether oral prednisolone is safe in pregnancy, given a friend has told her to refuse steroids.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 28 /min, HR 118 bpm, SpO2 93% RA, BP 124/78 mmHg, T 37.1 degC.
data_table.Examination: Speaking in short phrases, accessory muscle use, widespread polyphonic wheeze. CTG reactive.
data_table.Investigations: PEFR 210 L/min (50% of personal best 420). ABG not yet performed. CXR not indicated initially.

lead_in: Which management approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue maintenance inhaled corticosteroid but withhold all systemic corticosteroids in pregnancy due to perceived fetal teratogenic risk
Nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium if severe, continue ICS, oral prednisolone 37.5-50 mg for 5-10 days, plus controlled oxygen
Switch the patient to a leukotriene receptor antagonist (oral montelukast) alone as monotherapy maintenance throughout pregnancy
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes given as the immediate first-line therapy in pregnancy
Discharge home with a short-acting beta-2 agonist alone once PEFR has reached 60% of personal best

subtopic_detail: Asthma in pregnancy - acute exacerbation

stem:
A 28-year-old G2P0 woman with focal-onset epilepsy attends a joint obstetric-medicine/neurology pre-conception clinic three months before a planned pregnancy. She has been seizure-free for two years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily monotherapy, having previously failed levetiracetam (rash and breakthrough seizures) and carbamazepine (breakthrough seizures with intolerable somnolence) for seizure control. Her previous pregnancy ended in a first-trimester miscarriage while she was on lamotrigine monotherapy two years ago, and she has not used lamotrigine since.

She has no family history of neural tube defects or congenital malformations and her BMI is 23. She is concerned about teratogenicity having read media coverage of valproate, and asks specifically about: relative major congenital malformation rates of the commonly used AEDs, the appropriate periconceptional folate dose for women on AEDs versus the general population, the likely need for therapeutic drug monitoring during pregnancy (particularly for lamotrigine if used), and which medication she should ideally be established on by the time of conception.

She is keen to plan a pregnancy within the next six months and is willing to delay conception if a medication switch is recommended, but wants a clear plan that balances seizure control against teratogenic risk and includes the practical issue of how to monitor any new agent through pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 76 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Neurologically normal. BMI 23.
data_table.Investigations: Recent EEG and MRI stable. Valproate level within therapeutic range. Renal and hepatic function normal.

lead_in: Which combination of recommendations is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue sodium valproate, commence folate 0.5 mg daily, with no need for AED drug levels during pregnancy
Switch to phenytoin before pregnancy as it carries the lowest teratogenicity profile of all the AEDs available
Switch (via neurology) from valproate to lamotrigine or levetiracetam pre-conception, folate 5 mg daily, with therapeutic AED level monitoring
Continue valproate, add lamotrigine to permit valproate dose reduction, and use folate 0.5 mg daily throughout
Stop all antiepileptic medications before conception entirely to eliminate teratogenic risk to the developing fetus completely

subtopic_detail: Epilepsy in pregnancy - AED selection and teratogenicity

stem: A 27-year-old G1P0 at 7 weeks is referred for Graves disease. She was diagnosed 6 months ago with tremor, weight loss and palpitations; currently on carbimazole 15 mg daily with normal TFTs and TRAb 5.2 IU/L (positive). She has no goitre and no ophthalmopathy. She is asymptomatic. She and her obstetric medicine team are reviewing her medication plan for the pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Clinically euthyroid. No tremor. No goitre. No ophthalmopathy.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.4 mIU/L, free T4 14 pmol/L, free T3 4.2 pmol/L (all within trimester-specific reference). TRAb 5.2 IU/L (positive).

lead_in: Which management plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Switch to propylthiouracil (PTU) in trimester 1 then back to carbimazole in trimester 2-3; monthly maternal TFTs; fetal growth/goitre scans; neonatal TFTs and TRAb at birth
Continue carbimazole at the current dose throughout pregnancy as the fetus is not at risk of aplasia cutis or any other carbimazole embryopathy
Stop antithyroid drugs entirely as pregnancy is naturally immunosuppressive and Graves disease usually remits spontaneously without medication intervention
Switch to radioactive iodine ablation now to provide definitive treatment despite the absolute fetal contraindication to radioiodine exposure in utero
Switch to PTU throughout pregnancy without switching back to carbimazole in the second trimester despite the cumulative maternal hepatotoxicity risk

subtopic_detail: Graves disease in pregnancy

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman with longstanding primary autoimmune hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 100 microg daily attends the antenatal clinic at 6 weeks gestation by certain LMP with a positive home pregnancy test which she did this morning. Her TSH four weeks ago, pre-conception, was 2.0 mIU/L on her current dose and she has been clinically euthyroid. She is asymptomatic with no symptoms of hypothyroidism (no cold intolerance, fatigue, constipation, dry skin or weight change).

She asks the GP about the dose adjustment to make now (if any), the optimal frequency of thyroid function testing through pregnancy, and the trimester-specific TSH target range she should be aiming for, given that the laboratory reference interval she sees on her result printout (0.4-4.0 mIU/L) is for non-pregnant adults. Her previous pregnancy two years ago was complicated by first-trimester pregnancy loss at 8 weeks when her TSH was found retrospectively to be 6.5 mIU/L early in that pregnancy because she had not increased her dose at conception.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/70 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Euthyroid clinically. No goitre.
data_table.Investigations: Pre-conception TSH (4 weeks ago): 2.0 mIU/L on levothyroxine 100 microg daily. Anti-TPO positive.

lead_in: Which combined management plan most closely matches current guidance?

options.text: Continue 100 microg daily, recheck TSH at 28 weeks gestation, target TSH <4.0 mIU/L throughout the entire pregnancy
Reduce levothyroxine by 25% because pregnancy is associated with a hyperthyroid physiological state secondary to beta-hCG cross-reactivity
Cease levothyroxine completely now to assess underlying endogenous thyroid function before any further dose adjustment is made in pregnancy
Increase levothyroxine 25-30% now (e.g. 125 microg daily), check TSH 4-weekly until 20 weeks, with trimester-specific target
Increase dose by 25-30% but only check TSH if she develops overt clinical symptoms of hypothyroidism in this pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Hypothyroidism in pregnancy - levothyroxine and TSH targets
Combined first-trimester screen - next-step after high risk
stem:
A 36-year-old G2P1 woman attends her general practitioner with the result of her combined first-trimester screen, performed at 12 weeks and 4 days gestation with the recommended ultrasound markers (crown-rump length 62 mm, nuchal translucency 3.2 mm, present nasal bone) and maternal serum PAPP-A and free beta-hCG. The laboratory adjusted risk for trisomy 21 has come back as 1 in 80, with trisomy 18 risk 1 in 950 and trisomy 13 risk 1 in 1100.

Her first child is well at age 4 with no chromosomal abnormality. There is no family history of aneuploidy or congenital structural malformations. Her booking bloods are unremarkable. She and her partner have read about NIPT and diagnostic testing online and want to know the most appropriate immediate next step. She is keen to avoid procedure-related miscarriage risk if reasonable.

The pregnancy is otherwise progressing well, fetal heart was 162 bpm on a brief ultrasound today and she has no bleeding, pain or symptoms of concern.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Soft, non-tender abdomen. Uterus not yet palpable abdominally.
data_table.Investigations: cFTS at 12+4: NT 3.2 mm, nasal bone present, PAPP-A 0.4 MoM, free beta-hCG 2.8 MoM. Adjusted T21 risk 1 in 80, T18 risk 1 in 950, T13 risk 1 in 1100.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in counselling and investigation for this woman?

options.text: Reassure that the cFTS result represents a low-risk pregnancy and proceed to a routine 18 to 20 week morphology scan
Repeat the combined first-trimester screen at 13+6 weeks to see if the risk falls before any further action is taken
Proceed directly to chorionic villus sampling today without further screening, since maternal age above 35 makes diagnostic testing mandatory
Offer NIPT as a contingent screening test, or diagnostic testing (CVS now or amniocentesis from 15 weeks) after counselling about procedure-related miscarriage risk
Arrange amniocentesis today at 12+4 weeks, given the high-risk result and the woman's preference to avoid further screening tests

subtopic_detail: NIPT interpretation - positive T21 result
stem:
A 41-year-old G3P2 woman attends a tertiary maternal fetal medicine clinic at 13 weeks and 2 days gestation. She declined combined first-trimester screening and instead self-funded non-invasive prenatal testing at 11 weeks. The result has been telephoned through by her general practitioner this morning as a high-probability positive for trisomy 21, with fetal fraction reported at 8.2% and no comment on sex chromosome or other autosomal findings.

Trisomy 18 and 13 results were low risk. Her two previous children were chromosomally normal. She has hypothyroidism on thyroxine 100 micrograms daily, has had a previous lower-segment caesarean for breech, and there is no significant family history of inheritable disease. Her booking bloods were unremarkable. An ultrasound today shows a viable singleton pregnancy with CRL consistent with dates, a nuchal translucency of 2.1 mm, present nasal bone, no other structural concerns, and a normally implanted placenta on the posterior uterine wall.

She is distressed and asks the maternal fetal medicine consultant for clear advice on what the NIPT result actually means and what the next step should be.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen. Uterus 13-14 week size.
data_table.Investigations: NIPT at 11 weeks: high probability trisomy 21, fetal fraction 8.2%, T18/T13 low risk. Today's USS: viable singleton, CRL 70 mm, NT 2.1 mm, nasal bone present, no structural anomalies, posterior placenta.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for counselling and management?

options.text: Counsel that NIPT has very high positive predictive value at her age and proceed directly to termination of pregnancy if she wishes, without further confirmatory testing
Proceed directly to amniocentesis today at 13+2 weeks for the most accurate confirmatory result
Repeat the NIPT on a fresh maternal sample to confirm the result before any consideration of diagnostic testing
Reassure her because the nuchal translucency today is normal at 2.1 mm and there are no structural anomalies; defer further testing to the 20 week morphology scan
Counsel that NIPT remains a screening test and offer confirmatory diagnostic testing by chorionic villus sampling now, or amniocentesis from 15 weeks, before any irreversible decision is made

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic testing - CVS vs amniocentesis timing and risk
stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 woman is reviewed in a maternal fetal medicine clinic at 11 weeks and 5 days gestation by certain dates and a confirmatory ultrasound. Her combined first-trimester screen returned a risk of 1 in 60 for trisomy 21, with a nuchal translucency of 3.6 mm and PAPP-A of 0.3 MoM. The fetus has a present nasal bone and no structural anomaly is visible on this morning's ultrasound.

She has reviewed both contingent NIPT and definitive diagnostic options with her midwife and consultant and has decided that she wants a definitive answer in the shortest time possible because she has finite leave from work and significant anxiety. Her previous child has Down syndrome diagnosed postnatally and she does not want to wait until 15 weeks. The placenta is anterior and easily accessible by transabdominal route.

She is RhD positive, has no allergies, and is fit and well.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, anterior accessible placenta on ultrasound today.
data_table.Investigations: cFTS adjusted T21 risk 1 in 60. NT 3.6 mm. PAPP-A 0.3 MoM. USS today: CRL consistent with 11+5, no structural anomalies, anterior placenta.

lead_in: Which diagnostic procedure is most appropriate today and what is the approximate procedure-related miscarriage risk in an experienced Australian unit?

options.text: Transcervical chorionic villus sampling today, with procedure-related miscarriage risk approximately 2 to 3%
Amniocentesis today at 11+5 weeks, with procedure-related miscarriage risk approximately 0.5 to 1%
Defer diagnostic testing and arrange NIPT today, with procedure-related miscarriage risk of zero
Transabdominal chorionic villus sampling today, with procedure-related miscarriage risk approximately 0.1 to 0.2%
Defer diagnostic testing until 18 to 20 weeks and proceed to morphology scan only, with procedure-related miscarriage risk of zero

subtopic_detail: Morphology scan - soft marker (echogenic intracardiac focus)
stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 woman attends her general practitioner for review of her 19 week and 4 day morphology scan, performed at an accredited Australian fetal medicine imaging service. She had a low-risk combined first-trimester screen at 12+5 weeks (adjusted T21 risk 1 in 4200, NT 1.4 mm). The morphology scan report describes normal biometry on the 50th centile, a structurally normal fetus on the standard RANZCOG/ASUM views, a normally implanted posterior placenta clear of the os, normal amniotic fluid volume, and an isolated echogenic intracardiac focus in the left ventricle as the only abnormal finding.

The cardiac four-chamber view, outflow tracts and three-vessel view are otherwise normal. There are no other soft markers (nuchal fold normal, no echogenic bowel, no pyelectasis). She has no significant medical history, no family history of congenital heart disease and is not on any medications. She is anxious because she has read online that EIF is associated with Down syndrome and asks her general practitioner what this finding means in her context and what she should do next.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 76 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, fundus at the umbilicus.
data_table.Investigations: cFTS at 12+5: T21 risk 1 in 4200, NT 1.4 mm. Morphology scan 19+4: biometry 50th centile, structurally normal, isolated left ventricular EIF, no other soft markers, normal placenta and fluid.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling and management plan?

options.text: Offer additional non-invasive prenatal testing today to further confirm low aneuploidy risk before reassuring her about the isolated EIF finding
Refer urgently to maternal fetal medicine and offer amniocentesis given the increased risk of trisomy 21 from the isolated EIF
Arrange a fetal echocardiogram urgently to exclude an associated structural cardiac anomaly given the EIF finding
Repeat the morphology scan in four weeks to confirm persistence of the EIF before deciding on further investigations
Isolated echogenic intracardiac focus in this low-risk woman does not meaningfully alter her aneuploidy risk; reassure and continue routine antenatal care

subtopic_detail: Anti-D prophylaxis - sensitising event before 12 weeks
stem:
A 24-year-old G2P0 woman presents to a regional Australian emergency department with a single episode of moderate per-vaginal bleeding requiring two pads in two hours, associated with mild lower abdominal cramping. Her last menstrual period dates her at 9 weeks and 1 day, and a transvaginal ultrasound today shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with CRL consistent with 8+6 weeks, present fetal cardiac activity at 158 bpm, no retained products in the uterus and a small subchorionic haematoma.

There is no cervical motion tenderness, the os is closed and no products of conception are visible. Her booking blood group from the GP last week is documented as O RhD negative with a negative antibody screen, and she had no prior pregnancies carried beyond miscarriage at 6 weeks one year ago. The general practice doctor in ED asks the obstetric registrar whether routine anti-D Rh(D) immunoglobulin is indicated for this episode and at what dose, given Australian National Blood Authority guidance.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.7 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, mild suprapubic tenderness. Speculum: small amount of fresh blood, os closed, no products. No CMT.
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative, antibody screen negative. TV USS: viable IUP at 8+6, FHR 158 bpm, small subchorionic haematoma, no retained products. Beta-hCG 28 000 IU/L.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate anti-D Rh(D) immunoglobulin management today?

options.text: Administer 625 IU anti-D Rh(D) immunoglobulin IM now, since any bleeding in an RhD-negative woman after 9 weeks is a sensitising event
Administer 1500 IU anti-D Rh(D) immunoglobulin IM now as a single antenatal dose covering both 28 week and 34 week prophylaxis until delivery
Administer 250 IU anti-D Rh(D) immunoglobulin IM now and order a Kleihauer-Betke test today to titrate any further required dose
Anti-D is not indicated today; she continues routine 28 and 34 week prophylaxis of 625 IU IM with 625 IU post-event from 12 weeks onwards
Defer all anti-D decisions until 12 weeks gestation, then administer 625 IU IM only if vaginal bleeding persists or recurs at that time

subtopic_detail: GBS screening - intrapartum prophylaxis with penicillin allergy
stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman presents to the birth suite at 38 weeks and 5 days gestation in established labour with regular painful contractions every 3 minutes and intact membranes. Her vaginal-rectal swab taken at 36 weeks for universal group B Streptococcus screening was positive for Streptococcus agalactiae, sensitive to penicillin and reported as resistant to clindamycin and erythromycin. Her chart documents an immediate hypersensitivity reaction (generalised urticaria and tongue swelling without anaphylaxis) following oral amoxicillin in childhood, judged by the allergy team as high-risk for severe penicillin allergy.

Her previous baby is well at age 3 with no neonatal sepsis. Vital signs are normal, the baby is cephalic and engaged, fetal heart rate is reassuring on intermittent auscultation, and the obstetric registrar wants to commence intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. The midwife asks which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate given the patient's penicillin allergy and the documented GBS antibiotic sensitivities.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/74 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, fully effaced, vertex at -1 station. Contractions 3 in 10 strong.
data_table.Investigations: GBS swab at 36 weeks positive, sensitive to penicillin, resistant to clindamycin and erythromycin. FBC normal. Group O RhD positive.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis regimen?

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth as standard first-line intrapartum prophylaxis
IV cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every 8 hours until birth as the recommended alternative for low-risk penicillin allergy
IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) loading then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours until birth
IV clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours until birth, given the documented high-risk penicillin allergy and inability to use beta-lactams
Oral erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours until birth, given documented penicillin allergy and need to avoid intravenous antibiotic therapy

subtopic_detail: Ectopic pregnancy - methotrexate eligibility
stem:
A 29-year-old G2P0 woman is reviewed in a tertiary early pregnancy assessment unit at 6 weeks and 4 days gestation by last menstrual period after referral from her general practitioner with mild right iliac fossa pain and intermittent light per-vaginal spotting for 48 hours. Her previous pregnancy was a first-trimester miscarriage; she has no history of pelvic infection, prior ectopic, tubal surgery, IUD or assisted reproduction.

She is haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and has no shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or peritonism. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with no intrauterine gestational sac, no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, and an unruptured right adnexal mass measuring 28 mm containing a yolk sac but no fetal pole or cardiac activity. There is no haemoperitoneum. Her beta-hCG today is 3800 IU/L (yesterday 3500 IU/L).

Liver function tests, full blood count and renal function are normal. She lives 20 minutes from the hospital, has reliable transport, can attend for follow-up blood tests, and is keen to avoid surgery if reasonable. The obstetric registrar is considering single-dose intramuscular methotrexate as outpatient management and is checking each eligibility criterion against the RANZCOG and RCOG protocols.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 82 bpm, T 36.7 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Mild RIF tenderness, no peritonism. Soft abdomen. No CMT. No active bleeding.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 3800 IU/L (yesterday 3500). FBC, UEC, LFTs normal. TV USS: empty uterus, no free fluid, right adnexal mass 28 mm with yolk sac, no fetal cardiac activity.

lead_in: Which of the following findings, if present in this woman, would be an absolute contraindication to single-dose intramuscular methotrexate?

options.text: An adnexal mass measuring 28 mm with a yolk sac present but no fetal cardiac activity
A serum beta-hCG of 3800 IU/L with a 24-hour rise of 300 IU/L
Fetal cardiac activity demonstrated on the transvaginal ultrasound today within the right adnexal mass
Mild right iliac fossa tenderness without peritonism, fever or haemodynamic instability
Baseline ALT 65 U/L (reference <40) and AST 58 U/L with otherwise normal synthetic liver function and no underlying chronic liver disease

subtopic_detail: Pregnancy of unknown location - serial beta-hCG and discriminatory zone
stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 woman presents to an early pregnancy assessment unit with a positive urine pregnancy test, light per-vaginal spotting for 3 days and intermittent mild lower abdominal cramping. By last menstrual period she is approximately 6 weeks gestation but her cycles have been irregular over the last 12 months while she has been training for a half-marathon. She is haemodynamically stable, with no peritonism, shoulder-tip pain or dizziness.

A high-quality transvaginal ultrasound performed by an experienced sonographer today shows an empty uterus with a thin endometrium, no intrauterine gestational sac, no adnexal mass and normal-appearing ovaries bilaterally. Her serum beta-hCG today is 1200 IU/L. She is well, has reliable transport and is willing to attend for repeat blood tests. The clinic registrar must decide whether to expectantly manage with serial hCG and rescanning above the discriminatory zone, image again immediately, treat empirically as ectopic with methotrexate, or reassure as presumed early viable intrauterine pregnancy below the imaging threshold.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no peritonism, no CMT. Os closed, minimal brown spotting.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 1200 IU/L today. TV USS: empty uterus, thin endometrium, no adnexal mass, no free fluid, normal ovaries.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence single-dose IM methotrexate 50 mg/m2 today as presumed ectopic pregnancy based on the empty uterus on transvaginal ultrasound
Arrange diagnostic laparoscopy today for definitive diagnosis and possible salpingectomy because of the empty uterus and positive pregnancy test
Repeat the serum beta-hCG in 48 hours and rescan once it exceeds the discriminatory zone of 1500 to 2000 IU/L, with clear safety-netting
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound today by a second sonographer to confirm absence of an intrauterine pregnancy before any follow-up
Reassure that this is a normal early intrauterine pregnancy and arrange routine antenatal booking for 8 to 10 weeks

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis - severity assessment and admission criteria
stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 woman at 10 weeks and 2 days gestation presents to an emergency department with three weeks of progressively worsening nausea and vomiting. Over the last 48 hours she has been unable to keep down oral fluids, has vomited at least eight times per day, and has lost 4 kg from her booking weight of 62 kg (>5%).

She is exhausted, intermittently tearful, and has missed two days of work. Her partner reports she has had episodes of postural light-headedness. Examination shows dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 to 3 seconds, mild ketotic breath, HR 108 bpm, BP 100/62 mmHg lying and 88/55 mmHg standing, T 36.7 degC. Urinalysis shows ketones 3+, specific gravity 1.030, no nitrites or leucocytes.

Her PUQE-24 score today is 14 out of 15 (severe). Bloods reveal sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, urea 7.8 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. Beta-hCG and TFTs are pending. A transabdominal scan shows a viable singleton pregnancy at 10+2 with no molar features. She has tried oral pyridoxine 25 mg TDS at home with no relief.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 100/62 lying, 88/55 standing, HR 108 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Dry mucosa, CR 2 to 3s, ketotic breath. Soft abdomen. Uterus not yet palpable.
data_table.Investigations: PUQE-24 14/15 (severe). Weight loss 4 kg (>5%). Urine ketones 3+, SG 1.030. Na 132, K 3.1, urea 7.8, creat 92. USS: viable singleton, no molar features.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Admit for IV normal saline rehydration, IV thiamine before any dextrose, IV potassium replacement, and stepwise antiemetics with serial electrolyte monitoring
Discharge with oral doxylamine-pyridoxine and a metoclopramide PRN script with a written safety-net to return for ongoing vomiting
Admit for total parenteral nutrition via a central venous catheter to bypass the gut entirely while severe vomiting resolves over coming days
Admit for IV dextrose 5% rehydration to provide immediate energy substrate and commence IV ondansetron monotherapy without giving prior thiamine
Arrange urgent termination of pregnancy at 10 weeks as the only definitive treatment for refractory severe vomiting unresponsive to oral therapy

subtopic_detail: Molar pregnancy - recognition and surveillance
stem:
A 22-year-old G1P0 woman presents to her general practitioner at an estimated 11 weeks gestation by uncertain last menstrual period with three weeks of persistent nausea, intermittent vaginal spotting and one episode of passing what she describes as small grape-like tissue. She has no significant medical history. Examination shows a uterus palpable above the symphysis to a size consistent with 14 weeks, soft and non-tender.

Blood pressure today is 138/86 mmHg (previously 110/70 at GP visit at 8 weeks). She has dry mucous membranes and reports mild postural symptoms. A transvaginal ultrasound at the local imaging service today shows a heterogeneous intrauterine mass with multiple small cystic spaces (described as 'snowstorm' appearance), no fetal pole, no fetal cardiac activity, and bilateral theca lutein cysts on the ovaries measuring 4 to 5 cm.

The serum beta-hCG is 285 000 IU/L. Thyroid function tests show TSH 0.05 mU/L and free T4 22 pmol/L (mildly elevated). She has been referred to the local gynaecology team and her GP wants to confirm the recognition and what the next steps are.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Uterus size at 14 weeks (LMP-dated 11 weeks). Dry mucosa. Mild postural light-headedness.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 285 000 IU/L. TSH 0.05 mU/L, fT4 22 pmol/L. TV USS: heterogeneous 'snowstorm' mass, no fetal pole, bilateral theca lutein cysts 4 to 5 cm.

lead_in: Which sequence of management most accurately reflects current Australian guidance for this presentation?

options.text: Single-dose IM methotrexate 50 mg/m2 as outpatient with weekly hCG until undetectable, then 6-monthly surveillance for the following 12 months
Suction curettage in theatre with histology, weekly hCG until three negative samples then monthly for 6 months (complete) or 1 month (partial), with reliable contraception
Expectant management with weekly serum beta-hCG only, given that many molar pregnancies will resolve spontaneously without surgical or medical intervention
Total abdominal hysterectomy as primary treatment given the high reported risk of choriocarcinoma associated with this histology
Medical evacuation of the mole with methylergometrine and misoprostol, followed by weekly serum beta-hCG until undetectable for three consecutive weekly samples

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic bacteriuria - significance and treatment
stem: A 24-year-old G1P0 at 12 weeks is asymptomatic with a normal dipstick today. The booking MSU MC&S sent a week ago reports pure growth of GROUP B STREPTOCOCCUS 10^8 CFU/L (sensitive to penicillin). No symptoms, no costovertebral tenderness, observations normal, no allergies. The GP asks the obstetric registrar what management this asymptomatic finding warrants.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no costovertebral angle tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: MSU MCS: pure growth E. coli 10^8 CFU/L, sensitive to amoxicillin, cefalexin, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim. Dipstick today negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Treat with oral antibiotics now (penicillin V or amoxicillin) per Therapeutic Guidelines, and arrange intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin GBS prophylaxis at delivery
No treatment as patient is asymptomatic and dipstick is negative
Treat with antibiotics now but no intrapartum prophylaxis required
Repeat MSU in 4 weeks before any treatment to confirm the finding
Commence continuous suppressive nitrofurantoin until delivery

subtopic_detail: Heterotopic pregnancy after ART - discrimination from PUL/ectopic
stem:
A 34-year-old G3P0 woman conceived through a single fresh embryo transfer IVF cycle two weeks ago and presents to a tertiary early pregnancy assessment service at 6 weeks and 5 days gestation by transfer date. She has had two previous tubal ectopic pregnancies managed with laparoscopic salpingectomy (left partial and right partial), with severe periadhesive disease documented at the second operation, and an extensive endometriosis history with bilateral chocolate cysts treated 4 years ago.

Over the last 72 hours she has developed unilateral left iliac fossa pain that is intermittent but increasing, with one episode of dizziness this morning when standing. She has had no vaginal bleeding and is haemodynamically stable on arrival. Vital signs: BP 108/68 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 36.6 degC, SpO2 99%, respiratory rate 16. Abdominal examination reveals tenderness in the left iliac fossa without peritonism; the cervical os is closed and there is no active bleeding on speculum.

Serum beta-hCG today is 12 000 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound by an experienced fetal medicine sonographer demonstrates a single intrauterine gestational sac containing a yolk sac and a viable fetal pole with CRL 7 mm and fetal cardiac activity at 122 bpm. There is a separate left adnexal complex mass measuring 30 mm with a hyperechoic ring (sometimes called the 'tubal ring' or 'bagel sign') and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas (approximately 50 mL). Her LFTs, FBC, renal function and group/screen are normal; she is RhD positive. The on-call gynaecology consultant has been called and is en route.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/68 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Left iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism. Os closed. No active bleeding.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 12 000 IU/L. TV USS: viable intrauterine pregnancy at 6+5 (CRL 7 mm, FH 122 bpm) AND separate left adnexal complex mass 30 mm with echogenic ring; small free fluid POD ~50 mL.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Single-dose IM methotrexate 50 mg/m2 to treat the left adnexal ectopic, with serial beta-hCG monitoring to track resolution while continuing the intrauterine pregnancy
Expectant management with serial 48-hour beta-hCG and repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 1 week, given haemodynamic stability and the presence of a viable intrauterine pregnancy
Admit for observation and analgesia with 6-hourly observations, planning to operate only if she develops haemodynamic compromise
Ultrasound-guided potassium chloride injection into the adnexal mass with continued expectant care of the intrauterine pregnancy
Urgent laparoscopic salpingectomy of the left adnexal ectopic with intra-operative care to preserve the intrauterine pregnancy, plus anti-D if RhD negative

stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 attends her 28-week antenatal visit. Her partner attends every visit, answers questions for her, and asked the midwife last visit to keep him informed of all her results. Today she is quiet, has a fading bruise on her left forearm she attributes to a kitchen accident, and SFH/fetal heart are appropriate. The clinic has a private room, an interpreter line and an on-site social worker. The midwife steps out and asks the GP registrar what to do next; the partner is in the room with her.

data_table.Examination: SFH 28 cm, fetal heart 142, longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation; healing 4 cm bruise left forearm
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L, MCV 84 fL, urinalysis NAD
data_table.Social: Lives with partner and 3-year-old son; partner attends all visits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to enable safe domestic violence enquiry?

options.text: Ask the screening questions in front of the partner to demonstrate transparency and gather his perspective
Find a clinical reason to see her alone (e.g. urine sample, listen to baby in another room) and enquire privately using a validated framework such as HARK or RADAR
Defer the enquiry to the postnatal home visit, where the partner is less likely to attend
Avoid direct enquiry today and place a 1800RESPECT leaflet in her hand-held antenatal record for her to see
Contact NSW Police immediately because the forearm bruise constitutes evidence of an assault

stem:
A 22-year-old G1P0 Aboriginal woman from a regional NSW community books for antenatal care at 11 weeks. She has no medical conditions, BMI 24, supportive partner, lives with her mother and cousins. She tells the booking midwife she felt unsafe at a previous gynaecology appointment because she did not feel listened to and had to bring her own information; she has missed two prior follow-up appointments at other services for the same reason.

The hospital offers: standard midwifery group practice (MGP); a local Aboriginal Maternal and Infant Health Service (AMIHS) co-led by an Aboriginal Health Worker and continuity midwife linked with the regional ACCHO; obstetrician-led clinic; GP shared care; and telehealth. All five pathways can access morphology USS, OGTT and specialist obstetric review.

data_table.Booking bloods: Hb 122 g/L, blood group O Rh+, rubella immune, syphilis EIA non-reactive, HIV negative, HBsAg negative
data_table.Social: Lives with mother and cousins; supportive partner; previous disengagement from non-culturally-safe services

lead_in: Which model of care is most likely to optimise engagement and outcomes for this woman?

options.text: AMIHS continuity-of-carer model integrating midwife and Aboriginal Health Worker, with ACCHO linkage
Standard midwifery group practice with referral to a separate Aboriginal Health Worker as needed
Obstetrician-led care because all Aboriginal pregnancies are inherently high-risk and require specialist supervision
GP shared care with the regional GP to minimise hospital contact
Telehealth-only antenatal care to reduce her travel burden regardless of her preference

stem:
A 26-year-old G2P1 Aboriginal woman from a remote NT community presents for booking at 12 weeks. She has a documented history of acute rheumatic fever aged 10 with subsequent moderate mitral regurgitation on echo last year and is on monthly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin (BPG) 1.2 million units secondary prophylaxis through the local clinic. Her last dose was 2 weeks ago.

She has had one previous uncomplicated SVD at term with no cardiac decompensation, breastfed for 12 months, and is currently well with no exertional dyspnoea, no orthopnoea, and NYHA class I. Examination: BP 108/64, HR 82, soft pansystolic murmur at apex unchanged from previous, no peripheral oedema, clear chest. Repeat booking echo shows unchanged moderate MR, mild LA dilation, normal LV function, and pulmonary artery pressure 28 mmHg.

She asks whether she should continue the monthly injections during pregnancy because a friend told her to stop because the penicillin might harm the baby.

data_table.Examination: Soft PSM apex unchanged; no signs of failure; SFH appropriate; fetal heart 156
data_table.Investigations: Echo: moderate MR, mild LA dilation, normal LVEF 60%, PASP 28 mmHg; Hb 120 g/L; ECG sinus
data_table.Medications: Benzathine benzylpenicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 28 days; pregnancy multivitamin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her secondary prophylaxis during pregnancy?

options.text: Continue 4-weekly IM BPG at the standard dose throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period
Switch to oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg BD for the duration of pregnancy to avoid IM injections
Cease benzathine benzylpenicillin prophylaxis until after delivery because penicillin readily crosses the placenta
Shorten the BPG interval to every 3 weeks because pregnancy increases drug clearance and lowers troughs
Convert to azithromycin 1 g monthly as an alternative because penicillin allergy is more common in pregnancy

stem:
A 31-year-old G3P2 Aboriginal woman from a remote community, with known severe rheumatic mitral stenosis (MVA 1.0 cm2, mean gradient 14 mmHg, PASP 56 mmHg on third-trimester echo, NYHA II antenatally) presents to a regional referral centre at 39+2 weeks in spontaneous labour. She has been on monthly BPG, metoprolol 50 mg BD, and prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily, ceased 18 hours ago.

She is 6 cm dilated, contracting 4-in-10, the fetus is cephalic with reassuring CTG, and an epidural has been sited and is providing good analgesia. Over the last 30 minutes she has become increasingly breathless, oxygen saturation has fallen from 98% to 91% on room air, HR has risen from 96 to 132 (sinus tachycardia on ECG with no shortened diastole arrhythmia and no fibrillatory waves), BP is 105/68, JVP is elevated, and she has bibasal crackles.

Chest x-ray shows pulmonary venous congestion with no focal consolidation. Bedside echo confirms unchanged severe MS with no left atrial thrombus and preserved LV function. The cardiac-obstetric-anaesthetic team is gathering at the bedside, blood is cross-matched, and a high-dependency bed is available.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 105/68, HR 132 sinus, RR 28, SpO2 91% RA -> 95% on 4 L NP, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: JVP +4 cm, bibasal crackles, loud P2, mid-diastolic rumble apex; gravid uterus contracting 4-in-10
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachy, no AF; CXR pulmonary congestion; ABG pH 7.40, pO2 78 mmHg on O2, lactate 1.8; troponin negative
data_table.CTG: Baseline 145, variability normal, accels present, no decels
data_table.Medications: Metoprolol 50 mg BD, BPG monthly, enoxaparin 40 mg ceased 18 h ago, epidural sited

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention to stabilise her acutely?

options.text: IV furosemide plus additional IV beta-blocker to lower heart rate and reduce filling pressures
Tocolyse with IV salbutamol to halt labour and proceed to emergency percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty
Proceed to immediate category 1 caesarean section under general anaesthesia for acute pulmonary oedema
Give an IV crystalloid bolus of 500 mL Hartmann's to maintain preload before considering further intervention
Commence IV amiodarone infusion for presumed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

stem:
A 24-year-old G2P0 woman in regional Victoria presents at 23+1 weeks by dating ultrasound requesting termination of pregnancy. Morphology ultrasound at 21 weeks showed a fetal cardiac anomaly initially read as a ventricular septal defect, but on tertiary review at 23 weeks was confirmed as hypoplastic left heart syndrome with associated coarctation. She has discussed the diagnosis with paediatric cardiology, including the staged Norwood pathway and its long-term survival and morbidity, and feels unable to proceed with the pregnancy.

She has no medical comorbidities, her support network is intact, she has accessed counselling, and her first pregnancy ended in a first-trimester miscarriage. She specifically asks about the legal pathway in Victoria, whether she must travel interstate, and whether an ethics committee or panel needs to approve the procedure before she can be referred to the tertiary service

data_table.Examination: SFH 24 cm; uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Tertiary fetal echo: hypoplastic left heart syndrome with coarctation; karyotype normal; Hb 120 g/L

lead_in: Which statement best describes the lawful pathway for termination of pregnancy in Victoria at this gestation?

options.text: Termination is lawful on request without any additional consultation up to 24 weeks gestation in Victoria
Termination is unlawful after 20 weeks in Victoria and the patient must travel interstate to obtain care
Termination is lawful: she is under the 24-week on-request limit and is referred to a tertiary service
Termination requires approval by a formal hospital ethics committee at any gestation in Victoria
Termination is only lawful where the fetal anomaly is incompatible with life as defined by statute

subtopic_detail: Termination of pregnancy - Australian state-specific gestational limits

stem:
A 30-year-old G3P2 woman presents to ED 10 days after a medical TOP at 8 weeks using mifepristone-misoprostol from her GP. The procedure was reported as successful with passage of products on day 1 and tapering bleeding for 6 days. Over the last 36 hours she has had heavy bleeding soaking 1 large pad per hour, lower abdominal cramping, low-grade fever (37.8 deg C), foul-smelling discharge, and feels lightheaded on standing.

She has no significant past history, takes no medications, blood group O Rh positive, and breastfed her two prior children. On arrival: BP 96/58, HR 116, T 37.9, RR 18, SpO2 99%. Abdomen tender suprapubically with guarding but no peritonism. Speculum: open external os with brisk bleeding and brown malodorous discharge, products visible at the os. Bedside USS: heterogeneous endometrial collection 38 mm with vascularity on colour Doppler and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Bloods: Hb 88 g/L, WCC 16.4 x 10^9/L, CRP 142 mg/L, lactate 1.6, group-and-hold sent.

data_table.Examination: Tender suprapubic with guarding; open cervical os with brisk bleed, products visible, foul discharge
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, WCC 16.4, CRP 142, beta-hCG 1820 IU/L, lactate 1.6; USS endometrial collection 38 mm vascular
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Outpatient repeat misoprostol 800 microg vaginal plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days, review in 48 hours
Resuscitate with IV access, fluids, group-and-hold, and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, then proceed to urgent surgical evacuation of retained products
Admit for IV oxytocin infusion with close observation, deferring evacuation pending blood culture results
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV with observation and serial Hb without antibiotic cover until culture results
Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 for presumed ongoing intrauterine pregnancy and discharge home to GP

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 woman at 30 weeks gestation discloses intimate partner violence during a private antenatal visit after the midwife has seen her alone. Her partner has been verbally and physically abusive for 3 years; the frequency and severity have escalated over the past 6 weeks since she told him she was pregnant. Last week he choked her with both hands until she briefly lost consciousness, threatened to kill her if she left, and removed her mobile phone so she could not contact her sister.

He has access to firearms because he is a licensed recreational shooter. She has two children aged 4 and 6 at home, no immediate family support locally, and no current Apprehended Domestic Violence Order. She has not previously disclosed to a clinician. She is asking what to do; she is frightened, oriented, and engaged. There is a social worker on site this afternoon and a state-funded specialist DV service with crisis accommodation available.

data_table.Examination: Tender 4 cm bruise left flank, faint petechiae over neck, no current acute injury; SFH appropriate, FH 144
data_table.Social: Two children at home (4 and 6), no AVO, partner has firearms access, escalating frequency
data_table.Risk factors: Strangulation, threats to kill, controlling behaviour (phone removed), pregnancy, firearms access

lead_in: Which combination of features in this disclosure most strongly indicates EXTREME risk of intimate partner femicide and mandates immediate crisis-response activation?

options.text: Frequency of arguments and verbal abuse over the past 3 years without any physical injury
A past episode of pushing without injury approximately 18 months ago and now resolved
Recent non-fatal strangulation, threat to kill, escalation in pregnancy, and firearm access
Disclosure occurring during the antenatal visit itself, without any other contextual features
Absence of any Apprehended Domestic Violence Order despite the long abusive relationship history

subtopic_detail: Domestic violence in pregnancy - escalation risk assessment

stem:
A 34-year-old G4P3 woman in NSW discloses ongoing intimate partner violence during her postnatal home visit at day 14. There have been two physical assault episodes in the past 2 weeks, both witnessed by her 5- and 8-year-old children. The youngest child has begun bedwetting and the older child has been refusing school. The newborn is feeding well and gaining weight; there are no injuries on the infant.

She is asking that nothing be reported to child protection because she fears the four children will be removed from her care. She has agreed to a safety plan, accepted a warm referral to a specialist DV service, and confirmed she is safe to remain at her sister's house tonight. The midwife is a mandated reporter under the NSW Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998, and exposure of children to intimate partner violence meets the threshold of Risk of Significant Harm under the NSW Mandatory Reporter Guide.

data_table.Examination: Maternal: healing perineal repair, no acute injury, EPDS 16. Infant: alert, no injuries, weight gaining
data_table.Social: Two children witnessing assault; behavioural change in both; partner unaware of disclosure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding child protection reporting?

options.text: Honour the woman's request not to report because reporting would breach therapeutic trust and engagement
Report only the children's behavioural change to the GP and do not lodge any child protection report
Lodge a Risk of Significant Harm report to the NSW Child Protection Helpline and continue the safety plan
Contact NSW Police directly to seek an Apprehended Domestic Violence Order on behalf of the woman
Wait until the next clinic visit in a fortnight to allow the woman more time to consider

stem:
A 26-year-old woman disclosed intimate partner violence 4 weeks ago and you drew up a written safety plan (code words, packed bag at her sister's, 1800RESPECT number). Today she reports her partner has been kind, brought flowers, and agreed to attend couples counselling; she is reconsidering whether she still needs the plan. No acute injuries. The previous incident involved choking, which she had not initially disclosed.

She is calm, oriented, has no children, joint rental, independent income, family interstate. She asks whether the change means the cycle of abuse is over and whether joint counselling would now be safe.

data_table.Examination: No acute injury; old healed bruising right upper arm
data_table.Social: No children; joint rental; independent income; family interstate; partner currently in 'reconciliation' phase per her description

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Validate her experience, explain the reconciliation/honeymoon phase of the cycle, advise against joint couples counselling (which is unsafe in active IPV with prior strangulation), reinforce the safety plan and offer ongoing review
Reassure her that the apology phase usually means violence will not recur and discard the safety plan
Insist she leave the relationship today as the only safe option
Recommend joint couples counselling because the partner has agreed to attend
Discharge her from clinical follow-up because she now feels safe

subtopic_detail: Domestic violence - cycle and safety planning

stem:
A 23-year-old woman presents to ED 5 days (120 hours) after non-consensual unprotected vaginal intercourse with an unknown male at a party. She did not present sooner because of fear of judgement. She is otherwise well, has no medical history, no allergies, takes no regular medications, has a regular 28-day menstrual cycle with last period 11 days ago (so currently around day 11 and within the fertile window), and has previously had her three-dose HPV vaccine and a full primary hepatitis B course as a child.

The local sexual assault medical service is contactable, the on-call gynaecology registrar can insert a copper IUD today, and the assailant's HIV status is unknown.

data_table.Examination: No acute injury; healing 1 cm abrasion left knee; speculum: no acute trauma, no visible discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative; baseline HIV Ag/Ab, HBsAg/HBsAb/anti-HBc, HCV Ab, syphilis EIA, NAATs for chlamydia/gonorrhoea/trichomonas sent
data_table.Cycle: Day 11 of regular 28-day cycle; previous LMP 11 days ago

lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate component of management at this time?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally as a single-dose emergency contraceptive within the 72-hour licensed window
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally as a single-dose emergency contraceptive within the 120-hour licensed window
Copper IUD insertion as emergency contraception, with empirical STI prophylaxis and sexual assault referral
Commence HIV non-occupational post-exposure prophylaxis with tenofovir-emtricitabine-dolutegravir for a full 28-day course
Accelerated hepatitis B vaccination course because the patient is presumed unprotected after childhood priming

stem:
A 19-year-old woman presents to ED 18 hours after a night out, with no memory of several hours of the evening, having woken in an unfamiliar bed beside someone she did not know, with disarranged clothing. She is concerned that her drink was spiked. She last urinated on waking 1 hour ago and has had three sips of water since.

She has had no alcohol or illicit drugs to her knowledge other than two drinks she ordered and saw poured. She has no known medical conditions and takes no regular medications. She is alert, oriented, distressed but cooperative. The local sexual assault medical service is contactable and a forensic medical examiner is available within the hour. She has not decided whether to report to police.

The forensic examiner will offer toxicology and asks which sample to collect first given the long window since exposure and the short half-lives of common drug-facilitated sexual assault agents such as GHB and benzodiazepines.

data_table.Examination: No acute injury identified; speculum to be performed by forensic examiner if she consents
data_table.Investigations: Pending forensic samples, baseline STI screen, beta-hCG
data_table.Timing: 18 hours since suspected event; first void available; minimal hydration

lead_in: Which sample provides the highest yield for detection of common drug-facilitated sexual assault agents at this presentation?

options.text: A clotted serum sample taken now for benzodiazepine and GHB quantification analysis
First-catch urine sample now and a repeat urine sample at the next void
Scalp hair sample taken now for later segmental analysis after a 4-week growth window
Gastric aspirate via nasogastric tube to recover any residual ingested drug from the stomach
Oral mucosal swab to recover any drug residues from saliva and the buccal mucosa surface

stem:
A 29-year-old G2P2 woman is reviewed at 5 weeks postpartum at her general practice. She has focal epilepsy controlled on carbamazepine 400 mg BD (level stable, no seizures for 3 years), is exclusively breastfeeding her baby (infant weight tracking the 50th centile, no concerns at the maternal-child health nurse review), and had a normal vaginal birth with no thromboembolic history, no migraine, normotensive, BMI 24, non-smoker, and a normal Hb of 122 g/L.

She has read about long-acting reversible contraception and is aware that carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer. She wishes to space the next pregnancy by at least 3 years and prefers a method that does not require daily adherence or rely on her remembering to attend for 3-monthly injections. She is happy with all options being on the table, including LARCs and combined methods, and asks the GP to recommend the most reliable option that will not be undermined by her antiepileptic.

data_table.Examination: Well, lactating; uterus involuted
data_table.Medications: Carbamazepine 400 mg BD; folic acid 5 mg daily (planned for future pregnancy)
data_table.Pregnancy plans: Spacing at least 3 years; LARC preferred

lead_in: Which contraceptive option is the most appropriate first-line recommendation?

options.text: Etonogestrel 68 mg subdermal implant (Implanon NXT) inserted in the inner upper arm
Combined oral contraceptive pill (ethinylestradiol 30 microg with levonorgestrel) taken daily
Progestogen-only pill (norethisterone 350 microg) taken at the same time every day
Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine device (Mirena) or copper IUD inserted as a LARC
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscularly every 12 weeks as her contraceptive method

stem:

She is bottle feeding by choice, normotensive, non-smoker, no migraine, no VTE history, and is on regular vitamin and iron supplementation post-bariatric. She is asking the GP for contraception and is happy with all options, including LARCs.

She specifically asks whether she can simply take her sister's combined oral contraceptive pill, because she has heard that any oral hormonal method is reliable. She also asks whether a return of regular cycles is required before she starts a method, given she is not yet menstruating because she is using progesterone-containing analgesia

data_table.Examination: Well, lactation suppressed; surgical scars from RYGB
data_table.Medications: Multivitamin, iron, vitamin B12 IM 3-monthly, calcium + vitamin D

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate consideration when selecting contraception for this woman?

options.text: Oral hormonal contraception is unaffected because Roux-en-Y bypass does not alter small-molecule absorption
Long-acting reversible methods are preferred because oral hormonal absorption is reduced post-bypass
Combined hormonal contraception is preferred to ensure cycle regularity post-bariatric surgery in this patient
Await return of regular menstrual cycles before starting any contraception in this patient
Permanent sterilisation should be recommended because pregnancy is unsafe after bariatric surgery

stem:
A 30-year-old G1P1 woman with well-controlled HIV (CD4 720, viral load <50 copies/mL on tenofovir alafenamide-emtricitabine-bictegravir) is reviewed at 6 weeks postpartum. She is formula feeding per current Australian guidance, an option chosen after counselling once viral suppression was sustained, and the infant has completed post-exposure prophylaxis per ASHM. She is normotensive, BMI 25, non-smoker, no migraine, no VTE history, and no other comorbidity.

She wants reliable contraception for at least 2 years, preferably long-acting and not requiring daily adherence. Her HIV physician confirms she will remain on bictegravir-based therapy and is not on any enzyme-inducing antiretroviral. She specifically asks whether the implant will still work on her HIV regimen and whether she needs efavirenz to be added for the implant to be effective Her infectious-diseases physician has cleared any contraceptive method Her HIV physician noted no enzyme-inducing antiretrovirals on her regimen.

data_table.Examination: Well; uterus involuted
data_table.Medications: Tenofovir alafenamide-emtricitabine-bictegravir daily; no other medication
data_table.Investigations: CD4 720, HIV viral load <50 copies/mL

lead_in: Which contraceptive option is most appropriate without significant interaction concerns?

subtopic: Indigenous health (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander)
tags: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander maternal health
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 Aboriginal woman from a regional town presents at 11 weeks for booking with her local ACCHO. Her two previous pregnancies were complicated by gestational diabetes managed with diet and metformin, and both babies were macrosomic (birth weights 4.3 kg and 4.5 kg with shoulder dystocia in the second). Between pregnancies she lost touch with primary care and has not had her glucose checked.

Her BMI is 32 and BP is 122/76. There is a strong family history of type 2 diabetes (mother, two siblings). At booking, the GP arranges fasting venous plasma glucose and HbA1c as part of the early antenatal panel recommended by ADIPS and RANZCOG for high-risk women. Results: fasting venous plasma glucose 6.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.7% (50 mmol/mol), urine ketones negative. She is otherwise well, on folic acid and iodine, and asks whether she has GDM or something different.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no glycosuria today
data_table.Investigations: Fasting plasma glucose 6.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.7% (50 mmol/mol), urine ketones negative
data_table.Past obstetric: Two prior GDM, macrosomic infants 4.3 and 4.5 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Reassure that values are normal in pregnancy and re-screen with 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks
Diagnose diabetes in pregnancy, commence lifestyle measures and metformin, refer to multidisciplinary clinic
Diagnose gestational diabetes on the FPG threshold of >=5.1 and commence dietary advice only
Repeat the fasting plasma glucose in 4 weeks before initiating any pharmacological intervention
Commence insulin glargine immediately as monotherapy without any metformin or lifestyle intervention being trialled

stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman in Perth, Western Australia presents at 24+2 weeks gestation by ultrasound requesting termination of pregnancy. She has no medical comorbidities and no fetal anomaly. The pregnancy is unwanted but she had previously been undecided. She is certain of her decision now and asks her GP to refer her. The GP knows the new WA Public Health Amendment (Abortion) Act 2023 was enacted in early 2024 with different rules above and below 23 weeks.

data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound singleton live IUP 11+0 weeks; blood group O Rh positive

lead_in: Which statement most accurately reflects the legal pathway for her TOP in WA?

options.text: Lawful on request up to 23 weeks with one practitioner; at 24+2 she needs assessment and agreement by two practitioners, at least one being an O&G or in consultation with one
Unlawful in WA at this gestation under any circumstances; she must travel interstate to access termination of pregnancy at this stage of her current pregnancy
Partner consent is required before the procedure despite her capacity to consent and the disclosed intimate partner violence in the relationship
A mandatory 7-day waiting period applies from first consultation to procedure regardless of clinical urgency or any current safety concerns identified

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P1 woman is 34 weeks pregnant and has an active Apprehended Domestic Violence Order in NSW against her former partner, who is the father of the unborn child. The order prohibits him contacting her or approaching within 100 metres of her residence and workplace. She presents to the maternity day-assessment unit for routine review and is anxious because her former partner has been ringing the hospital switchboard asking for her appointment times and 'information about his child'.

She is fully engaged in antenatal care, has a written safety plan, is supported by a hospital social worker, and has a planned hospital birth. She asks specifically whether the ADVO applies inside the hospital, whether her former partner has any right to be told her appointment times because he is the father, and what the hospital can do to ensure he cannot find out when she will be in the building.

data_table.Examination: SFH 34 cm, fetal heart 142, cephalic
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal bloods normal
data_table.Social: Active ADVO; ex-partner attempting information access via switchboard; social worker engaged

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next action with respect to her hospital information access and safety?

options.text: Provide the former partner with appointment times because he has a paternal right to information about the unborn child
Flag the medical record as confidential, instruct switchboard and reception not to release any information, and notify security
Transfer her care to a different hospital to break the trail without involving her in the decision
Tell the partner the ADVO does not apply to the hospital so he may attend appointments
Restrict her from public maternity care until the ADVO is formally upgraded by the court

stem:
A 49-year-old G3P3 presents with a 9-month history of heavy menstrual bleeding. Cycles have shortened from 28 to 22 days, last 8 to 10 days, and she changes a fully soaked pad every 90 minutes on the worst two days with passage of 5-cent-piece-sized clots. She reports two episodes of intermenstrual bleeding in the last 3 months. Her BMI is 34, she has type 2 diabetes on metformin, and she has never been on hormonal contraception.

There is no postcoital bleeding, no dyspareunia, and her last cervical screen 18 months ago was HPV negative. She is not sexually active currently and uses no contraception. On examination her abdomen is soft with no palpable mass; speculum shows a healthy cervix and no cervical lesion; bimanual reveals a bulky but mobile uterus, no adnexal mass. Pregnancy test is negative. FBC shows Hb 98 g/L with MCV 74 fL and ferritin 6 microg/L. TSH and coagulation screen are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/84 mmHg, HR 82 bpm, T 36.6 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: BMI 34. Bulky mobile uterus. Cervix healthy. No adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L, MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 microg/L, TSH normal, coags normal, HPV negative 18 months ago.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Commence tranexamic acid 1 g tds during menses and review
Repeat the cervical screening test with HPV partial genotyping today
Pelvic MRI to characterise the bulky uterus before further management
Transvaginal ultrasound and outpatient endometrial biopsy at this visit
Outpatient hysteroscopy without prior endometrial sampling or pelvic imaging
