stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents with her fifth episode of vulvovaginal candidiasis in the past 12 months. Each episode features intense vulval pruritus, dyspareunia, thick white curd-like discharge, and erythematous vulval skin, and resolves with a single oral fluconazole 150 mg dose. Between episodes she is asymptomatic. She is in a stable monogamous relationship for 5 years, uses copper IUD for contraception, has no history of diabetes, and a recent HbA1c is 5.4% (35 mmol/mol).

She does not use scented soaps, wears cotton underwear, and has not used antibiotics in the last 6 months. She has no immunosuppression. Today on speculum examination there is thick white adherent discharge with vulval erythema and excoriation. Vaginal pH is 4.2. KOH microscopy shows numerous pseudohyphae and budding yeast. A high vaginal swab for fungal culture and speciation is collected and confirms Candida albicans sensitive to fluconazole.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, T 36.5 degC, BMI 24.
data_table.Examination: Thick white discharge, vulval erythema and excoriation.
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 4.2. KOH: pseudohyphae and budding yeast. HVS culture: Candida albicans, fluconazole sensitive. HbA1c 5.4% (35 mmol/mol).

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate ongoing management?

options.text: Single dose fluconazole 150 mg orally and reassure this is an isolated acute episode
Induction fluconazole 150 mg orally days 1, 4, 7, then suppressive fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months
Empirical oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for a 7-day course without further investigation
Refer her for an oral glucose tolerance test before any further antifungal therapy
Long-term intravaginal boric acid 600 mg nightly indefinitely as continuous suppressive antifungal therapy regimen

stem:
A 55-year-old G3P3 presents with 18 months of urinary leakage. She leaks small volumes when she coughs, laughs, sneezes, or lifts her grandchildren, has no urgency, no nocturia, and no leakage on the way to the toilet. She empties her bladder 6 times a day, never wakes overnight to void, and does not feel incomplete emptying. There is no haematuria, no dysuria, and no faecal incontinence.

She had three vaginal births with two episiotomies and a forceps delivery for her second child. Her last period was 14 months ago. BMI 31. She smokes 10 cigarettes/day. On examination, abdomen soft, no palpable bladder. On speculum a first-degree anterior wall prolapse is noted. A cough stress test in semi-recumbent and standing positions reproduces leakage of urine from the urethral meatus. Urinalysis is clear and post-void residual on bladder scan is 35 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 134/82 mmHg, BMI 31.
data_table.Examination: First-degree anterior wall prolapse. Positive cough stress test. No pelvic mass.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis clear. PVR 35 mL. Bladder diary not yet completed.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Refer for a mid-urethral sling (transobturator tape) surgical procedure now
Commence oral oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily as first-line monotherapy for symptoms
Three-day bladder diary, pelvic floor training for 3 months, weight loss and smoking cessation
Insert a ring pessary for the management of stress urinary incontinence
Urodynamic studies as the first step before any conservative therapy is trialled

stem:
A 68-year-old G4P4 woman presents with 6 months of a vaginal bulge worse at end of day. She also has bothersome stress urinary incontinence on coughing/sneezing and needs to splint to void fully. No faecal incontinence, no dyspareunia. Sexually active with husband, BMI 27, hypertension on perindopril, no other comorbidities. POP-Q: Ba 0, C -2, Bp -3 (stage 2 anterior compartment).

Post-void residual 80 mL. Urodynamic studies confirm urodynamic stress incontinence with no detrusor overactivity and good bladder capacity. She wants the option with the best evidence for both prolapse and urinary symptoms; she is prepared to consider surgery but would also consider a pessary.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 136/82 mmHg, BMI 27.
data_table.Examination: POP-Q: Ba = 0 (anterior wall at hymen on Valsalva), C = -2, Bp = -3. Stage 2 anterior compartment prolapse.
data_table.Investigations: PVR 80 mL. Urinalysis clear.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Trial vaginal ring pessary and supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy, with reassessment of urinary symptoms after prolapse reduction
Anterior colporrhaphy with concomitant retropubic midurethral sling
Sacrocolpopexy with synthetic mesh under general anaesthesia
Indwelling urinary catheter to manage the elevated post-void residual long-term
Topical oestrogen as monotherapy with no other intervention

stem:
A 32-year-old G0 presents with 14 months of constant pelvic pain rated 5/10 at baseline and 8/10 cyclically. The pain has both cyclical features (worse in the 4 days prior to and during her period) and non-cyclical features (dull background ache present every day for the last 8 months). She reports dyspareunia on deep penetration, dyschezia during menses, and increased urinary frequency without dysuria or haematuria.

She has been trying to conceive for 9 months without success. There is no fever, no postmenopausal bleeding, and no haematuria. Her mother had endometriosis diagnosed at laparoscopy. On bimanual examination there is uterosacral nodularity and a fixed retroverted uterus with cervical excitation. A pelvic ultrasound 2 months ago showed a 3 cm left ovarian endometrioma with ground-glass appearance and normal uterine cavity. STI screen today is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.6 degC, BMI 23.
data_table.Examination: Uterosacral nodularity. Fixed retroverted uterus. Cervical excitation. No palpable adnexal mass on bimanual.
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: 3 cm left ovarian endometrioma. Normal uterine cavity. STI screen pending. Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure that endometriosis is confirmed on ultrasound and commence the COCP continuously without further investigation
Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device now and review her symptoms in 6 months
Start a GnRH agonist with add-back tibolone for 6 months and reassess symptoms
Proceed directly to diagnostic laparoscopy without prior imaging or specialist multidisciplinary review at all
Refer to a multidisciplinary endometriosis service, arrange MRI for deep infiltrating disease, and address fertility

stem:
A 29-year-old G1P1 presents for preconception counselling. Her first child was born 18 months ago at 39 weeks via uncomplicated vaginal birth weighing 3450 g. She takes sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy (last seizure 4 years ago) and is co-managed by neurology. She is otherwise well. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defects, no diabetes, no malabsorption, and a BMI of 24.

She is up to date with her cervical screening (HPV negative 8 months ago) and her booking bloods from her last pregnancy showed she was rubella immune and varicella immune. She smokes 5 cigarettes a day, drinks 4 standard drinks twice a week on weekends, and does not use any other supplements. She would like to start trying for a second child in 3 months and asks what she should do to prepare.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 70 bpm, BMI 24.
data_table.Examination: Well, no abnormal findings.
data_table.Investigations: Rubella IgG immune (last pregnancy). Varicella IgG immune. Cervical screen HPV negative 8 months ago. HbA1c 5.2% (33 mmol/mol).

lead_in: Which is the most important pre-conception intervention?

options.text: Folic acid 0.5 mg orally daily for 3 months pre-conception and the first trimester only
Iodine 150 microg daily plus vitamin D level testing only without any medication change overall
Reassure her that no change to current AED therapy is needed because she is presently seizure-free
Administer MMR and varicella booster immunisations now before any pregnancy attempt is made by this patient
Refer to neurology to switch to a safer anti-seizure medication and prescribe folic acid 5 mg daily

stem:
A 33-year-old G3P0 presents after her third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage. The first was a missed miscarriage at 9 weeks managed expectantly, the second was a complete miscarriage at 8 weeks managed at home, and the third was a missed miscarriage at 10+2 managed with misoprostol 4 weeks ago. She conceives easily within 1 to 2 cycles each time and has regular 28-day ovulatory cycles.

She has no personal history of venous thromboembolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke, or pulmonary embolism, no symptoms of systemic lupus erythematosus (no malar rash, no arthralgia), no autoimmune disease, no fertility treatment, and no live births. She has never smoked, drinks one standard drink per week, has a BMI of 27, and is otherwise well. There is no family history of recurrent miscarriage, balanced translocation, congenital malformation, or genetic disease, and no consanguinity.

A transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal uterine cavity, both ovaries normal, and no fibroids; antral follicle count is normal. Karyotype of products of conception from the third miscarriage was 46,XX (euploid). TSH is 1.8 mIU/L and HbA1c is 5.4% (35 mmol/mol). She asks what should be tested before her next pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, BMI 27.
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: normal uterine cavity, no fibroids, both ovaries normal. POC karyotype third miscarriage 46,XX (euploid). TSH 1.8 mIU/L. HbA1c 5.4% (35 mmol/mol).

lead_in: Which is the most important next investigation?

options.text: Parental peripheral blood karyotype testing as the very first single investigation in this workup
Inherited thrombophilia screen including factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene, protein C, protein S, antithrombin
Diagnostic hysteroscopy with directed biopsies regardless of any prior pelvic ultrasound findings reported recently
Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-1 antibodies repeated on two occasions 12 weeks apart
Peripheral blood natural killer cell assay as the very first single investigation here

subtopic_detail: Recurrent pregnancy loss - antiphospholipid syndrome workup

stem:
A 30-year-old G0 and her 32-year-old male partner present after 13 months of trying to conceive with regular unprotected intercourse 2 to 3 times per week, including timed intercourse around predicted ovulation in the last 4 cycles. She has regular 29-day cycles with predictable ovulatory symptoms (mid-cycle mucus change and mittelschmerz). She has no dysmenorrhoea, no dyspareunia, and was up to date with cervical screening 6 months ago (HPV negative).

BMI 24, non-smoker, no alcohol, no caffeine excess. She takes folic acid 0.5 mg daily and iodine 150 microg daily. Her partner is well, BMI 26, non-smoker, no known fertility issues, no previous children, takes no medications, drinks 6 standard drinks per week, and his work as an electrician does not involve heat exposure. She is concerned and asks what investigations should be done now.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, BMI 24.
data_table.Examination: Normal pelvic examination.
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screen HPV negative 6 months ago. Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial set of investigations?

options.text: Semen analysis, day-21 progesterone, TSH and transvaginal ultrasound; reserve HSG for after initial workup
Refer immediately for IVF without any further investigation of the couple
Continue trying for another 12 months before any investigation of the couple
Hysterosalpingogram and diagnostic laparoscopy as the first-line investigations of the couple
AMH for ovarian reserve only and reassure her she can wait given young age

stem:
A 15-year-old presents with her mother because of worsening period pain and bleeding. Menarche was at 12; cycles are regular at 28 days but have become increasingly painful since age 14, now causing her to miss 3 to 5 school days per month. Pain begins 24 hours before bleeding, peaks on day 2, and is associated with nausea, vomiting, and inability to get out of bed.

She soaks through a fully saturated super pad every 90 minutes on days 1 and 2 and reports passing 5-cent-piece-sized clots. She has tried paracetamol 1 g qid and ibuprofen 400 mg tds with only partial relief. Her mother had endometriosis diagnosed at laparoscopy at age 22 and a paternal aunt has known endometriosis. There is no dyspareunia (she is not sexually active), no dyschezia, no haematuria, and no postcoital bleeding.

She is no longer attending netball training and has begun to refuse social outings and sleepovers during her periods, and her mother reports she has been increasingly tearful and withdrawn in the days leading up to bleeding. On abdominal examination there is mild suprapubic tenderness; she declines an internal examination. A pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/64 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, T 36.5 degC, BMI 22.
data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness. Declines internal examination.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative. FBC: Hb 116 g/L, MCV 82 fL, ferritin 18 microg/L.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Naproxen 500 mg bd (day -1 to 3), continuous COCP and pelvic ultrasound; refer if no improvement
Reassure her that severe period pain in adolescence is normal and continue her current analgesia regimen long-term
Proceed directly to diagnostic laparoscopy without trialling any medical management as the first step
Commence a GnRH agonist with hormone add-back therapy as the next immediate step in management
Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system without trialling any prior medical therapy first

stem:
A 14-year-old presents to the emergency department with a 4-hour history of sudden severe left iliac fossa pain. The pain began abruptly while she was playing netball, is sharp, constant, radiates to the left flank, and has been associated with vomiting four times in the last 2 hours. She had two previous brief episodes of less severe left-sided pain in the last 6 months, each lasting 30 minutes and resolving spontaneously.

Menarche was at 13; her last menstrual period was 12 days ago and was normal. She has never been sexually active. There is no fever, no urinary symptoms, and no chronic illness. On examination she is in obvious distress, BP 110/68, HR 116, T 37.0, with marked left iliac fossa tenderness and guarding, and a tender palpable mass. Abdomen is otherwise soft.

Beta-hCG is negative. White cell count is 13.4 x 10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L. A transabdominal pelvic ultrasound with Doppler shows a 7 cm complex left adnexal mass with peripherally displaced follicles, a hyperechoic whirlpool sign at the suspected pedicle, and absent venous flow with reduced arterial flow within the left ovary. The right ovary is normal. There is no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, T 37.0 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Marked left iliac fossa tenderness with guarding. Tender left adnexal mass palpable.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative. WCC 13.4 x 10^9/L. CRP 18 mg/L. TVUS Doppler: 7 cm complex left adnexal mass, peripherally displaced follicles, whirlpool sign, absent venous flow, reduced arterial flow. Right ovary normal. No free fluid.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation and analgesia and repeat the ultrasound in 12 hours
Pelvic MRI to confirm diagnosis before any surgical decision is made
Emergency laparoscopy for detorsion and ovarian preservation, with oophoropexy considered intraoperatively
Emergency laparoscopy with planned left salpingo-oophorectomy because the ovary appears non-viable on Doppler
Commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and admit for suspected pelvic inflammatory disease

NCSP - self-collection in under-screened woman with prior LSIL
stem:
A 42-year-old Aboriginal woman attends an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service. Her last cervical screening was 9 years ago on the pre-2017 cytology-based program and was reported as low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL); she was scheduled for a 12-month repeat at the time but did not attend, and has been lost to follow-up since. She declines a clinician-collected speculum today, citing childhood sexual trauma and significant distress with previous examinations.

She has no postcoital bleeding, no intermenstrual bleeding, and no pelvic pain. She is G3P3 (all vaginal), in a monogamous relationship, no immunosuppression, BMI 27. She did not receive HPV vaccination (predates routine cohort). The clinic is accredited to offer self-collection. She wants to participate in screening in a way she can tolerate. There is no visible lesion at external genital examination (which she has agreed to).

The clinician is weighing whether her prior abnormal cytology and long screening gap warrant insisting on clinician-collected sampling or whether self-collected HPV testing is an appropriate program-defined entry point.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 76 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no palpable mass. External genital examination unremarkable. Clinician-collected speculum declined today.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Offer a self-collected vaginal HPV swab today as her cervical screening test, with explicit pathway counselling that any oncogenic HPV result on a self-collected sample will require clinician-collected reflex LBC or direct colposcopy depending on HPV type
Refer to gynaecology for examination under anaesthesia and cervical sampling
Decline screening today and rebook for clinician-collected sample at a later visit
Send a self-collected urine sample for HPV testing in lieu of vaginal sampling
Send her for direct colposcopy without any HPV test based on the prior LSIL alone, bypassing screening

subtopic_detail: NCSP - non-16/18 oncogenic HPV with pLSIL reflex cytology
stem:
A 38-year-old G2P2 returns for her cervical screening result: HPV oncogenic non-16/18 detected; reflex liquid-based cytology shows possible HIGH-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (pHSIL). She is asymptomatic; cervix appeared normal at the time of the sample. She is in a monogamous relationship of 12 years, last screened 7 years ago (normal Pap), non-smoker, BMI 24, no immunosuppression. She received Gardasil as a teenager.

She uses the LNG-IUS. She is anxious and asks specifically whether 'non-16/18' means she should just have another screen in 12 months rather than colposcopy.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no palpable mass. Cervix appeared normal at speculum at the time of sample with no visible lesion and no contact bleeding.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly to colposcopy now
Repeat clinician-collected HPV test in 12 months from today
Repeat HPV test in 6 months as an interim safety check
Return to routine 5-yearly screening as cytology is described as only 'possible'
Refer to colposcopy at 6 months if she develops symptoms, otherwise routine screening

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic cervical cancer - postcoital bleeding workup overrides routine screening
stem:
A 35-year-old G1P1 woman attends her GP with a 4-month history of intermittent postcoital bleeding occurring after most episodes of intercourse, with one episode of intermenstrual bleeding lasting 2 days. She has had no abnormal discharge, no dyspareunia and no pelvic pain. Her last cervical screening test was 18 months ago and showed HPV not detected on a clinician-collected sample.

She received Gardasil as a teenager and is otherwise well. She is a current smoker (15 pack-years) and uses the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has one child after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. There is no significant family history. She has been treated empirically by another clinician for presumed chlamydial cervicitis with azithromycin 1 g stat 6 weeks ago, with chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT both negative; symptoms have persisted unchanged. BMI is 24. She has no fevers, no weight lossymptoms. She is asking for a 'repeat HPV swab to make sure'.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no masses. Speculum: cervix has a friable area at 4 o'clock with contact bleeding on swab; no obvious exophytic lesion. Bimanual: uterus normal size, no adnexal mass, no cervical motion tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative. Chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT negative 6 weeks ago. HPV screening test 18 months ago: HPV not detected.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat the routine NCSP HPV cervical screening test and act on the result
Empirical treatment for cervicitis with doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days
Reassure patient that symptoms will likely resolve and review in 6 months
Perform a co-test (HPV + LBC) and refer for colposcopy regardless of result
Discontinue the combined oral contraceptive pill as likely cause, review 3 months

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding - TVUS endometrial thickness >4 mm threshold
stem:
A 64-year-old G3P3 woman attends her GP with two episodes of fresh vaginal bleeding over the past 3 weeks. She experienced natural menopause at age 51 with no further bleeding until now. She has no postcoital bleeding, no discharge and no pelvic pain. Her last cervical screening test was 4 years ago, HPV not detected. She has type 2 diabetes (metformin 1 g BD, last HbA1c 7.4%), essential hypertension on perindopril 5 mg daily, BMI 34, and a 25-year history of regular menses prior to menopause.

She has never used hormone therapy or tamoxifen. Family history is unremarkable for gynaecological malignancy and Lynch syndrome screening criteria are not met. She does not smoke. She walks 3 km daily and has no urinary or bowel red flags. She has had no recent intercourse and is not on anticoagulation. She is not anaemic on point-of-care testing. She is anxious because her neighbour was recently diagnosed with endometrial cancer.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.5 degC.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no masses. Speculum: atrophic vaginal mucosa, no cervical lesion, small amount of blood at the os, no friability. Bimanual: uterus normal size, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L (115-165). Urinalysis negative. Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrium 8 mm with heterogeneous echotexture; no focal mass identified; both ovaries normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy with directed and Pipelle endometrial biopsy
Trial topical vaginal oestrogen for presumed atrophic vaginitis and review in 6 weeks
Reassure as a single episode and review in 3 months if symptoms persist
Order a serum CA-125 to risk-stratify endometrial pathology before further imaging
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 6 weeks to assess for any change

subtopic_detail: Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia - management in postmenopausal woman
stem:
A 58-year-old G2P2 postmenopausal woman is referred to gynaecology after 4 weeks of intermittent vaginal bleeding. TVUS demonstrated an endometrial thickness of 12 mm with a heterogeneous appearance and no focal mass. Outpatient hysteroscopy with directed and Pipelle biopsies reports endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (also called endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, EIN); no invasive disease seen on the available tissue. She has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.6%, metformin 1 g BD), hypertension treated with perindopril 5 mg daily, BMI 38, and natural menopause at age 53.

She has no family history of Lynch-associated cancers. She has completed her family. She does not wish to continue hormonal therapy long term. She has no thromboembolic history and a normal cardiac assessment on preoperative review. She asks specifically about the risk that this finding already represents cancer.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 140/84 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no masses. Bimanual: uterus normal size, mobile, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Pipelle + hysteroscopic directed biopsy: endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (EIN). Hb 122 g/L. TVUS: ET 12 mm heterogeneous, both ovaries normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as definitive surgical management
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system with 6-monthly endometrial sampling for surveillance
Oral medroxyprogesterone acetate with repeat biopsy in 12 months
Endometrial ablation to control bleeding and reduce cancer risk
Watchful waiting with repeat TVUS and endometrial biopsy in 6 months

subtopic_detail: Ovarian cancer recognition - vague abdominal symptoms + CA-125
stem:
A 62-year-old G2P2 postmenopausal woman attends her GP with a 3-month history of progressive abdominal bloating, early satiety, mild lower abdominal discomfort, increased urinary frequency without dysuria, and unintentional 4 kg weight loss. She initially thought she had developed IBS. There is no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit beyond mild constipation, and no postmenopausal bleeding. She has no significant past medical history, no family history of ovarian, breast or bowel cancer, and is not known to carry BRCA1/2.

She does not smoke and drinks alcohol minimally. She has had no abdominal surgery. Her last cervical screening test was 2 years ago, HPV not detected. She has not used hormone therapy. Examination reveals mild abdominal distension and a vaguely palpable left adnexal fullness. There is no overt ascites but a low-volume effect cannot be excluded clinically. She is afebrile, with stable observations. The GP has already started her on a fibre supplement which has not relieved symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 80 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen mildly distended. Vague left lower-quadrant fullness, no peritonism. Bimanual: left adnexal mass approximately 7 cm, partly fixed; uterus normal size.
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal. Urea, creatinine, LFTs within normal limits. Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Colonoscopy as the initial investigation for presumed bowel pathology and constipation
Serum HE4 alone as a more specific tumour marker than CA-125
Trial of antispasmodic and follow up if symptoms persist beyond 6 weeks
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast as first-line imaging investigation
Pelvic transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound with serum CA-125 for RMI/IOTA risk stratification

subtopic_detail: Ovarian torsion - emergency recognition and detorsion
stem:
A 24-year-old G0 woman presents to ED at 02:00 with sudden-onset severe right iliac fossa pain that woke her from sleep 4 hours ago, associated with nausea and two episodes of vomiting. The pain is colicky, radiates to the right groin and posterior thigh, and is currently 9/10 in intensity despite paracetamol 1 g PO taken 90 minutes ago. She had a recent pelvic ultrasound 2 weeks ago for cyclical pelvic discomfort showing a 6 cm right ovarian dermoid (mature cystic teratoma); she was awaiting an outpatient gynaecology appointment.

Her last menstrual period was 10 days ago, regular 28-day cycles, and she has no intermenstrual bleeding or discharge. She is sexually active in a long-term relationship, uses condoms, and beta-hCG taken on arrival is negative. On examination she is in obvious distress, splinted on the right, with cool peripheries from pain.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, HR 112 bpm, RR 22, T 37.1 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen: marked right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding, no peritonism. Bowel sounds present. Bimanual: very tender right adnexal mass, palpable approximately 7 cm, with severe pain on cervical motion. Uterus normal size, anteverted.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative. WCC 13.2 x10^9/L, CRP 12 mg/L. Urinalysis negative. Bedside TVUS: enlarged right ovary 9 cm with peripheral follicles and a 6 cm complex mass; minimal Doppler flow within the ovarian parenchyma compared with the left.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit for serial observation, IV analgesia and a formal radiology TVUS at 08:00
Emergency CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast before any surgical decision
Right salpingo-oophorectomy via laparotomy because the ovary is likely non-viable
Urgent diagnostic laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian-preserving cystectomy under general anaesthetic
IV opioid analgesia and discharge with outpatient gynaecology follow-up next week

subtopic_detail: Lichen sclerosus - ultrapotent topical steroid + cancer surveillance
stem:
A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman attends a vulval clinic with a 12-month history of progressive vulval pruritus, soreness, and dyspareunia limiting intercourse with her long-term partner. She has noticed white, paper-thin skin around the labia minora and perineum, with occasional fissuring and contact bleeding when itching at night and during attempts at intercourse. Multiple courses of clotrimazole pessaries and over-the-counter hydrocortisone 1% over the past 6 months have not helped.

She has had no postmenopausal bleeding from the cervix and her last cervical screening test 12 months ago was HPV not detected. On examination there is well-demarcated 'figure-of-eight' white atrophic change involving the labia minora, clitoral hood and perianal skin, with partial resorption of the labia minora, narrowing of the introitus, and early posterior fourchette adhesion. There is one persistent indurated nodule 8 mm in diameter on the right labium majus that has been present for 6 weeks and has not responded to topical hydrocortisone.

data_table.Examination: Atrophic, paper-thin white change in classic figure-of-eight distribution. Loss of labia minora architecture. Discrete 8 mm indurated nodule on right labium majus, firm, non-tender. No inguinal lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening 12 months ago: HPV not detected.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Punch biopsy the indurated nodule and start clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment nightly
Trial topical oestrogen cream for presumed atrophic vaginitis and review in 6 weeks
Commence clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment nightly and review again in 12 weeks
Refer for wide local excision of the entire affected vulval area
Refer to dermatology for systemic methotrexate as steroid-sparing therapy now

subtopic_detail: Bartholin abscess - Word catheter as primary care management
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P1 woman presents to her GP with a 3-day history of progressively painful right-sided labial swelling. The swelling is now egg-sized, tense, exquisitely tender and is interfering with sitting and walking. She has had a low-grade fever of 37.8 degC at home but has not had rigors. She is in a monogamous relationship of 5 years and her most recent STI screen 4 months ago was negative for chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV.

She had a similar but smaller episode on the same side 2 years ago that resolved with incision and drainage in ED but recurred 3 months later as a painless cyst that has since fluctuated in size.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 37.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Tense, fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the right posterior introitus (5 o'clock position), overlying erythema, exquisitely tender. No inguinal lymphadenopathy. No vulval ulceration. Speculum deferred due to pain.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management of this Bartholin abscess?

options.text: Simple incision and drainage with packing, no catheter or marsupialisation
Outpatient oral antibiotics alone (e.g. amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg BD) without drainage
Incision and drainage with Word catheter insertion retained in situ 4-6 weeks
Excision of the Bartholin gland under general anaesthetic as definitive management
Sitz baths and oral analgesia, with re-review in 1 week if not improving

subtopic_detail: Test of cure after LLETZ for HSIL
stem:
A 34-year-old G0 woman had a LLETZ procedure 11 months ago for biopsy-proven HSIL (CIN3) detected after a screening HPV test reported HPV 16 with possible HSIL on reflex cytology. The LLETZ histology confirmed CIN3 with clear excision margins (ectocervical, endocervical and deep margins all clear of dysplasia, no glandular involvement, no microinvasion). Post-LLETZ recovery was uncomplicated with no secondary haemorrhage and no cervical stenosis on subsequent review.

She is asymptomatic, with no postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding and no discharge. She is in a monogamous relationship of 2 years and is using the etonogestrel implant for contraception. She is a non-smoker, BMI 24, has no immunosuppression, takes no regular medications and has no family history of cervical or other gynaecological malignancy. She received Gardasil as a teenager and completed her course. She attends her GP today asking what surveillance she now needs and when she can return to routine 5-yearly NCSP screening.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft. Cervix at speculum: smooth, no obvious lesion, no contact bleeding.

lead_in: Which surveillance pathway should she follow under the Australian NCSP?

options.text: Annual HPV cervical screening for 5 years, then return to routine 5-yearly screening
Single co-test at 24 months and return to routine 5-yearly screening if negative
Return to routine 5-yearly NCSP screening now because excision margins were clear
6-monthly colposcopy for 2 years regardless of cytology or HPV result
Co-test at 12 and 24 months; both negative returns to 5-yearly screening

subtopic_detail: Tamoxifen-related endometrial bleeding - investigate symptoms, do not screen asymptomatic
stem:
A 64-year-old G2P2 woman has been taking tamoxifen 20 mg daily for 4 years as adjuvant endocrine therapy for ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative left breast cancer treated 4 years ago with breast-conserving surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy. She was previously postmenopausal (natural menopause age 52, no bleeding for 12 years prior to commencing tamoxifen) and is now referred to gynaecology after presenting to her GP with two episodes of fresh vaginal bleeding over the past 3 weeks, each lasting 2-3 days and requiring two pads daily.

She has had no postcoital bleeding, no dischargery or bowel symptoms. Her last cervical screening 18 months ago was HPV not detected on a clinician-collected sample. She has hypertension (perindopril 5 mg daily, BP 138/82 on review), a BMI of 31, and well-controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.9%, metformin 1 g BD). She has no personal or family history of Lynch-associated cancers and meets no Lynch testing criteria. She has never used hormone therapy or unopposed oestrogen pre-tamoxifen.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 76 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft. Speculum: atrophic mucosa, small amount of blood at the os, no cervical lesion. Bimanual: uterus normal size, mobile, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L (115-165). TVUS performed by GP: endometrium 9 mm, heterogeneous, with several small cystic spaces; no focal mass identified; ovaries normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discontinue tamoxifen and substitute an aromatase inhibitor without further gynaecological investigation
Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy with directed and Pipelle endometrial biopsy
Repeat TVUS in 3 months to assess for any change in endometrial thickness
Reassure as endometrial thickness is acceptable for tamoxifen users; review if bleeding recurs
Commence routine 6-monthly TVUS surveillance and biopsy only if thickness exceeds 8 mm

stem:
A 44-year-old G2P2 woman attends her GP with an 8-month history of progressively heavier menstrual bleeding. Cycles are regular at 28 days but bleeding now lasts 9 days with flooding through super tampons hourly on days 2-3 and passage of large clots up to 3 cm in size. She reports increasing tiredness, palpitations on minor exertion, and exertional shortness of breath climbing one flight of stairs.

Her work as a primary school teacher has been disrupted and she has had to change pads during teaching sessions. She is not currently sexually active, has had no postcoital bleeding, no intermenstrual bleeding, and no postcoital spotting. There is no abdominal or pelvic pain. There is no easy bruising, no gum bleeding last cervical screening test was negative for oncogenic HPV 18 months ago.

BMI is 34. She has hypertension treated with perindopril 5 mg daily and takes no anticoagulants, no antiplatelets and no over-the-counter NSAIDs. She has had two normal vaginal deliveries with no postpartum haemorrhage. She has not yet had pelvic imaging or endometrial sampling in this presentation.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae. Abdomen soft, no palpable mass. Bimanual: uterus bulky, mobile, anteverted, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L (115-165), MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 mcg/L. Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: In addition to a transvaginal ultrasound and full blood count with ferritin, which further investigation is most important at this visit?

options.text: FSH and oestradiol to assess for perimenopausal anovulation as cause
Coagulation screen and von Willebrand panel as the first-line bleeding work-up
Endometrial Pipelle biopsy at this visit, with TSH and coagulation screen as adjuncts
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy as the sole investigation in place of TVUS today
Serum CA-125 to screen for occult ovarian malignancy in this patient

subtopic_detail: Heavy menstrual bleeding - structured PALM-COEIN workup

stem:
A 39-year-old G1P1 woman has a 2-year history of heavy regular menstrual bleeding with cycle-related bulk symptoms including urinary frequency, mild lower-abdominal pressure, and occasional nocturia. She passes large clots during menses and floods through super tampons every 1-2 hours on the heaviest days. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 4 cm intramural fibroid (FIGO type 4, not distorting the cavity) and a 3 cm subserosal fibroid; the endometrial cavity is regular and the endometrium is 6 mm.

Endometrial biopsy returns benign proliferative endometrium with no atypia. She has completed her family, is in a monogamous relationship using condoms for contraception, and would prefer to avoid surgery if possible. She does not want to lose her fertility surgically and is open to a long-acting hormonal device. She has tried tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses with only modest improvement and has not tolerated mefenamic acid. BMI 26.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, lower-uterine mass palpable just above pubis. Bimanual: bulky irregular uterus approx 12-week size, mobile.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 101 g/L (115-165), ferritin 14 mcg/L. TVUS as above. Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line medical therapy?

options.text: GnRH agonist (e.g. goserelin 3.6 mg SC monthly) with add-back oestrogen
Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system (Mirena) insertion now
Tranexamic acid 1 g orally three times daily during menses only
Mefenamic acid 500 mg orally three times daily during menses only
Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy under GA

subtopic_detail: Uterine fibroids - choice of medical therapy

stem:
A 27-year-old nulligravid woman presents with 4 years of cyclical pelvic pain (peaks day 1-2, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia during menses, cyclical back pain). She has tried regular ibuprofen and heat-pack regimen with minimal benefit. She is not planning conception in the next 18-24 months but does want children eventually. She has no migraine with aura, no smoking, no VTE history, BMI 24.

Pelvic USS normal (no endometrioma). Bimanual examination shows tender uterosacral nodularity. She is now keen for the most evidence-based next step that does not commit her to surgery if it can be avoided.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no masses. Bimanual: uterus anteverted, mobile, mildly tender. No palpable nodularity in the pouch of Douglas. No adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic USS: normal-appearing ovaries, no endometrioma, no deep infiltrating lesion visualised.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial continuous combined oral contraceptive pill with NSAID for breakthrough pain, with review at 3-6 months and laparoscopy if refractory or fertility planning advances
Diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal biopsy before any medical therapy
Serum CA-125 to support the working diagnosis
MRI pelvis as the next investigation to confirm the working diagnosis
GnRH agonist with add-back HRT as first-line therapy

subtopic_detail: Endometriosis - diagnostic pathway

stem:
A 33-year-old nulligravid woman attends her GP with 6 months of secondary amenorrhoea following a 12-month history of progressively irregular cycles. She reports new hot flushes (around 6-8 per day), troublesome night sweats with disturbed sleep, vaginal dryness with deep dyspareunia, low mood, reduced libido and increased fatigue. She is in a stable long-term relationship and is open to future fertility consideration, although they have not actively been trying to conceive.

There is no recent significant weight change, no excessive exercise, no medication changesoms. She has had no chemotherapy, no pelvic radiotherapy and no previous ovarian surgery. She had menarche at age 12 with previously regular 28-day cycles. Family history: her mother had menopause at age 41 and her maternal aunt had menopause in her early forties; one cousin has Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

BMI 23. She is not using contraception currently. Beta-hCG is negative today. Initial bloods 5 weeks ago: FSH 56 IU/L, oestradiol low, prolactin normal, TSH normal, total testosterone normal. Today's repeat FSH and oestradiol have been collected and are pending.

data_table.Examination: BMI 23. No goitre. No visual field defect. Speculum: pale dry vaginal mucosa.
data_table.Investigations: Five weeks ago: FSH 56 IU/L (premenopausal <10), oestradiol low, LH 38, prolactin normal, TSH 1.8, beta-hCG negative. Today: bloods repeated, pending.

lead_in: If today's repeat FSH is similarly elevated (>25 IU/L), which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure and recheck FSH in 6 months as a single elevated FSH is non-diagnostic alone
Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill solely for menopausal symptom control without further workup needed
Bone density scan and fertility counselling referral, but defer hormonal therapy until age 40 years
Refer to endocrinology for an adrenal failure work-up before initiating any hormonal therapy in her
Systemic HRT, fertility counselling, screen for adrenal/thyroid antibodies and karyotype, plus baseline bone densitometry

subtopic_detail: Premature ovarian insufficiency - diagnosis and HRT

stem: A 21-year-old sexually active woman presents with 4 days of lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, mucopurulent vaginal discharge, fever 38.4 C, HR 110, BP 100/64. Examination: bilateral lower-quadrant tenderness, cervical motion tenderness, mucopurulent endocervical discharge, AND a 6 cm tender right adnexal mass with bedside USS demonstrating a multilocular cystic mass with internal debris consistent with tubo-ovarian abscess. She is unable to tolerate oral intake due to nausea and vomiting. Urine beta-hCG negative. WCC 18, CRP 180. NAAT swabs sent. She has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 37.1 degC.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen: bilateral lower abdominal tenderness. Bimanual: cervical motion tenderness, mucopurulent endocervical discharge, no palpable adnexal mass.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit and commence IV ceftriaxone, doxycycline (or azithromycin if intolerant) and metronidazole, with surgical or interventional drainage if no improvement at 48-72 hours
Outpatient ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus oral doxycycline plus oral metronidazole for 14 days despite the imaging-confirmed tubo-ovarian abscess here
Single-dose IM ceftriaxone and discharge home with safety-net advice despite the imaging-confirmed tubo-ovarian abscess on the recent pelvic scan
Proceed immediately to laparoscopy and salpingectomy as the primary intervention before any trial of intravenous antibiotic therapy for the abscess
Oral amoxicillin monotherapy for 14 days despite the polymicrobial pelvic infection with anaerobic and gonococcal coverage gaps in this regimen

subtopic_detail: PID - Therapeutic Guidelines regimen

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P2 woman attends her 6-week postnatal check with her local GP. She had an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal birth of a healthy term infant 6 weeks ago and is exclusively breastfeeding on demand, day and night, with no formula supplementation and no expressed-milk bottle feeds. The baby is feeding 8-12 times in 24 hours and weight gain is on track.

She has not yet had a return of menses. She wishes to space pregnancies for at least 2 years and would prefer the most reliable method that is compatible with breastfeeding. She has no history of VTE, no thrombophilia25. She does not smoke. She has not used the lactational amenorrhoea method as her sole strategy and is concerned about pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Well. BP 118/74. BMI 25. Soft well-involuted uterus, no lochia, perineum healed. Lactating breasts, no mastitis.
data_table.Investigations: None required today; routine 6-week postnatal review.

lead_in: Regarding contraception, which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The combined oral contraceptive pill is the first-line choice as BP has normalised and gestational hypertension has resolved
Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) is acceptable as a sole contraceptive method indefinitely while she remains amenorrhoeic
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system or copper IUD can be inserted today, and etonogestrel implant or progestogen-only pill are also suitable
Etonogestrel implant should be delayed until 6 months postpartum because of an adverse effect on milk supply
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is contraindicated during breastfeeding and should not be used at all here

subtopic_detail: Postnatal contraception in a breastfeeding woman

stem:
A 38-year-old woman has her routine 5-yearly cervical screening test through her general practice. She is not pregnant, has had two previous CSTs at ages 28 and 33 which were both negative for oncogenic HPV, and has had no abnormal vaginal bleeding, no postcoital bleedingpelvic pain. She is in a stable monogamous relationship of 11 years and uses the LNG-IUS 52 mg (Mirena, inserted 4 years ago for both contraception and HMB control) and is currently amenorrhoeic.

She has had a total of 4 lifetime sexual partners and has never had a sexually transmitted infection identified. She received the quadrivalent HPV vaccine series at age 14 through the school-based program. Her practitioner-collected sample returns: oncogenic HPV detected (non-16/18 type); reflex liquid-based cytology performed automatically by the laboratory shows no intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. She is immunocompetent and has no history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or cervical excisional treatment. She does not smoke.

data_table.Examination: Routine speculum normal at time of collection.
data_table.Investigations: HPV test: oncogenic non-16/18 detected. Reflex LBC: negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy.

lead_in: Under the Australian National Cervical Screening Program, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Direct referral for colposcopy with cervical biopsy now
Repeat HPV testing in 12 months (intermediate-risk pathway)
Return to routine 5-yearly cervical screening immediately
Repeat HPV test for partial genotype in 6 months
Refer for excisional treatment (LLETZ) without further investigation

subtopic_detail: Cervical screening - oncogenic non-16/18 HPV management

stem:
A 62-year-old G3P3 woman presents to her general practice with a 6-week history of intermittent painless vaginal bleeding. She has been menopausal since age 51 (last menstrual period at 51) and has had no episodes of bleeding in the intervening 11 years until now. The current bleeding is light to moderate, requires a pad most days, and has been ongoing intermittently for the last 6 weeks.

There is no associated abdominal or pelvic pain, no urinary symptoms, no bowel change and no weight loss. She has never been on menopausal hormone therapy, has never used tamoxifen, and has no family history of endometrial, ovarian, breast or bowel cancer (specifically no features of Lynch syndrome on family history). Her BMI is 33, she has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1 g twice daily (HbA1c 6.6%), and her hypertension is well controlled on perindopril 5 mg daily.

She has had three previous spontaneous vaginal births, none complicated, and no postpartum haemorrhage. Her last cervical screening test was negative for oncogenic HPV 18 months ago. She is on no anticoagulants and no antiplatelets. A transvaginal ultrasound is being arranged today.

data_table.Examination: BMI 33. Speculum: small amount of dark blood at cervix, no visible cervical lesion. Bimanual: uterus mobile, normal size, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L, platelets 240. UEC and LFTs normal. Beta-hCG not indicated. Cervical screening negative 18 months ago.

lead_in: Regarding TVUS endometrial thickness in this clinical setting, which statement is most accurate?

options.text: If TVUS endometrial thickness is <=2 mm then endometrial sampling is mandatory regardless of other factors
A TVUS endometrial thickness of 3 mm essentially excludes endometrial cancer and no further investigation is needed even if recurrent bleeding
Tamoxifen use makes TVUS thickness measurement unreliable due to subepithelial cysts; saline sonohysterography or hysteroscopy is preferred
She should proceed directly to hysteroscopy without prior TVUS, given her constellation of risk factors
Endometrial thickness >=4 mm on TVUS warrants endometrial sampling (Pipelle), with hysteroscopy if focal lesions or non-diagnostic sampling

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding - TVUS endometrial thickness threshold

stem:
A 53-year-old G2P2 woman presents to her GP with 18 months of disabling vasomotor symptoms: 8-12 hot flushes per day with drenching night sweats requiring change of nightwear most nights, fragmented sleep with average 4-5 hours, persistently low mood (PHQ-9 score 11), and reduced libido. She has tried fan, cooling clothing, regular exercise, alcohol avoidance and trigger-diary approaches with limited benefit.

Her last menstrual period was 14 months ago and she is therefore postmenopausal by clinical criteria. She has an intact uterus and has had no episodes of postmenopausal bleeding. Her BMI is 31, BP 132/84 mmHg, fasting lipids in target range and HbA1c 5.5%. She had a single provoked DVT after a long-haul flight 8 years ago and was anticoagulated for 3 months; no thrombophilia was identified and she has had no subsequent VTE.

She has no personal or family history of breast cancer, no ischaemic heart disease, and no migraine with aura. She does not smoke. Cervical screening and mammography are up to date and normal. She does not want a monthly bleed and would prefer a no-bleed regimen if possible.

data_table.Examination: BMI 31. BP 132/84. Breast examination normal. Pelvic examination unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: Fasting lipids: total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 3.1. HbA1c 5.5%. TSH 1.6 mIU/L. Mammogram normal 10 months ago.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate MHT regimen for her?

options.text: Oral oestradiol 1 mg daily plus cyclical medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg for 12 days each month
Oral conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625 mg daily plus continuous medroxyprogesterone acetate 2.5 mg orally
Tibolone 2.5 mg orally once daily as monotherapy for menopausal symptom control alone
Transdermal oestradiol patch 50 mcg/24 h twice weekly plus levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD (Mirena)
Transdermal oestradiol patch 50 mcg/24 h applied twice weekly alone, with no progestogen at all

subtopic_detail: MHT - regimen selection and route

stem:
A 67-year-old woman presents to her GP with 18 months of progressive vaginal dryness, deep dyspareunia and urinary urgency without incontinence. She has had three episodes of culture-confirmed E. coli urinary tract infection in the past 12 months, each requiring antibiotics, with no upper-tract involvement. She had a left-sided early-stage T1N0 oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer treated with breast-conserving lumpectomy, sentinel node biopsy, adjuvant radiotherapy and 5 years of adjuvant tamoxifen completed 12 months ago.

She did not receive an aromatase inhibitor. She is currently in remission with no evidence of disease on her most recent annual surveillance mammogram and clinical breast examination 4 months ago. She is not on systemic MHT. She has tried over-the-counter water-based vaginal lubricants for intercourse and a non-hormonal hyaluronic acid-based vaginal moisturiser (Replens) used three times weekly consistently for 4 months with only modest symptomatic benefit. She is sexually active with her long-term partner and her quality of life and intimate relationship are significantly affected.

data_table.Examination: Speculum: pale thin atrophic vaginal mucosa, friable, loss of rugae. No discharge, no lesions. Bimanual: normal-sized uterus, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Urine MCS today: no growth. Last surveillance mammogram and clinical breast examination 4 months ago: no evidence of disease.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Avoid all oestrogen-containing therapies indefinitely and continue non-hormonal vaginal moisturisers and lubricants only
Commence systemic oestradiol patch 50 mcg/24 h plus an LNG-IUS for endometrial protection
Trial low-dose vaginal oestriol cream after discussion with breast oncologist, continuing non-hormonal moisturisers
Refer for fractional CO2 vaginal laser treatment as first-line alternative in this patient
Commence ospemifene orally as the first-line therapy for her dyspareunia in this setting

subtopic_detail: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause - local oestrogen

stem:
A 64-year-old G2P2 postmenopausal woman has a 6-year established diagnosis of vulval lichen sclerosus, biopsy-confirmed at the time of diagnosis. She has been managed with topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment using a structured regimen (nightly for 4 weeks, then alternate nights for 4 weeks, then twice weekly maintenance long-term) and has been reasonably symptom-controlled until recently, with annual review by her gynaecologist.

Over the past 4 months she has noticed a persistent fissured area on the right labium majus that has not healed despite optimisation of her steroid technique (correct application, adequate quantity confirmed at recent review). Symptoms include localised pruritus that has worsened, occasional spotting when wiping after micturition, and increasing discomfort with intercourse despite use of personal lubricant. She has no postcoital bleeding aside from the localised spotting described.

She is on no immunosuppressive medications and is otherwise well, with controlled hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily. There is no history of previous vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, no previous vulval surgery, and her last cervical screening 18 months ago was negative for oncogenic HPV.

data_table.Examination: Vulva: classic white atrophic 'cigarette paper' skin extending in a figure-of-eight around vulva and perianal area, loss of labia minora architecture. New finding: 1.2 cm hyperkeratotic, fissured, indurated plaque on right labium majus that has not healed.
data_table.Investigations: None done today; review appointment for chronic LS surveillance.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase topical clobetasol propionate to nightly application for a further 8 weeks and review symptoms
Add topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment as a second-line steroid-sparing agent for symptomatic control of disease
Reassure that surveillance is not required after 5 years of stable disease and discharge to self-management with PRN steroid only
Refer for wide local excision of the suspicious vulval lesion without prior histology being obtained
Refer urgently to gynaecology/vulval clinic for punch biopsy of the persistent fissured lesion, continuing topical clobetasol and at least annual surveillance

subtopic_detail: Lichen sclerosus - surveillance and malignancy risk

stem:
A 27-year-old G1P0 at 40+3 in spontaneous labour has had an epidural sited two hours ago with a top-up given 25 minutes ago for a left-sided breakthrough. Her booking BMI was 24, she is a non-smoker, has no medical comorbidities, and the GBS swab at 36 weeks was negative. The last vaginal examination 40 minutes ago showed 8 cm dilatation, +0 station, direct OA, intact caput, no moulding.

Membranes ruptured spontaneously 6 hours ago with clear liquor. Oxytocin augmentation was started 90 minutes ago for slow progress between 6 and 8 cm and is currently at 12 mU/min with contractions 4 in 10, lasting 70 seconds, palpating moderate. The CTG over the last 30 minutes shows a baseline of 145 bpm, reduced variability of 3 to 5 bpm, no accelerations, and recurrent late decelerations occurring with more than 50% of contractions for the last 25 minutes.

There has been no prolonged deceleration. The mother is comfortable and the partogram shows progress consistent with primary dysfunctional labour. The obstetric registrar is at the bedside and theatre is available.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: 8 cm, +0, direct OA, clear liquor. Uterus soft between contractions. Palpates 4 in 10 moderate.
data_table.Investigations: CTG: baseline 145 bpm, variability 3-5 bpm, no accelerations, recurrent late decelerations >50% of contractions x 25 min. No tachysystole on tocodynamometer.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?

options.text: Stop oxytocin, reposition to left lateral, give 500 mL IV crystalloid, perform fetal scalp lactate within 15 minutes
Continue oxytocin and observe for a further 30 minutes to determine if the pattern resolves spontaneously
Proceed immediately to a category 1 caesarean section with a 30-minute decision-to-delivery interval
Administer terbutaline 250 microg subcutaneously for acute tocolysis and continue oxytocin at the current rate
Perform an artificial rupture of membranes and apply a fetal scalp electrode without further intrauterine resuscitation

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum CTG - recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 at 39+1 in spontaneous labour at 6 cm has an epidural in situ that was sited 90 minutes ago and has provided good analgesia until the last hour, when she began to feel a sharp left-sided sensation with contractions. Her booking BMI was 27, she has no cardiac, respiratory or neurological comorbidities, no allergies, no anaphylaxis history, and her booking bloods including FBC and group and screen were unremarkable.

Five minutes ago the anaesthetic registrar gave a top-up of 10 mL of 0.1% ropivacaine with 2 microg/mL fentanyl for breakthrough pain. Her BP has now dropped from 122/74 to 84/46 mmHg with a maternal HR of 102. She feels light-headed but is conscious and is not nauseated, has no perioral numbness, no tinnitus and no metallic taste. The CTG shows a prolonged deceleration to 80 bpm that has now been ongoing for 4 minutes after previously reassuring features (baseline 140, variability 10-15, accelerations present).

There has been no vaginal bleeding, the uterus is soft between contractions (no hypertonus), the liquor was clear at ARM 30 minutes earlier, and there is no concern for cord prolapse on bedside vaginal examination. The anaesthetic registrar is at the bedside and IV access is patent through a 16G cannula.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 84/46 mmHg, HR 102 bpm (maternal), T 36.7 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Awake, light-headed. Uterus soft between contractions. No PV bleeding. Cord not palpable.
data_table.Investigations: CTG: prolonged deceleration to 80 bpm for 4 minutes following epidural top-up.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Ephedrine 6 mg IV bolus, repeat at 1-2 minute intervals as needed
Metaraminol 0.5 mg IV bolus, repeat at 1-2 minute intervals as needed
Phenylephrine 100 microg IV bolus, repeat at 1-2 minute intervals as needed
Adrenaline 10 microg IV bolus and prepare for category 1 caesarean
Atropine 600 microg IV bolus to correct the maternal heart rate

subtopic_detail: Prolonged deceleration after epidural top-up - vasopressor choice

stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 40+1 in spontaneous labour, admitted 6 hours ago at 5 cm, is re-examined and is now 6 cm at +0 station in direct OP position with mild caput and no moulding. Membranes ruptured spontaneously 4 hours ago with clear liquor. Contractions: palpate 3 in 10 lasting 40 seconds, mild intensity. CTG normal. Hb 124. Her mother is reminding the registrar that her own labour had to be 'started with the drip' and asks them to do the same.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: 6 cm, +0, direct OP, mild caput, no moulding. Contractions 3 in 10, 40 s, mild.
data_table.Investigations: CTG normal. GBS negative. Hb 124 g/L.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence IV oxytocin infusion starting at 1-2 mU/min, titrated every 30 minutes to achieve 4-5 contractions per 10 minutes
Perform ARM and reassess in 4 hours before considering oxytocin
Proceed to category 2 caesarean section for failure to progress
Commence IV oxytocin infusion starting at 6 mU/min with no titration interval shorter than 60 minutes
Site an epidural and re-examine her in 6 hours without commencing any augmentation now

subtopic_detail: Failure to progress in active first stage - oxytocin augmentation

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 at 38+2 in spontaneous labour at 10 cm dilatation has just had a spontaneous rupture of membranes with a large gush of clear liquor. The midwife performing a vaginal examination immediately feels a pulsating loop of cord in the vagina at +0 station. The fetal head is at -2 station and direct OA, with 3/5 of the head still palpable abdominally.

The CTG was previously reassuring (baseline 140, variability 10, accelerations present, no decelerations) but now shows a prolonged deceleration to 70 bpm starting within the last minute. The mother is comfortable on her right side with an epidural in situ; her observations are BP 122/78, HR 88, T 36.9, SpO2 99%. She is otherwise well, has no obstetric or medical comorbidities, and her 36-week growth scan was unremarkable.

The emergency buzzer has been pulled and the obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams are en route. She has had no previous abdominal surgery, no caesarean section, and is otherwise low risk for surgical complications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: 10 cm, -2 station, direct OA, pulsating cord at +0 in vagina. Liquor clear. Bladder catheterised.
data_table.Investigations: CTG: prolonged deceleration to 70 bpm, starting within the last minute.

lead_in: Which immediate set of actions is most appropriate?

options.text: Reduce the cord back into the uterus through the cervix and proceed to instrumental vaginal delivery in the room
Continue oxytocin augmentation, reposition the mother to left lateral and reassess CTG again in 5 minutes
Administer terbutaline 250 microg subcutaneously and proceed immediately to assisted vaginal birth using a ventouse now
Manually elevate the presenting part off the cord, knee-chest or exaggerated Sims, fill bladder 500 mL if delay, category 1 caesarean
Wait for the next contraction at full dilatation and perform a fundal pressure delivery to expedite vaginal birth

subtopic_detail: Cord prolapse - immediate management at full dilatation

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 40+0 with an epidural is in active second stage. She has been pushing for 110 minutes without descent of the presenting part beyond +1 station. The fetal head is at +1, direct OA, with no caput or moulding palpable, and 0/5 of the head is palpable abdominally on Crichton assessment. The maternal pelvis was clinically adequate on assessment by both registrar and consultant.

The CTG shows a baseline of 145 with variability 5-10 bpm, no accelerations and variable decelerations with most contractions but no late or prolonged decelerations and no sinusoidal pattern. Membranes are ruptured with clear liquor of normal volume. Contractions are 4 in 10 with oxytocin running at 16 mU/min. The mother is exhausted, asking for help to deliver, and has had a thorough antenatal discussion of birth options including operative delivery.

The bladder is empty after recent catheter in/out. Adequate epidural top-up has been given and the block is dense to ice. The neonatal team has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, T 37.0 degC.
data_table.Examination: +1 station, direct OA, 0/5 head palpable abdominally, no caput, no moulding. Bladder empty. Epidural adequate.
data_table.Investigations: CTG suspicious (variable decelerations, reduced variability), not pathological.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate instrument and approach for this delivery?

options.text: Kielland's rotational forceps for a deep transverse arrest under regional anaesthesia
Low-cavity non-rotational outlet forceps (Neville-Barnes or Simpson) under regional anaesthesia
Sequential ventouse then forceps if the initial vacuum extraction attempt fails to descend
Kiwi OmniCup soft ventouse with traction synchronous with maternal contractions only and pulls
Proceed directly to a category 2 caesarean section now without attempted instrumental delivery

subtopic_detail: Instrumental birth - forceps vs ventouse selection

stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 at 39+4 having a trial of labour after caesarean (one previous LSCS for breech) is in active labour at 7 cm with epidural. The CTG develops a sudden prolonged deceleration to 60 bpm, not recovering after 4 minutes despite stopping oxytocin, left lateral, 500 mL crystalloid and exclusion of hypotension. Fresh PV bleeding develops, scar tenderness, and the previously palpable head becomes ballotable abdominally (suspected uterine rupture). The registrar calls a category 1 caesarean section.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 102/64 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Scar tender, fresh PV bleeding, head ballotable abdominally.
data_table.Investigations: CTG: prolonged deceleration 60 bpm, not recovering at 4 minutes.

lead_in: Which combination most accurately describes the standards for category 1 caesarean and the immediate priorities?

options.text: Decision-to-delivery interval target 30 minutes; concurrent MTP activation, theatre transfer, anaesthetic preparation; do not delay for re-examination
Decision-to-delivery 15 minutes; defer MTP activation until intraoperative blood loss is confirmed
Decision-to-delivery 60 minutes; obtain confirmatory bedside ultrasound before transfer to theatre
Decision-to-delivery 75 minutes if epidural is already sited and theatre is in-house
Decision-to-delivery 45 minutes; abandon TOLAC pathway only after delivery is achieved

subtopic_detail: Decision-to-delivery interval for category 1 caesarean

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 28+3 is admitted with a 24-hour history of severe frontal headache, blurred vision and right upper quadrant pain. She booked at 14 weeks with a BP of 116/72 and no proteinuria; her booking BMI was 23 and she has no chronic hypertension, no diabetes and no autoimmune disease. The 20-week morphology scan was normal and the most recent growth scan at 26 weeks showed an appropriately grown fetus with normal Dopplers.

Her BP on arrival is 178/116 mmHg confirmed on repeat with a manual cuff after 5 minutes' rest, with 3+ proteinuria on dipstick and a urine PCR of 380 mg/mmol. She is reflexively brisk at 3+ with no clonus, no focal neurology, and no visual field defect on confrontation. Bloods show platelets 92, ALT 184, urate 0.42, creatinine 88, LDH normal, no haemolysis on film, INR 1.0, fibrinogen 4.2.

A magnesium sulfate loading dose of 4 g IV over 20 minutes was given 30 minutes ago and a maintenance infusion of 1 g/h is now running. Despite the magnesium load her headache and blurred vision persist and her BP remains 174/112. The CTG is currently reassuring with a baseline of 138 and normal variability.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 174/112 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Headache, blurred vision persist. Hyperreflexia 3+, no clonus. RUQ tender.
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 92 (x10^9/L), ALT 184 U/L, urate 0.42 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, urine PCR 380 mg/mmol, no haemolysis. CTG reassuring.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate additional antihypertensive intervention?

options.text: IV hydralazine 5 mg bolus, then 5-10 mg every 20 minutes (max 30 mg) titrated to BP <160/110
IV labetalol 20 mg bolus, then 40 mg, then 80 mg every 10 minutes (max 220 mg) titrated to BP <160/110
Oral nifedipine immediate-release 10 mg, repeated every 30 minutes to a maximum of three doses for control
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg capsule bitten and swallowed, repeated every 20 minutes as required to a maximum of three doses
Increase the magnesium sulfate maintenance infusion from 1 g/h to 2 g/h to achieve blood pressure control in her

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia at 28 weeks - antihypertensive selection

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 37+3 has just had a spontaneous vaginal birth of Twin 1 (cephalic, 2.6 kg) with intact membranes of the second sac. She has an epidural in situ. After delivery of Twin 1 her uterus relaxes and bedside ultrasound now shows Twin 2 in a transverse lie with the back inferior and the membranes still intact.

The estimated fetal weight of Twin 2 at the 36-week scan was 2.8 kg. The CTG of Twin 2 is reassuring with a baseline of 140 bpm, variability 10-15, accelerations present, no decelerations. The cervix remains fully dilated. The obstetric consultant is in theatre attached to the room, and the anaesthetist confirms a working epidural with a dense block. There is no PV bleeding and the uterus is currently soft. The team has been briefed and the mother had a thorough antenatal discussion of intrapartum options for twin birth.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 88 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Cervix fully dilated. Twin 2 transverse, back inferior, membranes intact. Uterus relaxed.
data_table.Investigations: USS at bedside: transverse lie, back inferior. CTG reassuring.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of Twin 2 at this point?

options.text: External cephalic version under tocolysis followed by ARM when cephalic and longitudinal
ARM immediately to allow the head to descend by gravity
Immediate emergency caesarean section for delivery of the second twin
Wait 60 minutes for spontaneous version before any intervention
Internal podalic version with breech extraction performed under continued epidural anaesthesia

subtopic_detail: Twin delivery - second twin with non-cephalic lie

stem:
A 36-year-old G4P3 at 39+4 has just had a spontaneous vaginal birth at 09:42 after a 4-hour labour augmented with oxytocin from 5 cm for slow progress, ending with a second stage of 30 minutes and an intact perineum. The placenta was delivered by controlled cord traction at 09:48 and active third-stage management with IM oxytocin 10 units had been given immediately after the birth.

Two minutes after delivery of the placenta she suddenly develops dyspnoea, agitation and a sense of impending doom while talking to her partner. Within 60 seconds she becomes cyanotic, loses consciousness and her monitor shows BP 60/40 mmHg, HR 130 bpm, SpO2 78% on 15 L/min via Hudson mask, with the trace transitioning to a narrow-complex tachycardia. Within 90 seconds she becomes pulseless with a rhythm of PEA on the defibrillator.

There is now brisk PV bleeding from the uterus despite a soft contracted fundus on bimanual palpation, and oozing from her peripheral IV site and recent venipuncture. She has no history of cardiac disease, no epidural was sited at any point, no local anaesthetic was used apart from 5 mL of 1% lidocaine for a perineal infiltration after the birth, and there were no transfusions or blood products administered during labour. CPR is commenced with manual left uterine displacement and the obstetric, anaesthetic, ICU and haematology teams are paged through the MET emergency call.

data_table.Vital signs: Pre-arrest: BP 60/40 mmHg, HR 130 bpm, SpO2 78% on 15 L/min O2. Now pulseless with PEA.
data_table.Examination: Cyanotic, unconscious. Brisk PV bleeding from soft contracted uterus. Oozing from IV site.
data_table.Investigations: Bloods drawn: anticipate prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, low platelets. CTG no longer relevant.

lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?

options.text: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiopulmonary collapse and DIC
Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) from perineal lidocaine infiltration
Eclamptic seizure with secondary cardiopulmonary cardiac arrest
Acute pulmonary embolism with right heart failure
Acute coronary syndrome with cardiogenic shock and arrest

subtopic_detail: Maternal collapse in labour ward - amniotic fluid embolism

stem: A 33-year-old G1P0 at 41+5 is undergoing induction of labour for prolonged pregnancy. She has received two doses of dinoprostone 2 mg vaginal gel 6 hours apart, the second 8 hours ago. Cervix today: 1 cm long, posterior, firm, 1 cm dilated, head at -3 (Bishop score 3). No regular contractions. CTG reassuring, membranes intact. EFW 3.4 kg, no contraindications to mechanical methods, no previous caesarean, no antepartum haemorrhage, no fetal compromise. Local protocol permits maximum 2 doses of dinoprostone gel in 24 hours and prefers mechanical ripening when prostaglandins fail. She has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Bishop score 3 (1 cm long, posterior, firm, 1 cm dilated, -3 station). Membranes intact.
data_table.Investigations: CTG reassuring. EFW 3.4 kg.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a transcervical Foley catheter (16 Fr) with balloon inflated to 30-60 mL for up to 24 hours for mechanical cervical ripening
Administer a third dose of dinoprostone 2 mg vaginal gel today
Perform artificial rupture of membranes and commence IV oxytocin infusion
Perform a membrane sweep at the bedside and reassess in 24 hours
Proceed directly to category 4 elective caesarean section for failed induction of labour

subtopic_detail: Failed induction - unfavourable cervix after prostaglandins

stem:
A 38-year-old G5P4 has had a postpartum haemorrhage after spontaneous vaginal birth of a 4.2 kg neonate following oxytocin augmentation. Despite 40 IU oxytocin infusion, IM ergometrine, three doses IM carboprost, IV tranexamic acid 1 g, and a Bakri balloon at 500 mL, she continues to bleed. Total EBL 3500 mL. BP 88/52, HR 134, peripheries cool. Fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, platelets 68.

MTP active, packed cells/FFP/platelets running. She has completed her family. Consultant obstetrician is at the bedside, gynae-oncology is in-house, interventional radiology is on site, anaesthetic team is in theatre.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/52 mmHg, HR 134 bpm, T 36.0 degC.
data_table.Examination: Atonic uterus despite Bakri 500 mL. Cool peripheries. In theatre, laparotomy imminent.
data_table.Investigations: Total EBL 3500 mL. Fibrinogen 1.4 g/L. Platelets 68 (x10^9/L). Massive transfusion protocol active.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to laparotomy with uterine-sparing measures first (B-Lynch compression suture +/- stepwise uterine artery ligation), escalating to peripartum hysterectomy if bleeding persists
Proceed directly to peripartum hysterectomy without trialling uterine-sparing surgery
Insert a second balloon alongside the Bakri and arrange transfer to interventional radiology for embolisation
Re-inflate Bakri to 750 mL and observe for 30 minutes before further intervention
Bilateral internal iliac artery ligation as the first surgical step

subtopic_detail: Intractable PPH - surgical escalation pathway

stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 39+5 in spontaneous labour has been at full dilatation with a working epidural for 2 hours. She has been pushing actively for 90 minutes. The fetal head is at 0 station in occiput transverse with moderate caput and 1+ moulding. CTG: baseline 145, variability 5-10, no accelerations, occasional early decelerations. Contractions 3 in 10 lasting 45 seconds, palpate moderate. Liquor clear. EFW 3500 g, gynaecoid pelvis. She is exhausted but cooperative.

data_table.Examination: Full dilatation, +1 station, direct OA, mild caput, no moulding.
data_table.CTG: Baseline 140 bpm, variability 10-15, accelerations present, no decelerations.
data_table.Contractions: 4 in 10, 60 seconds, palpate moderate to strong.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue active pushing for a further hour as delay is defined only after 3 hours in nulliparous women with epidural
Obstetric review for assessment of arrest of descent with consideration of rotational instrumental or caesarean
Immediate Kielland's rotational forceps in the room without senior review
Commence oxytocin augmentation and continue pushing for another 2 hours
Stop pushing and observe passively for spontaneous descent for the next 4 hours

subtopic_detail: Normal labour - duration of second stage in nulliparous woman with epidural

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 at 41+2 with an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy attends the day assessment unit for induction of labour for post-dates. Her previous birth was a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39+4 weeks with a normal third stage and no perineal trauma beyond a small first-degree tear. She has no medical comorbidities, no allergies caesarean. The fetus is cephalic with a reassuring CTG today, an estimated fetal weight on the 60th centile at her 36-week scan and normal umbilical and middle cerebral artery Dopplers at that time.

Liquor volume is normal. Membranes are intact and there has been no PV bleeding, no PV loss and no offensive odour. On vaginal examination the cervix is 1 cm dilated, 1 cm long, firm in consistency, posterior in position, and the presenting part is at -3 station, giving a Bishop score of 3. She has not had any contractions and reports normal fetal movements.
