She is keen to maximise her chance of vaginal birth and to remain as ambulant as possible, and she asks about the safest first agent to use to begin induction at her cervical state.

data_table.Examination: Cervix: 1 cm dilated, 1 cm long, firm consistency, posterior position. Station -3. Cephalic, membranes intact.
data_table.Bishop score: Dilatation 1 (1), length 1 cm (2), consistency firm (0), position posterior (0), station -3 (0) = 3.
data_table.Past obstetric: One previous SVD at 39+4, no perineal trauma, no PPH, no instrumental.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial induction method?

options.text: Artificial rupture of membranes followed by an IV oxytocin infusion
Mechanical cervical ripening with a transcervical Foley balloon catheter as priming
Oxytocin infusion commenced at 2 mU/min and titrated to contractions
Misoprostol 200 microg oral every 2 hours until contractions established
Stretch and sweep at the bedside and discharge home for review in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Bishop score and selection of induction agent in an unfavourable cervix

stem:
A 39-year-old G2P1 at 39+0 with a BMI of 34 attends antenatal clinic. EDD has been confirmed by an 8-week scan. The fetus is cephalic, growth on the 50th centile, normal AFI and Dopplers, reassuring CTG today. Bishop score 4 (cervix 1 cm, 30%, firm, posterior, station -2). Booking BP 118/74, today 122/76 with no proteinuria. She has gestational diabetes diet-controlled with normal home glucose monitoring.

Her previous birth was a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 40 weeks with no complications. She is anxious about a long pregnancy but feels well. She asks about timing of induction.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74, HR 78, T 36.6, urinalysis negative.
data_table.Examination: Bishop 6. SFH 38 cm at 41+0. Reassuring CTG.
data_table.Investigations: 8-week dating scan confirms gestation. 36-week growth scan: 50th centile, normal AFI, normal Dopplers.

lead_in: Which evidence-based threshold best supports a recommendation to induce labour for this woman?

options.text: Maternal age >=35 alone independently justifies induction at 39 weeks regardless of other factors
Diet-controlled GDM with appropriate growth supports induction at 39-40+6 weeks to reduce stillbirth risk
BMI 34 alone is an evidence-based indication for induction before 39+0 weeks
Bishop score >=8 is required before induction can be offered at any gestation
Induction at 39+0 reduces caesarean section rates compared with expectant management to 41+0

subtopic_detail: Indications for induction of labour - post-dates threshold in Australian practice

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 at 39+6 is in spontaneous labour, currently 7 cm dilated, with oxytocin augmentation at 8 mU/min for slow progress between 5 and 7 cm. Contractions are 5 in 10 lasting 60 seconds, palpate strong with no tachysystole. She has an epidural with good analgesia. Maternal BP 110/68, HR 88, T 36.8. Liquor clear, ARM 4 hours ago.

The 36-week scan was unremarkable and GBS swab was negative. The CTG over the last 25 minutes shows a baseline of 150 bpm, variability of 5 to 8 bpm, no accelerations, and recurrent decelerations occurring with more than 50% of contractions. The decelerations begin gradually after the peak of each contraction, reach a nadir 60 seconds after the contraction peak and recover slowly after the contraction ends. There has been no prolonged deceleration and no vaginal bleeding. The obstetric registrar is at the bedside and theatre is available within 15 minutes.

data_table.CTG: Baseline 150, variability 5-8, no accelerations, recurrent late decelerations with >50% of contractions for 25 min.
data_table.Contractions: 5 in 10, 60 sec, strong on palpation. Oxytocin 8 mU/min.
data_table.Examination: 7 cm, +0 station, direct OA, clear liquor, no PV bleeding.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Continue oxytocin at current rate and repeat assessment in 30 minutes
Proceed immediately to a category 1 caesarean section in theatre now
Increase oxytocin to expedite delivery before further fetal compromise worsens further now
Stop oxytocin, left lateral, 500 mL IV crystalloid, exclude reversible causes, consider fetal scalp lactate
Administer terbutaline 250 microg subcutaneously for acute uterine tocolysis in this setting now

subtopic_detail: Management of recurrent late decelerations with intrauterine resuscitation

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 at 40+0 is in the active second stage at full dilatation following a 25-minute push, with an epidural providing good analgesia. The previous birth was an uncomplicated SVD. The fetus is cephalic with normal growth, and the GBS swab was negative. The CTG shortly before crowning showed a baseline of 140 bpm, variability 10, and mild variable decelerations recovering well.

Liquor is clear. The fetal head crowns and is delivered slowly with perineal support. A cord is palpated wrapped tightly around the neck. An attempt to slip the cord over the head fails because it is too tight and the loop cannot be loosened either way. The shoulders have not yet delivered and the head is in restitution to LOT.

No shoulder dystocia is recognised and the woman is pushing effectively with the next contraction expected within 30 to 60 seconds. The midwife asks the obstetric registrar what to do.

data_table.Examination: Head delivered, restituting to LOT. Tight nuchal cord, cannot be slipped over the head. No shoulder dystocia recognised.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Double-clamp and divide the umbilical cord immediately before delivery of the fetal shoulders begins
Apply firm traction to the fetal head to deliver the shoulders quickly before the cord tightens further
Ask the woman to stop pushing now and prepare for an emergency caesarean section
Cut the cord between two clamps only when shoulder dystocia is clearly diagnosed clinically
Perform somersault manoeuvre, keep the head close to maternal thigh as the body delivers, then unwind the cord

subtopic_detail: Management of a tight nuchal cord at delivery of the head

stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 40+2 is at full dilatation, head at +3 station, direct OA, distending the perineum. CTG has developed recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability for 12 minutes. The consultant has decided to perform a non-rotational Neville-Barnes forceps delivery in the room. Bladder empty, epidural topped up, consent obtained, paediatric team notified. EFW 3500 g, pelvis gynaecoid, head fully engaged. The registrar suggests cutting a midline episiotomy at the 12 o'clock position to maximise space.

data_table.Examination: Full dilatation, +3, direct OA, head distending perineum, no abdominal palpable head.
data_table.Indication: Non-rotational forceps for pathological CTG at +3.
data_table.Maternal: Epidural topped up, bladder empty, consent obtained, BMI 26.

lead_in: Which response is most appropriate regarding episiotomy in this birth?

options.text: Decline midline episiotomy; cut a mediolateral episiotomy at 60 degrees from the midline at crowning
Cut the midline episiotomy as the registrar suggests to maximise outlet space
Cut a mediolateral episiotomy at 30 degrees from the midline before crowning
Avoid episiotomy entirely as routine episiotomy is not recommended
Cut a J-shaped episiotomy starting midline then curving laterally at crowning

subtopic_detail: Episiotomy - indications and correct technique

stem:
A 25-year-old G1P0 at 40+4 has just had a spontaneous vaginal birth of a 4100 g infant with a mediolateral episiotomy following a 90-minute active second stage. Active management of the third stage has been completed with delivery of a complete placenta and intact membranes, with an estimated blood loss of 350 mL. On systematic per-vaginum and per-rectum examination by the obstetric registrar, there is a tear extending through the perineal skin, all layers of the perineal muscles, and approximately 60% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter complex.

The internal anal sphincter is identified as intact on PR examination, and the rectal mucosa is intact with no buttonhole tear. Bleeding is controlled with pressure, the woman is haemodynamically stable, and she has a working epidural that has been topped up. The registrar plans repair in theatre with appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis and postoperative care.

data_table.Examination: Tear through perineal skin, perineal muscles, partial external anal sphincter (~60% thickness). Internal anal sphincter intact on PR. Rectal mucosa intact, no buttonhole.
data_table.Maternal: BP 116/72, HR 84, working epidural, haemodynamically stable.

lead_in: Which classification and repair plan is correct?

options.text: Second-degree perineal tear, repaired on the labour ward using absorbable suture material as standard
Third-degree tear grade 3a, repair in theatre with end-to-end or overlap external anal sphincter repair
Third-degree tear grade 3c, repair in theatre with a separate internal anal sphincter repair done
Third-degree tear grade 3b, repair in theatre with end-to-end or overlap external sphincter repair plus antibiotics, laxatives and physio
Fourth-degree perineal tear, repaired in theatre with rectal mucosal closure as the first step

subtopic_detail: Perineal trauma classification and OASI repair principles

stem:
A 33-year-old G3P2 at 39+5 has just had an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal birth of a 3500 g infant. The baby is on the maternal chest, Apgar 9 at 1 minute, with delayed cord clamping at 90 seconds. Booked BP at 36 weeks was 138/86 and her booking BP today 1 hour ago was 145/92; she has been on labetalol for gestational hypertension since 32 weeks.

She has no proteinuria and was not on magnesium sulfate. Maternal observations are now BP 150/95, HR 90, EBL so far 200 mL, uterus palpable at the umbilicus. Active management of the third stage is planned per unit protocol.

data_table.Maternal: BP 150/95, HR 90, EBL so far 200 mL, uterus palpable at umbilicus.
data_table.Neonate: Apgar 9 at 1 min, on maternal chest, delayed cord clamping at 90 sec.
data_table.Risk factors for PPH: None: parity 3, no APH, no prolonged labour, no induction, no chorioamnionitis.

lead_in: Which uterotonic is the most appropriate component of active management for this woman?

options.text: Oxytocin 10 IU IM with delivery of the anterior shoulder, controlled cord traction and uterine massage
Syntometrine (ergometrine 500 microg + oxytocin 5 IU) IM with controlled cord traction and uterine massage
Ergometrine 500 microg IM with delivery of the anterior shoulder and uterine massage
Misoprostol 600 microg orally with controlled cord traction and uterine massage
Carbetocin 100 microg IV bolus with immediate cord clamping and uterine massage

subtopic_detail: Active management of the third stage of labour

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 at 40+1 has had a spontaneous vaginal birth of a 3400 g infant 45 minutes ago after a 7-hour labour with no oxytocin augmentation and no instrumental delivery. Active management of the third stage was performed with oxytocin 10 IU IM at delivery of the anterior shoulder, and controlled cord traction has been attempted multiple times by the experienced midwife and registrar without placental delivery.

There is no significant ongoing bleeding, total EBL is 350 mL. The uterus is palpable and contracted at the umbilicus and there is no apparent uterine inversion. The cord is intact, appears at the introitus, and shows no signs of having broken on traction. The woman has an epidural in situ that is providing good analgesia and remains haemodynamically stable.

Her previous birth was an uncomplicated SVD with a normal third stage 3 years ago. She had one D&C for a missed miscarriage at 10 weeks two years ago and an LLETZ for CIN2 four years ago. No previous caesarean. The placenta is therefore retained at 45 minutes despite active management with no third-stage haemorrhage. The midwife asks the obstetric registrar what should happen next, and the on-call consultant has been informed.

data_table.Maternal: BP 118/72, HR 86, EBL 350 mL, uterus contracted at umbilicus.
data_table.Third stage: 45 min, oxytocin 10 IU IM given, controlled cord traction unsuccessful.
data_table.Past history: One vaginal birth, one D&C for missed miscarriage, one LLETZ for CIN2.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue expectant management for a further 30 minutes given no significant bleeding evident
Inject 20 IU oxytocin diluted in 20 mL saline into the umbilical vein
Administer ergometrine 500 microg intramuscularly now and reattempt controlled cord traction in theatre
Perform manual removal at the bedside without anaesthesia since the woman has a working epidural
Transfer to theatre for manual placental removal under regional or general anaesthesia with IV antibiotics and oxytocin infusion

subtopic_detail: Retained placenta - timing and approach to manual removal

stem:
A 34-year-old G1P0 at 37+3 attends day assessment with a one-week history of frontal headaches not relieved by paracetamol and new BP elevation noted by her GP. Her booking BP was 110/68 and her booking BMI was 28, with no chronic hypertension, no renal disease, no autoimmune disease, no prior gestational hypertension and no family history of pre-eclampsia. Today her BP on arrival is 158/102 on repeat measurement 15 minutes apart in the seated position with an appropriately sized cuff, urine protein creatinine ratio is 65 mg/mmol, platelets are 145 x10^9/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, ALT 32 U/L, urate 0.39 mmol/L, and the fetus is appropriately grown on the 40th centile with normal umbilical artery Dopplers, normal AFI and a reassuring CTG.

She has had labetalol 200 mg orally with a fall to 142/92 after one hour and the headache has eased. There is no eclampsia, no epigastric pain, no visual disturbance, no clonus, no pulmonary oedema and no oliguria. On vaginal examination the cervix is closed, posterior, 2 cm long, firm, station -3, giving a Bishop score of 1. The on-call consultant reviews her in the unit and discusses options regarding admission, antihypertensive management, MgSO4 use and timing and route of delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/102 then 142/92 post-labetalol, HR 88, T 36.8, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Bloods: Platelets 145 x10^9/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, ALT 32 U/L, urate 0.39 mmol/L. uPCR 65 mg/mmol.
data_table.Fetal: 40th centile, normal Dopplers, normal AFI, reassuring CTG.
data_table.Cervix: Closed, posterior, 2 cm long, firm, station -3 (Bishop 1).

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home on oral labetalol with weekly clinic review until 39+0 then induce labour
Admit, continue oral antihypertensive to keep BP <140/90, induce labour this admission, MgSO4 only if severe features develop
Proceed to a category 2 caesarean section today given the unfavourable cervix on examination
Admit, give MgSO4 4 g loading then 1 g/h infusion regardless of severity, and induce labour now
Admit for 48 hours of betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 doses before any induction

subtopic_detail: Pre-eclampsia at term - timing of delivery and intrapartum management

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P1 at 39+0 attends in spontaneous labour at 5 cm. Her vaginorectal GBS screening swab at 36+2 was positive. Her previous birth was an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39+5 and the infant had no early-onset GBS sepsis and was discharged home well. She has a documented allergy to penicillin recorded in detail in her record as widespread urticarial rash starting 2 days into a course of amoxicillin for a dental infection three years ago, without angioedema, without wheeze, without hypotension and without anaphylaxis or hospitalisation.

Susceptibility testing on the GBS isolate from this pregnancy's swab is documented in the pathology report as susceptible to clindamycin and erythromycin. She has no other comorbidities, is afebrile, has a reassuring CTG, normal observations and no other risk factors for intrapartum infection. Membranes ruptured 30 minutes ago with clear liquor and CTG is reassuring with baseline 138, variability 10-15, accelerations and no decelerations. The midwife asks the resident which antibiotic regimen should be commenced now for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis.

data_table.Microbiology: GBS positive (vaginorectal swab 36+2). Isolate susceptible to clindamycin and erythromycin.
data_table.Allergy: Penicillin - widespread urticarial rash, no angioedema/wheeze/hypotension (non-severe, non-anaphylactic).
data_table.Labour: 5 cm, SROM 30 min ago, clear liquor, reassuring CTG.
data_table.Other risk factors: None: afebrile, no prolonged ROM, no preterm labour.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic regimen for GBS prophylaxis?

options.text: Benzylpenicillin 3 g IV loading then 1.8 g IV every 4 hours until delivery as prophylaxis
Clindamycin 600 mg IV every 8 hours until delivery as monotherapy intrapartum
Vancomycin 1 g IV every 8 hours until delivery as monotherapy intrapartum
Cefazolin 2 g IV loading then 1 g IV every 8 hours until delivery as prophylaxis
Oral amoxicillin 1 g every 8 hours until delivery as intrapartum prophylaxis

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis - regimen and penicillin allergy

stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 at 39+4 presents at 0200 with a sudden gush of clear fluid from the vagina that occurred 30 minutes ago while watching television. On sterile speculum examination there is a pool of clear amniotic fluid in the posterior fornix, with a positive fern test on a dried slide and a positive IGFBP-1 swab. There is no offensive odour and no PV bleeding visible.

The fetus is cephalic, the head is engaged on abdominal palpation, and the CTG is reassuring with a baseline of 138 bpm, good variability of 10-15 bpm, accelerations and no decelerations. The cervix is closed and 2 cm long on sterile speculum visualisation; digital examination has not been performed. She is afebrile at T 36.7, HR 78, BP 116/72 and her white cell count is 9 x10^9/L with CRP <5 mg/L.

Her booking BMI was 24, she has no medical comorbidities and her GBS vaginorectal swab at 36+1 was negative. She is having occasional irregular tightenings every 10-20 minutes but is not in established labour. She would prefer to avoid medical interventions if possible and is keen on as physiological a birth as is safe. The on-call obstetric registrar discusses her options.

data_table.Examination: SROM confirmed (pool, ferning, IGFBP-1 positive), clear liquor, no meconium, no foul odour, head engaged.

lead_in: Which best describes the optimal management plan for this woman?

options.text: Discharge home with daily review for up to 72 hours, then induce labour if not in labour
Offer immediate induction with oxytocin or expectant management to 24 hours, intrapartum GBS prophylaxis only if ROM >18 hours
Commence empirical IV ampicillin plus gentamicin immediately and induce labour with vaginal prostaglandin gel today
Perform digital vaginal examination to assess Bishop score and plan immediate caesarean section for delivery
Commence vaginal prostaglandin gel for cervical ripening overnight regardless of her stated preference now in admission

subtopic_detail: Term PROM - timing of induction versus expectant management

stem:
A 32-year-old G1P0 at 40+0 has been pushing actively in the second stage for 110 minutes with an epidural providing adequate sensory block. The fetal head is at +2 station, in direct OA, with no caput and no moulding on examination by the registrar. The CTG has developed recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability for 8 minutes, and the registrar wishes to expedite delivery.

The bladder has been catheterised and emptied, the maternal pelvis is clinically gynaecoid, and verbal consent for instrumental delivery in the room with theatre on standby has been obtained from the woman. Adequate epidural analgesia has been confirmed with cold testing, the paediatric team has been notified and the anaesthetist is in the room. The registrar applies Neville-Barnes forceps correctly with the operator's posterior wrist supported and performs three pulls with descent of the head from +2 to +3, and then no further descent on the fourth pull despite correct application, correct axis traction, and an effective maternal push with a contraction.

The fetal head has not yet crowned and the perineum is not yet stretched. The consultant is now at the bedside and reviews the scenario before deciding the next step.

data_table.Examination: Head +3 after three pulls, no further descent on fourth pull, direct OA, no caput/moulding initially.
data_table.CTG: Recurrent late decelerations, reduced variability, ongoing 8 min.
data_table.Maternal: Adequate epidural, bladder catheterised, consent obtained, theatre on standby, gynaecoid pelvis.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reapply forceps with a different cup angle and attempt two further pulls
Switch to a ventouse to complete delivery given the head is at +3
Transfer immediately to theatre for category 1 caesarean section with senior consultant present
Ask the mother to push without the forceps for one more contraction
Perform a symphysiotomy at the bedside to widen the pelvis for delivery

subtopic_detail: Operative vaginal delivery - prerequisites and failed forceps disposition

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 37+5 is in spontaneous labour. Twin 1 is cephalic and growth-appropriate on the 45th centile, twin 2 has been transverse throughout the third trimester on serial scans with the back inferior and is 200 g smaller than twin 1 (35th centile, within the 20% inter-twin discordance threshold and with no growth discordance suggestive of selective FGR).

There is no previous caesarean, no uterine surgery and no medical comorbidities. Both fetuses have reassuring CTGs on dual monitoring. The cervix is 6 cm, station of the leading twin is -1, membranes are intact for the leading twin and ARM has not been performed, and an experienced obstetric consultant with extensive twin delivery experience is available throughout the labour.

The anaesthetist is in the unit and an epidural has been sited and is providing good analgesia. She has expressed a clear preference for a vaginal birth if safe. After 4 hours she is fully dilated, twin 1 head is at +3, and she pushes for 25 minutes to deliver a 2900 g cephalic infant with normal Apgars. On bedside rescan by the consultant immediately after delivery of twin 1, twin 2 remains transverse with the back inferior.

The CTG of twin 2 is reassuring at this point, membranes of twin 2 are intact, and the consultant is at the bedside in the delivery suite with a theatre and a paediatric team on standby.

data_table.Antenatal: DCDA twins, twin 1 cephalic, twin 2 transverse back-inferior. EFW concordance within 20%.
data_table.After twin 1 delivery: Twin 2 remains transverse, back inferior, reassuring CTG, intact membranes.
data_table.Operator: Experienced consultant at bedside, theatre available, paediatrics on standby.
data_table.Maternal: Epidural in situ, good analgesia, haemodynamically stable.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step for delivery of twin 2?

options.text: Internal podalic version followed by breech extraction of twin 2
External cephalic version under ultrasound, then expect spontaneous cephalic delivery
Category 2 caesarean section for delivery of twin 2 now
Await spontaneous descent of twin 2 for up to 60 minutes before any intervention
Perform ARM of twin 2 membranes immediately to allow descent

subtopic_detail: Twin delivery - mode of birth with second twin non-cephalic

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P2 woman, three weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding her well term infant, presents to her GP with a 24-hour history of a tender, hot, wedge-shaped erythematous area in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. She feels feverish and shivery, has been continuing frequent feeds and effective expression after feeds, and the area has continued to enlarge over the last 12 hours.

There is no fluctuance, no skin breakdown and no axillary adenopathy. She is otherwise well. Her recorded drug allergy is to phenoxymethylpenicillin during childhood, when she developed an urticarial rash and lip swelling within 1 hour of a dose; she has never tolerated a penicillin or cephalosporin since. She has no other allergies, has not had antibiotics in the past 12 months, has no recent hospital contact and is not from a community with known high MRSA prevalence. She wishes to continue breastfeeding throughout treatment and her infant has no medical conditions and was born at term with no neonatal complications.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 degC, HR 104 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air.
data_table.Examination: Wedge-shaped erythema upper outer left breast, hot and tender, no fluctuance, no skin breakdown, no axillary lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis clear. Bedside ultrasound not yet performed.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate oral antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Flucloxacillin 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days
Cefalexin 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days
Clindamycin 450 mg orally three times daily for 7 days
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg orally twice daily for 7 days

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis - antibiotic choice in penicillin allergy

stem: A 27-year-old primipara, 6 weeks postpartum, exclusively breastfeeding her thriving term infant, attends with a 14-hour history of a discrete tender lump in the lower inner right breast. Overlying skin has faint pink mottling but no defined erythema. T 36.8, no rigors, no flu-like symptoms, infant feeding effectively. Recent change: baby has slept a longer 5-hour stretch the past two nights. No fluctuance, no axillary adenopathy. She has read online that 'aggressive deep massage' and 'pump-and-dump' are recommended.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 degC, HR 78 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16.
data_table.Examination: Tender 3 cm lump lower inner right breast, faint overlying pink mottling, no defined erythema, no fluctuance, no axillary adenopathy.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue feeding from both breasts on demand, apply cold packs between feeds, ibuprofen for pain, and review in 24 hours; avoid deep massage and pump-and-dump
Commence oral flucloxacillin 500 mg qid for 7 days now
Aggressive deep breast massage every 2 hours with hot compresses for 48 hours
Cease feeding from the affected breast and pump-and-dump for 48 hours
Urgent breast ultrasound and surgical referral for incision and drainage

subtopic_detail: Blocked duct vs inflammatory mastitis vs bacterial mastitis discrimination

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P3 woman, 4 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding, was diagnosed with right-breast bacterial mastitis 5 days ago and commenced flucloxacillin 500 mg orally four times daily with continued feeding and expression. Her fevers settled within 48 hours but the erythematous area has now developed a discrete, fluctuant tender lump over the past 24 hours despite ongoing antibiotics and effective drainage.

She is afebrile today, haemodynamically stable, and the skin overlying the lump is intact, non-necrotic and not under tension. Bedside ultrasound performed by the GP demonstrates a well-defined, unilocular hypoechoic collection measuring 38 mm x 24 mm at 1.5 cm depth, with no overlying skin necrosis. She has no recurrent abscess history, no immunosuppression breastfeeding. She is comfortable being managed in primary care if the lesion is amenable to office-based drainage and the local Breast Centre offers ultrasound-guided procedures on a same-day basis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 degC, HR 84 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg.
data_table.Examination: Right breast, 4 cm fluctuant tender mass, overlying skin intact and non-necrotic, no axillary adenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside USS: unilocular 38 x 24 mm hypoechoic collection, 1.5 cm depth, no skin necrosis. Hb 124 g/L, WCC 11.2 x10^9/L, CRP 48 mg/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue current oral flucloxacillin and review in 5 days without drainage
Refer for ultrasound-guided needle aspiration with culture; continue antibiotics, reaspirate if needed
Refer for theatre incision and drainage with packing under general anaesthetic
Stop breastfeeding from the affected breast and continue antibiotics only
Switch to oral clindamycin 450 mg three times daily and observe without drainage

subtopic_detail: Lactational breast abscess - drainage strategy

stem:
A 28-year-old primiparous woman attends with her 3-week-old term infant for a same-day appointment because she is convinced her milk supply has dropped. The baby is now feeding for 60-80 minutes per feed, 10-12 times in 24 hours, and is unsettled between feeds. She produces only 30 mL when she expresses after a feed and feels her breasts are softer than they were at 10 days.

The infant had a birthweight of 3.4 kg, was discharged at 3.15 kg on day 4 (regained birthweight by day 12), and today weighs 3.55 kg on the practice scales. The infant is alert, has 6-8 heavy wet nappies and 3-4 mustard-yellow stools per day, has no jaundice, and feeds with audible swallowing during feeds. She has been advised by family to start formula top-ups.

She is not on any medications, has no breast surgery history, has normal-appearing breasts that grew through pregnancy, and breastfed her older nieces' children briefly without difficulty.

data_table.Infant assessment: Birthweight 3.4 kg; day 4 discharge 3.15 kg; today 3.55 kg (mean gain ~30 g/day from nadir).
data_table.Feeding: 10-12 feeds/24h, audible swallowing, 6-8 heavy wet nappies, 3-4 mustard stools/day.
data_table.Maternal: Soft breasts, no surgery, infant alert.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence formula top-ups of 60 mL after each breastfeed to meet caloric requirements
Reassure: growth, nappy output and feeding behaviour indicate adequate transfer; review in 1 week
Commence domperidone 10 mg three times daily as a pharmacological galactagogue
Arrange measured pre-feed and post-feed test-weighs over 24 hours at home
Refer for maternal pituitary MRI to exclude Sheehan syndrome as the cause

subtopic_detail: Low milk supply - first step in assessment

stem:
A 30-year-old primiparous woman attends the GP at 3 weeks postpartum with her term infant. She has persistent bilateral cracked, bleeding nipples that have not improved despite three lactation consultant reviews focused on positioning and attachment; the latch has been optimised across multiple holds and she has tried nipple shields without lasting benefit. Feeds last 50-70 minutes and the infant frequently breaks suction with a clicking sound.

Infant weight gain has fallen below the expected trajectory: birthweight 3.5 kg, discharge weight 3.25 kg, today's weight 3.4 kg at 3 weeks (mean gain ~10 g/day from nadir, below the 20-30 g/day threshold). On examination by an experienced lactation consultant, the infant has a thin anterior tongue frenulum that restricts tongue elevation to less than midline when crying, a heart-shaped tongue tip when the tongue is lifted, and a Hazelbaker tongue-function score that meets criteria for ankyloglossia with impaired function. The infant has no other oral, craniofacial or neurological abnormalities and is otherwise well.

data_table.Infant assessment: Birthweight 3.5 kg, nadir 3.25 kg, today 3.4 kg at day 21 (~10 g/day from nadir, below threshold).
data_table.Feeding: 50-70 min feeds, audible clicking, nipple trauma persists.
data_table.Examination: Restricted tongue elevation, heart-shaped tongue tip, Hazelbaker confirms functionally significant anterior tongue tie.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to an experienced clinician for assessment and frenotomy of the anterior tongue tie
Continue positioning and attachment optimisation for another 4 weeks before considering frenotomy
Commence formula top-ups and discontinue breastfeeding given the persistent nipple trauma
Refer for posterior tongue tie and upper-lip tie release out of hours regardless of findings
Prescribe long-term nipple shields and review at the 6-week postnatal check

subtopic_detail: Tongue tie - indications for frenotomy referral

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P2 woman, 5 days post-vaginal birth of a healthy term infant, presents to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of pleuritic right-sided chest pain, mild dyspnoea on exertion and a swollen tender right calf. Bedside observations and ECG are detailed below. CTPA confirms a segmental right lower lobe pulmonary embolus and Doppler ultrasound shows acute right popliteal-femoral DVT.

She has no haemodynamic instability, no right heart strain and no hypoxia at rest. She is exclusively breastfeeding her term, well infant and is highly motivated to continue. She has no other medical conditions, takes no medications, has no allergies, no history of bleeding disorder and her postnatal Hb is 118 g/L with normal platelets, INR and APTT.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, T 37.0 degC.
data_table.Investigations: CTPA: segmental RLL PE. Doppler: right popliteal-femoral DVT. Hb 118 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, APTT 32 s, eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m2.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulant regimen?

options.text: Therapeutic enoxaparin transitioning to warfarin with bridging until INR therapeutic; continue breastfeeding
Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, continuing breastfeeding
Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily, continuing breastfeeding
Unfractionated heparin infusion only with discontinuation of breastfeeding for the treatment period
Aspirin 100 mg daily and graduated compression stockings as primary treatment for VTE

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation choice in breastfeeding mother

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P2 woman is reviewed in the GP-IBCLC combined clinic at 5 weeks postpartum with confirmed insufficient milk supply contributing to faltering infant growth despite four weeks of structured input. Positioning and attachment have been optimised, frequency of feeds increased, post-feed expression added, and a structural cause has been excluded (no tongue tie, no breast surgery, normal thyroid). Infant weight gain remains below 20 g/day with documented inadequate transfer on test-weighs over 24 hours.

The mother wishes to use a galactagogue as adjunctive therapy to maintain breastfeeding while continuing the non-pharmacological measures. She has no personal cardiac history, but on review of her medications she takes citalopram 20 mg daily for anxiety. Her resting baseline ECG today shows sinus rhythm at 78 bpm with QTc 460 ms (Bazett) and normal electrolytes including K+ 4.4 mmol/L and Mg2+ 0.85 mmol/L. She has no family history of sudden cardiac death and no syncope. The IBCLC asks specifically whether domperidone is appropriate in her situation.

data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm 78 bpm, QTc 460 ms (Bazett), no AV block.
data_table.Electrolytes: K+ 4.4 mmol/L, Mg2+ 0.85 mmol/L, Ca2+ corrected 2.35 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Citalopram 20 mg daily.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding domperidone?

options.text: Commence domperidone 10 mg three times daily for 7 days as a galactagogue
Avoid domperidone; review citalopram with her psychiatrist and intensify non-pharmacological measures
Increase domperidone dose to 20 mg four times daily to maximise the milk yield
Substitute metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily as a long-term galactagogue
Commence fenugreek 600 mg three times daily as a herbal galactagogue without other changes

subtopic_detail: Domperidone as galactagogue - safety considerations

stem: A 71-year-old G4P4 postmenopausal woman attends a urogynaecology outpatient clinic with 18 months of progressive vaginal pressure that is now associated with a visible bulge at the introitus when she stands at the end of the day, occasional difficulty completing defaecation that improves when she splints the posterior vaginal wall, and intermittent urinary hesitancy. Speculum and POP-Q examination on maximal Valsalva in the supine position record the following measurements: Aa -1, Ba +1, C +3, GH 5 cm, PB 3 cm, TVL 9 cm, Ap -2, Bp -2, D +1. The most dependent point of prolapse is therefore the cervix at +3 cm beyond the hymen.

data_table.POP-Q (supine, Valsalva): Aa -1, Ba +1, C +3, GH 5, PB 3, TVL 9, Ap -2, Bp -2, D +1.
data_table.Examination: Cervix descends 3 cm beyond hymen; anterior and posterior walls supported at hymen or above; PVR 30 mL.

lead_in: Which is the most accurate description of this prolapse?

options.text: POP-Q stage 2 anterior compartment prolapse (cystocele)
POP-Q stage 3 apical (uterine) prolapse
POP-Q stage 4 complete vaginal vault eversion
POP-Q stage 3 posterior compartment prolapse (rectocele)
POP-Q stage 1 mixed compartment prolapse

subtopic_detail: POP-Q staging and compartment identification

stem:
A 64-year-old G3P3 postmenopausal woman attends urogynaecology with 12 months of progressive vaginal vault prolapse 9 years after a total abdominal hysterectomy for benign menorrhagia. She has previously trialled a ring pessary for 6 months with recurrent expulsion despite refit, and supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy for 4 months with no symptomatic benefit. POP-Q examination shows vaginal vault descent to +4 with anterior wall to +2 and posterior wall to 0; TVL is 8 cm.

She is sexually active and wishes to preserve coital function; she has no obesity-related surgical risk (BMI 24), no significant cardiopulmonary disease, no diabetes and is otherwise healthy.

data_table.History: TAH 9 years ago. Pessary failed (recurrent expulsion). PFMT 4 months no benefit. Sexually active, BMI 24, no comorbidities.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate surgical procedure?

options.text: Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy with type 1 polypropylene mesh fixed to the anterior sacral ligament
Transvaginal mesh kit repair of the vaginal vault using a synthetic mesh device
Sacrospinous ligament fixation of the vaginal vault through a vaginal surgical approach
Le Fort colpocleisis with obliteration of the vagina for definitive vault support
Repeat pessary trial with a Gellhorn pessary plus indefinite topical oestrogen therapy

subtopic_detail: Vault prolapse after hysterectomy - surgical choice

stem:
A 78-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 24) presents to her GP with 9 months of urinary urgency, urge incontinence approximately twice daily and nocturia 3 times. She has had a structured trial of bladder training and supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy for 12 weeks under a continence nurse, with caffeine and evening fluid restriction implemented, and reports modest but inadequate improvement.

There is no stress component on her bladder diary, no haematuria, and PVR is 30 mL. Urinalysis is clear; recent FBC, UEC, glucose and Ca2+ are normal. She has well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg, no untreated narrow-angle glaucoma, no severe constipation and her resting heart rate is 72 bpm with BP 134/82 mmHg. She does not have severe uncontrolled hypertension. She is concerned about adding medications that might worsen her memory. Her geriatrician and GP agree to add pharmacotherapy to her ongoing conservative measures.

data_table.Bladder diary: Urgency, urge UI x2/day, nocturia x3, no stress component. PVR 30 mL.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate pharmacological agent?

options.text: Oxybutynin immediate-release 5 mg orally twice a day
Mirabegron 25 mg orally daily, titrating to 50 mg if needed
Solifenacin 5 mg orally daily as a long-acting antimuscarinic
Duloxetine 40 mg orally twice daily for the urinary symptoms
Desmopressin 0.1 mg orally at night for the urge incontinence

subtopic_detail: Urge incontinence pharmacological choice in older woman

stem:
A 52-year-old G3P3 woman attends with 12 months of urinary leakage. On a 3-day bladder diary she records: 8 leakage episodes total - 6 preceded by sudden urgency (mostly on the way to the toilet or hearing running water), and 2 small-volume leaks on coughing or sneezing. Daytime void frequency is 9, nocturia 2, urgency score on Patient Perception of Bladder Condition is severe, and quality-of-life impact is dominated by the urge episodes (she has stopped attending her grandson's school events because of fear of leakage with running to a toilet).

PVR is 40 mL, urinalysis is negative, and a cough stress test reproduces a small leak with full bladder. BMI 31, no smoking, no relevant medications. She declines surgery at this stage and has not yet had any structured conservative therapy or pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Bladder diary: 8 leakage episodes; 6 urge, 2 stress. Frequency 9, nocturia 2.
data_table.Tests: PVR 40 mL, urinalysis negative, cough stress test +ve (small leak).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management approach?

options.text: PFMT, bladder training, weight loss and caffeine reduction; review at 3 months
Refer immediately for a tension-free vaginal tape mid-urethral sling procedure
Commence an antimuscarinic plus duloxetine combination from the outset of management
Refer for invasive urodynamic studies before offering any conservative management
Insert a continence pessary and commence indefinite topical oestrogen therapy

subtopic_detail: Mixed urinary incontinence - prioritising treatment by predominant symptom

stem:
A 72-year-old G3P3 postmenopausal woman with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.4%, on metformin + dapagliflozin) presents with 6 months of small-volume continuous urinary leakage, daytime urinary frequency 12, nocturia 4 with leakage on rising, and a sensation of incomplete emptying. She has no urgency that precedes the leakage. Her GP has been treating her empirically as urge incontinence with oxybutynin for 8 weeks with worsening of her leakage.

On examination she has a palpable bladder to the umbilicus, mildly impaired ankle reflexes with reduced light touch and pinprick over both feet bilaterally, and no costovertebral angle tenderness. Speculum reveals a stage 2 cystocele to the hymen with no other prolapse. Urinalysis: protein 1+, no nitrites, no leucocytes. Bedside bladder scan post-void shows a PVR of 720 mL. Bloods: Hb 118 g/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 88), eGFR 36 mL/min/1.73m2 (down from 68), K+ 5.3 mmol/L, HbA1c 8.4%. Renal tract ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/84 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, T 36.5 degC.
data_table.Examination: Palpable bladder to umbilicus, peripheral neuropathy, stage 2 cystocele.
data_table.Investigations: PVR 720 mL on bladder scan. Creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 88), eGFR 36, K+ 5.3 mmol/L. Renal USS: bilateral hydronephrosis. Urinalysis: protein 1+, no infection.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease oxybutynin, insert indwelling catheter and refer urgently to urology
Add mirabegron 50 mg daily to the oxybutynin and review again in 4 weeks
Refer for urgent mid-urethral sling surgery for presumed stress urinary incontinence now
Commence furosemide 40 mg daily to manage her presumed nocturnal polyuria
Arrange outpatient urodynamics in 6 weeks and continue current therapy unchanged

subtopic_detail: Overflow incontinence with chronic urinary retention

stem:
A 55-year-old G3P3 woman is referred to urogynaecology after 12 months of stress urinary incontinence symptoms refractory to a documented 6-month program of supervised pelvic floor muscle training and weight loss (lost 7 kg, BMI now 28). Her bladder diary shows leakage with cough/sneeze/exertion only, no urgency or urge episodes, no voiding difficulty. PVR is 20 mL and a positive cough stress test reproduces leakage in clinic.

There is no haematuria and no recurrent UTI; POP-Q examination shows Ba -1 (no prolapse beyond the hymen). She has been counselled about a mid-urethral sling and an autologous fascial sling and is keen to proceed surgically. She has not had urodynamic studies. The clinical fellow asks whether urodynamics should be performed before sling surgery. She has not had any previous incontinence surgery, no pelvic radiotherapy and no relevant neurological disease.

data_table.Diary: Pure stress symptoms; no urgency or urge.
data_table.Tests: PVR 20 mL, positive cough stress test, no prolapse beyond hymen.
data_table.Trials: 6 months PFMT + 7 kg weight loss without resolution.

lead_in: Which approach to urodynamics is most consistent with current guidance?

options.text: Routine urodynamic studies in every woman before any incontinence surgery
Urodynamics not required before primary sling here; reserve for mixed or complex
Urodynamic studies only after a failed primary mid-urethral sling procedure
Urodynamic studies required only when the post-void residual exceeds 100 mL
Urodynamics is mandatory whenever any pharmacotherapy is being considered

subtopic_detail: Indications for urodynamic studies

stem:
A 48-year-old G3P3 woman attends the gynaecology outpatient clinic 4 weeks after a total laparoscopic hysterectomy for symptomatic fibroids. The procedure was complicated by adhesions at the vesicouterine peritoneum requiring sharp dissection from the bladder; the surgeon documented bladder integrity at the end of the case using bladder filling without leak observed. For the past 8 days she has had continuous painless watery leakage into her underwear regardless of position or activity, with no urge, no stress trigger, and unchanged daytime voids of normal volume.

There is no fever, no flank pain. Urinalysis is negative for blood, nitrites and leucocytes. Speculum examination reveals clear fluid pooling in the vaginal vault but no visible defect on direct inspection. The vault is well healed; there is no apparent vault dehiscence. She is on no medications other than recent post-operative paracetamol and is otherwise well.

data_table.History: Continuous painless watery leakage 8 days after TLH complicated by bladder dissection.
data_table.Examination: Clear fluid in vault, no visible defect, vault intact.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis clear, no infection, no haematuria.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Three-swab dye test: instil dilute methylene blue into the bladder and inspect vaginal swabs
Empirical oral antibiotics for 7 days then outpatient review of the leakage pattern
Urodynamic studies as first-line to characterise the pattern of continuous leakage
MRI pelvis with rectal contrast to define the suspected genitourinary tract fistula
Outpatient pelvic floor physiotherapy with re-review in 3 months without imaging

subtopic_detail: Vesicovaginal fistula - diagnostic approach

stem:
A 38-year-old woman with HIV (CD4 540, viral load undetectable on ART) is referred to a vulval clinic with 9 months of mild vulval pruritus. Examination shows two well-demarcated, slightly raised, pigmented and acetowhite plaques on the right labium minus measuring 8 mm and 12 mm, with no ulceration, induration or vascular atypia. There is no clitoral hood resorption, no labial fusion and no porcelain-white skin.

Vulvoscopy-directed punch biopsy from each lesion shows high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (vulvar HSIL, also called usual-type VIN) with full-thickness dysplasia, koilocytotic change and p16 block-positive immunohistochemistry consistent with HPV-driven disease; there is no invasion, no microinvasion and no features of differentiated VIN (no basal atypia on a background of lichen sclerosus). She has had previous CIN 2 treated by LLETZ 5 years ago and is up to date with HPV-based cervical screening.

She is sexually active with one partner, both fully HPV-vaccinated, no immunosuppressive medications other than ART, no other comorbidities and is keen to preserve vulval anatomy if possible.

data_table.Lesions: Two pigmented/acetowhite plaques right labium minus (8 mm and 12 mm), no induration.
data_table.Histology: Vulvar HSIL (uVIN), p16 block-positive (HPV-driven), no invasion.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Topical imiquimod 5% three times weekly for up to 16 weeks
Watchful waiting with annual vulvoscopy and no active treatment
Radical vulvectomy with bilateral inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy for vulval HSIL
Topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment to lesions for 12 weeks
Topical 5-fluorouracil cream applied daily indefinitely as primary therapy

subtopic_detail: VIN - management of HSIL (uVIN) vs differentiated VIN

stem:
A 28-year-old nulliparous woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively painful right vulval swelling, now interfering with walking. T 37.1, no rigors, no STI symptoms. Examination: 4 cm fluctuant tender mass at the right posterolateral introitus (5 o'clock) consistent with a Bartholin abscess; intact non-necrotic skin, no cellulitis spreading beyond. This is her THIRD Bartholin abscess at the same site in the last 12 months.

The two previous episodes were treated with simple incision and drainage with packing, and both recurred within 3 months. She is otherwise well, on no medications, and wants definitive treatment that minimises further recurrence.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.1 degC, HR 84 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg.
data_table.Examination: 4 cm fluctuant tender mass right posterolateral introitus at 5 o'clock, intact non-necrotic skin, no cellulitis.
data_table.History: No prior Bartholin episodes, no STI symptoms.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Simple incision and drainage with packing under local anaesthetic
Marsupialisation under general anaesthetic
Word catheter insertion under local anaesthetic for 4-6 weeks
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days without drainage
Excision of the Bartholin gland as primary management

Epilepsy - preconception folate dose
stem:
A 27-year-old woman with focal epilepsy attends her GP for preconception counselling. She has been seizure-free for 4 years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily as monotherapy, prescribed by her neurologist who has been unable to wean her without seizure recurrence. She is in a stable relationship, drinks no alcohol, BMI 24, no other medications. There is no personal or family history of neural tube defects.

She wishes to conceive within the next 6 months and has not yet started any vitamins. She has read online that 'folic acid 5 mg' is recommended in epilepsy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, weight 68 kg, BMI 24 kg/m2.
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable, no neurocutaneous markers, no goitre.
data_table.Medications: Lamotrigine 200 mg BD. No other medications. No allergies.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preconception advice?

options.text: Continue valproate, start folic acid 5 mg daily and aim to conceive in 6 months
Refer to neurology for transition to a less teratogenic antiepileptic (e.g. lamotrigine or levetiracetam) and start folic acid 5 mg daily, deferring conception until stable on the new agent
Stop valproate today without neurology input and start folic acid 400 mcg daily
Continue valproate and add lamotrigine to allow pregnancy on combination therapy
Continue valproate and start folic acid 400 mcg daily, the standard dose for low-risk women

subtopic_detail: Asthma - continuation of inhaled corticosteroid
stem: A 24-year-old G1P0 at 9 weeks gestation has had asthma since childhood, well-controlled on budesonide 200 mcg bd plus salbutamol PRN. Over the past month she has needed reliever 4-5 times per week with two episodes of nocturnal cough. Spirometry today: FEV1 78% predicted (baseline 95% pre-pregnancy). No infective symptoms, no exposure changes. She tells you a friend advised her to stop the budesonide because 'steroids cross the placenta'. She is up to date with influenza vaccination and folic acid.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 99% on air.
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no wheeze, peak flow at her usual personal best.
data_table.Medications: Budesonide 200 micrograms BD inhaled, salbutamol 100 micrograms PRN.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her asthma now?

options.text: Continue current budesonide 200 mcg bd and reassess in 4 weeks
Step up inhaled corticosteroid (e.g. budesonide-formoterol combination) per the Australian Asthma Handbook and continue throughout pregnancy
Stop budesonide and use salbutamol alone for the duration of pregnancy
Switch to oral prednisolone 10 mg daily for the duration of pregnancy
Switch to montelukast 10 mg daily as monotherapy

subtopic_detail: Acute severe asthma in pregnancy - escalation
stem:
A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 28 weeks gestation presents to the obstetric assessment unit with two days of worsening cough, breathlessness and wheeze on a background of moderate persistent asthma. She had a viral upper respiratory infection last week and her partner had similar symptoms. She is on budesonide/formoterol 200/6 micrograms twice daily and reports using salbutamol every 30 minutes overnight without sustained relief.

She has had two previous emergency department presentations with asthma in the last 18 months but no ICU admissions and no history of intubation. She has no fevers, no chest painal movements; she received corticosteroid coverage for lung maturity two days ago at booking with respiratory. On arrival 30 minutes ago she was given continuous nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 500 micrograms, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and high flow oxygen titrated to SpO2 95%, with minimal subjective improvement.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 32, HR 132 bpm, BP 134/86 mmHg, T 37.4 degC, SpO2 94% on 8 L/min mask, peak flow 38% of personal best.
data_table.Examination: Sitting forward, audible wheeze, accessory muscle use, unable to complete full sentences. SFH 28 cm, CTG normal baseline 140 with variability and accelerations.
data_table.Investigations: ABG on 8 L: pH 7.36, PaCO2 36 mmHg, PaO2 78 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 3.4 mmol/L. CXR (with shielding): hyperinflated, no consolidation.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next pharmacological step in management?

options.text: Oral leukotriene receptor antagonist loading dose of montelukast 20 mg
Intravenous aminophylline loading dose then maintenance infusion
Subcutaneous adrenaline 500 micrograms intramuscular every 5 minutes
Emergency caesarean delivery to improve maternal oxygenation now
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes once now

subtopic_detail: Hypothyroidism - thyroxine dose escalation on confirming pregnancy
stem:
A 33-year-old woman with primary hypothyroidism after thyroidectomy for benign multinodular goitre two years ago presents at 6 weeks of a confirmed singleton pregnancy. She has been stable on levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily for 18 months with TSH consistently between 1.2 and 1.8 mIU/L. Her last TSH four months ago was 1.4 mIU/L. She conceived spontaneously after stopping the combined oral contraceptive eight weeks ago and reports nausea but no vomiting.

She has no other medical problems and is on no other regular medications. She has commenced folic acid 500 micrograms daily and iodine 150 micrograms daily as advised by her GP. She has not yet had pregnancy bloods drawn and asks whether she should change her thyroxine dose now or wait for the booking blood results, which she will have done in the next few days. She has not had any change in body weight, energy, cold tolerance or constipation. There is no family history of thyroid autoimmunity.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, weight 64 kg.
data_table.Examination: Well, no goitre (thyroidectomy scar healed), no proximal weakness, reflexes normal.
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods not yet returned. Last TSH 4 months ago 1.4 mIU/L (free T4 within range).
data_table.Medications: Levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, folic acid 500 micrograms, iodine 150 micrograms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate adjustment to her levothyroxine?

options.text: Maintain 100 micrograms daily and recheck TSH in 4 weeks
Stop iodine supplementation because she is taking levothyroxine
Double the dose to 200 micrograms daily and recheck in 6 weeks
Switch to liothyronine 20 micrograms three times daily here
Increase to approximately 125 micrograms daily and recheck TSH in 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: Graves disease - antithyroid choice by trimester
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman with Graves disease diagnosed 18 months ago is reviewed at her booking visit at 7 weeks gestation. Initial treatment was with propylthiouracil and propranolol, but she was switched to carbimazole 10 mg daily six months ago after biochemical control was achieved and has remained euthyroid since. Her TSH is 2.1 mIU/L and free T4 is within range on bloods drawn yesterday.

She has no eye signs and no goitre on examination today. TSH receptor antibody titre four months ago was mildly elevated at 2.5 IU/L (cut-off 1.75 IU/L).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/64 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, weight 68 kg.
data_table.Examination: No goitre, no exophthalmos, no tremor, no proximal weakness.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mIU/L, free T4 within range, TRAb 2.5 IU/L 4 months ago (mildly raised).
data_table.Medications: Carbimazole 10 mg daily, folic acid 500 micrograms, pregnancy multivitamin.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her antithyroid medication for this stage of pregnancy?

options.text: Continue carbimazole 10 mg daily throughout the pregnancy and recheck thyroid function tests every trimester
Refer for definitive radioactive iodine ablation this week and commence levothyroxine replacement therapy immediately afterwards
Stop all antithyroid medication now and monitor maternal TSH and free T4 every two weeks until delivery
Switch to propylthiouracil now and review at the start of the second trimester for return to carbimazole
Add propranolol 40 mg three times daily to her current carbimazole and continue both throughout pregnancy

subtopic_detail: SLE - anti-Ro/La and neonatal lupus risk
stem:
A 30-year-old G2P0 woman with SLE diagnosed seven years ago is reviewed in a combined obstetric medicine clinic at 11 weeks gestation. She has been in clinical remission for two years on hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily and low dose prednisolone 5 mg daily. Her one previous pregnancy ended in a first-trimester miscarriage at 9 weeks with no known cause identified at the time.

Her most recent rheumatology bloods three months ago confirmed normal complement, negative dsDNA, and positive anti-Ro at 120 U/mL (positive >10) and positive anti-La at 70 U/mL. She has no past history of lupus nephritis, no thromboembolism and her antiphospholipid antibody screen has been repeatedly negative on three occasions over the last two years. She has commenced folic acid 5 mg daily and aspirin 100 mg daily for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis at 11 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/64 mmHg, HR 70 bpm, weight 62 kg.
data_table.Examination: No active joint synovitis, no rash, no oral ulcers.
data_table.Investigations: Anti-Ro 120 U/mL positive, anti-La 70 U/mL positive, dsDNA negative, C3/C4 normal, APL screen repeatedly negative, urine PCR 3 mg/mmol.
data_table.Medications: Hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily, prednisolone 5 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, folic acid 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which surveillance plan is the most appropriate addition for this pregnancy?

options.text: Serial fetal echocardiograms from 16 to 28 weeks for congenital heart block
Stop hydroxychloroquine at the start of the second trimester now
Empirical IVIG infusions from 16 weeks to prevent congenital heart block
Stop aspirin because anti-Ro positive SLE increases bleeding risk
Routine empirical low molecular weight heparin from 12 weeks gestation

subtopic_detail: HIV - mode of delivery decision by viral load
stem:
A 30-year-old G1P0 woman with HIV diagnosed three years ago attends her 36 week obstetric review. She has been on combination antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir disoproxil, emtricitabine and dolutegravir) since diagnosis and has been virologically suppressed throughout this pregnancy. Her viral load four weeks ago was undetectable (<20 copies/mL) and her CD4 count was 620 cells/microlitre. She has no opportunistic infections, no co-infections (HBV and HCV negative) and no other comorbidities.

Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated with a normally grown cephalic fetus on the 50th centile and reassuring serial umbilical artery Dopplers. She wishes to plan a vaginal birth and asks the obstetric registrar what the recommendation is regarding mode of delivery given her status and her preference. She has no obstetric contraindications to vaginal birth and there are no concerns on CTG today. She has not yet ruptured membranes and is not in labour. The infectious diseases physician has been co-managing her care.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 114/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: SFH 36 cm, cephalic, FHR 140, longitudinal lie.
data_table.Investigations: HIV viral load <20 copies/mL at 36 weeks, CD4 620 cells/microlitre, HBV/HCV negative, syphilis negative.
data_table.Medications: Tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine/dolutegravir once daily, pregnancy multivitamin.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation regarding mode of delivery?

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean section at 38 weeks regardless of viral load
Plan a vaginal birth at term with continuation of antiretroviral therapy
Stop antiretroviral therapy two weeks before planned vaginal birth
Plan an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks plus intravenous zidovudine
Induction of labour at 37 weeks to minimise duration of ruptured membranes

subtopic_detail: HIV - infant prophylaxis and feeding choice in Australia
stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 woman with HIV diagnosed prior to pregnancy is reviewed postnatally on the maternity ward six hours after a normal vaginal birth at 39+2 weeks of a 3.2 kg infant. She has been on combination antiretroviral therapy throughout pregnancy and her most recent HIV viral load at 36 weeks was <20 copies/mL. The infant is well and feeding cues are emerging.

She is hepatitis B surface antigen negative and hepatitis C negative. She has no other comorbidities and her partner is HIV negative and on PrEP. She lives in a major Australian city, has stable housing, a refrigerator, reliable formula supply and supportive family. She asks the midwife about safe feeding choices and what medication, if any, the baby needs. The neonatologist is also reviewing the infant and confirms the baby is well, term and not requiring resuscitation. The infectious diseases physician has been involved throughout pregnancy and is available to discuss the neonatal plan.

data_table.Vital signs (mother): BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.8 degC, well.
data_table.Vital signs (neonate): HR 138 bpm, RR 40, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 98% on air, weight 3.2 kg.
data_table.Investigations: Maternal HIV VL <20 copies/mL at 36 weeks. HBsAg negative. HCV antibody negative.

lead_in: Which combination of advice and prophylaxis is most appropriate for this infant in an Australian setting?

options.text: Formula feeding plus oral triple antiretroviral therapy to the infant for 6 weeks
Exclusive breastfeeding for six months plus oral zidovudine for the infant
Exclusive formula feeding plus oral zidovudine monotherapy for 2-4 weeks
Mixed feeding (breast and formula) plus zidovudine to the infant for 2 weeks
Exclusive formula feeding alone with no antiretroviral prophylaxis required

subtopic_detail: Hepatitis B - infant immunoprophylaxis and maternal tenofovir
stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman who emigrated to Australia from a high HBV prevalence country is reviewed at 26 weeks gestation in the obstetric medicine clinic. She was diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B 8 years ago during routine antenatal screening in her first pregnancy. She is HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, anti-HBe negative, and her HBV DNA at 24 weeks is 2.3 x 10^8 IU/mL.

Her ALT is 28 U/L, platelets 220 x10^9/L, INR 1.0 and her FibroScan was 5.6 kPa six months ago, consistent with minimal hepatic fibrosis. She has no co-infection with HIV, HCV or HDV on booking serology and no clinical features of chronic liver disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, SFH 26 cm.
data_table.Investigations: HBsAg+, HBeAg+, anti-HBe-, HBV DNA 2.3 x 10^8 IU/mL, ALT 28 U/L, platelets 220, INR 1.0, FibroScan 5.6 kPa (low fibrosis).
data_table.Medications: None.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate maternal intervention to reduce vertical transmission in this pregnancy?

options.text: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin to the mother at 28 weeks gestation
Entecavir 0.5 mg daily from 28 weeks until 4-12 weeks postpartum
Tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg daily from 28 weeks until 4-12 weeks postpartum
Routine elective caesarean section at 39 weeks to reduce transmission risk
Advise no breastfeeding because of high maternal HBV DNA levels here

subtopic_detail: Hepatitis C - antenatal counselling and breastfeeding
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman with chronic hepatitis C diagnosed two years ago presents at her booking visit at 10 weeks gestation. She acquired HCV through past injecting drug use and has been abstinent for three years with current support from an addiction medicine service. Her HCV RNA is 5.2 x 10^5 IU/mL with genotype 1a and ALT 32 U/L. She has no co-infection with HIV or HBV.

Her liver synthetic function is preserved with INR 1.0, albumin 38 g/L, platelets 220 x10^9/L and a FibroScan of 5.1 kPa nine months ago indicating minimal fibrosis. She has not commenced direct-acting antiviral therapy. She has no other medical issues, takes folic acid 500 micrograms daily and has no allergies. She is in stable accommodation with her supportive partner who is HCV antibody negative. She asks the obstetric team about treatment in pregnancy, vertical transmission risk and whether she will be able to breastfeed her baby.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 76 bpm.
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no chronic liver disease stigmata.
data_table.Investigations: HCV RNA 5.2 x 10^5 IU/mL, genotype 1a, ALT 32 U/L, albumin 38 g/L, INR 1.0, platelets 220, FibroScan 5.1 kPa.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate advice to give now?

options.text: Defer direct-acting antiviral therapy and plan breastfeeding once nipples intact
Start sofosbuvir/velpatasvir at 12 weeks and continue for 12 weeks total
Plan elective caesarean section at 39 weeks to reduce vertical transmission
Advise no breastfeeding because of detectable HCV RNA in her serum
Test the newborn with HCV antibody within 48 hours of delivery here

subtopic_detail: ITP - platelet threshold for neuraxial anaesthesia
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman with ITP diagnosed three years ago presents to obstetric day assessment at 36 weeks gestation. Her ITP has previously responded to oral prednisolone but she has been off all therapy for the past 12 months with platelet counts between 90 and 110 x10^9/L. Today her routine bloods show a platelet count of 72 x10^9/L, down from 95 x10^9/L two weeks ago.

She has no bleeding, no petechiae and no bruising, and the rest of her FBC and a peripheral blood film show isolated thrombocytopenia consistent with her known ITP. She has no signs of pre-eclampsia, no other medical problems and no allergies. She is on iron supplementation only and her booking HIV, HBV and HCV serology was negative. She is keen to have an epidural in labour. The obstetric anaesthetist and obstetric haematologist are reviewing her at 36 weeks and discussing a plan to optimise her platelets prior to expected delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm.
data_table.Examination: No petechiae or bruising. SFH 36 cm, cephalic.
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 72 x10^9/L (95 two weeks ago), Hb 116 g/L, WCC 7.0, INR 1.0, blood film: isolated thrombocytopenia consistent with ITP.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan with respect to neuraxial anaesthesia and delivery?

options.text: No treatment required because platelets above 50 x10^9/L allow epidural use
Commence oral prednisolone aiming for platelets above 80 x10^9/L by labour
Plan immediate platelet transfusion to bring the count above 100 x10^9/L
Start eltrombopag 50 mg orally daily and continue throughout pregnancy
Splenectomy after delivery is no longer indicated for chronic ITP

subtopic_detail: IBD - medication safety in pregnancy
stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 woman with Crohn disease presents for preconception counselling. She has been in clinical and biochemical remission for 18 months on azathioprine 150 mg daily and adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every two weeks. Three years ago, before stable remission, she had a flare during which she received a 6-month course of methotrexate that was subsequently stopped. She is now planning pregnancy in the next three months.

She has no other medical problems and no allergies. Her gastroenterologist is part of the discussion and her preconception bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP and faecal calprotectin <50 micrograms/g) are reassuring. She has commenced folic acid 5 mg daily. She asks specifically which of her current and past medications might need to change before conception. Her vaccinations including MMR, varicella and pertussis are up to date and her partner is well with no relevant medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, weight 60 kg.
data_table.Examination: No active perianal disease. Soft abdomen. No mucocutaneous EIM.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs normal, CRP 2 mg/L, faecal calprotectin <50 micrograms/g.
data_table.Medications: Azathioprine 150 mg daily, adalimumab 40 mg SC fortnightly, folic acid 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate medication advice for preconception?

options.text: Stop azathioprine preconception and switch to oral budesonide as her sole maintenance therapy for the pregnancy
Continue azathioprine and adalimumab; ensure methotrexate has been stopped for at least 3-6 months
Stop adalimumab at conception and avoid all biologic therapy for the duration of the pregnancy
Restart methotrexate 15 mg weekly if any biochemical evidence of flare during this pregnancy emerges
Switch azathioprine to mycophenolate mofetil preconception for stronger maintenance immunosuppression during pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Type 1 diabetes - preconception HbA1c target
stem:
A 26-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 11 attends preconception clinic with her partner. She uses multiple daily injections (insulin glargine 18 units nocte and insulin aspart with meals) with continuous glucose monitoring. Her most recent HbA1c is 8.4% (68 mmol/mol), down from 9.2% (77 mmol/mol) six months ago. She has background diabetic retinopathy on screening last year but no proliferative changes, urine ACR 1.8 mg/mmol, normal renal function and no neuropathy.

She has no other medical problems, no allergies and is not on any other regular medication. She is taking a standard prenatal multivitamin but no separate folic acid supplement. She has been smoke free for two years and drinks no alcohol. She tells you she would like to start trying to conceive in the next six months and asks whether her current glucose control and supplementation are adequate. Her partner is well.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, BMI 26 kg/m2.
data_table.Examination: No peripheral neuropathy, monofilament intact, fundoscopy: background retinopathy.
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.4% (68 mmol/mol), urine ACR 1.8 mg/mmol, eGFR >90, TSH normal.
data_table.Medications: Insulin glargine 18 units nocte, insulin aspart with meals, standard prenatal multivitamin.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her preconception care?

options.text: Switch from insulin to metformin 1 g twice daily before conception and continue throughout the pregnancy
Reassure that the current HbA1c of 8.4% is acceptable for proceeding immediately to conception attempts
Intensify glucose management aiming for HbA1c below 6.5% and start folic acid 5 mg daily
Advise indefinitely against pregnancy because of background diabetic retinopathy and the current HbA1c level
Start a SGLT2 inhibitor such as empagliflozin preconception to reduce HbA1c rapidly before conception attempts

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum glucose targets in pre-existing diabetes
stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman with type 1 diabetes for 15 years is admitted in spontaneous labour at 38+3 weeks. She has been on insulin pump therapy throughout pregnancy with an HbA1c at 36 weeks of 5.9% (41 mmol/mol). Growth has tracked along the 80th centile with an estimated fetal weight 3.7 kg one week ago. There is no polyhydramnios. She has no diabetic complications other than background retinopathy and no pre-eclampsia.

She is currently 4 cm dilated, contracting regularly and requesting an epidural. On admission her capillary blood glucose is 8.2 mmol/L and she has trace ketones on urine dip. The midwifery team is asking the obstetric registrar about the appropriate glucose target during labour and the optimal way to manage her insulin from now on. She has no allergies and no other regular medications. The neonatal team has been notified to attend delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm/fully effaced, station -2, contractions 3:10, CTG normotypical baseline 140.
data_table.Investigations: CBG 8.2 mmol/L, urine ketones trace, U&E normal, recent HbA1c 5.9%.
data_table.Medications: Insulin pump (basal aspart). Folic acid 5 mg until 12 weeks (stopped), iodine.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum glucose management?

options.text: Continue subcutaneous insulin pump unchanged with 4-hourly capillary glucose monitoring
Switch to variable-rate IV insulin infusion targeting CBG 4-7 mmol/L
Stop all insulin in labour and recommence after delivery of the placenta
Aim for capillary glucose 8-10 mmol/L to reduce maternal hypoglycaemia risk
Give a single dose of long-acting insulin glargine 20 units now

subtopic_detail: Mechanical mitral valve - anticoagulation by trimester
stem:
A 34-year-old G1P0 woman with a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve replacement for rheumatic heart disease attends preconception clinic with her cardiologist and an obstetric physician. Her rheumatic disease was acquired in childhood before she immigrated to Australia at age 12; surveillance now demonstrates only the prosthetic valve as a residual lesion. She has been on warfarin 4 mg daily with stable INR 2.5-3.5 since her surgery five years ago, monitored at a community anticoagulation clinic, with no thrombotic or bleeding events.

She is currently in sinus rhythm, NYHA functional class I with no exertional symptoms during stair climbing, and her most recent transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal mechanical valve function with no regurgitation, no left atrial enlargementft ventricular ejection fraction of 60%.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 76 bpm regular.
data_table.Examination: Mechanical S2, no murmurs, no signs of failure, NYHA I.
data_table.Investigations: INR 2.8, LVEF 60%, normal valve function on TTE.
data_table.Medications: Warfarin 4 mg daily, folic acid 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which anticoagulation strategy is most appropriate to plan from conception through to delivery?

options.text: Use therapeutic-dose enoxaparin with anti-Xa monitoring for the entire pregnancy from positive test until 36 weeks then switch to unfractionated heparin
Continue warfarin at the same dose from conception through to elective induction at term to minimise mechanical valve thrombosis risk throughout pregnancy
Switch to therapeutic-dose enoxaparin from positive pregnancy test, return to warfarin from 13-36 weeks, switch back to LMWH from 36 weeks to delivery
Switch to rivaroxaban 20 mg orally daily preconception and continue this direct oral anticoagulant throughout the entire pregnancy and puerperium
Stop all anticoagulation in the first trimester to avoid warfarin embryopathy and reintroduce therapeutic LMWH at 14 weeks gestation

subtopic_detail: Postnatal VTE prophylaxis - risk-based dosing
stem:
A 36-year-old G3P2 woman delivers a healthy 3.6 kg infant by emergency caesarean section at 39+1 weeks for failure to progress in the first stage of labour. Her BMI on booking was 33 kg/m2 and her current weight is 92 kg with proportionate gestational weight gain. She is otherwise well with no personal or family history of thrombosis, no known thrombophilia and no immobilising disease.

The caesarean was technically straightforward with estimated blood loss 600 mL, no transfusion required and no postpartum haemorrhage. She is now on the postnatal ward six hours after delivery, observations stable, mobilising with assistance, no signs of bleeding, lochia normal and the wound dressing dry.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, dressing dry, lochia normal, calves soft and non-tender, no oedema.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 108 g/L (booking 122), platelets 240 x10^9/L, U&E normal, INR 1.0.
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol PRN, ibuprofen PRN. No anticoagulant yet.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate VTE prophylaxis plan for this patient?

options.text: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily orally for 7 days post-discharge
Mechanical thromboprophylaxis with TED stockings alone for duration of admission
Therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 90 mg twice daily for 6 weeks postpartum
Prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for at least 10 days postoperatively
Aspirin 100 mg orally daily for 6 weeks postpartum as VTE prophylaxis

subtopic_detail: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy - UDCA and delivery timing
stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 35+2 weeks presents with two weeks of progressive generalised itching that is worst on the palms and soles and worse at night. She has no rash, no jaundice and no right upper quadrant pain. She has no significant past medical history and her booking bloods including viral screen were normal. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated.

Her LFTs today show ALT 110 U/L (ULN 35), AST 88 U/L (ULN 35), bilirubin 12 micromol/L, GGT 60 U/L, ALP 280 U/L, and total fasting bile acids 56 micromol/L. Her INR is 1.0 and platelets are 220 x10^9/L. She has no signs of pre-eclampsia, urine PCR is 4 mg/mmol and her CTG is reassuring. Liver ultrasound shows no gallstones, normal hepatic parenchyma and patent portal vessels. She has had no other liver insults and is on no regular medications other than a pregnancy multivitamin.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Excoriations on palms, soles, abdomen. No jaundice. SFH 35 cm. CTG normotypical.
data_table.Investigations: ALT 110 U/L, AST 88 U/L, GGT 60 U/L, ALP 280 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, fasting bile acids 56 micromol/L, INR 1.0, platelets 220, urine PCR 4 mg/mmol.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate combined plan for medication and timing of delivery?

options.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily and plan delivery at 37-38 weeks
