Topical emollients only and plan delivery at term 39-40 weeks
Colestyramine 4 g three times daily and plan immediate delivery now
Oral dexamethasone 12 mg daily for 7 days as definitive symptomatic therapy
Antihistamine therapy with chlorphenamine and expectant management to 40 weeks

subtopic_detail: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy versus HELLP
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 woman at 36+4 weeks presents to the maternity assessment unit with 36 hours of nausea, vomiting and right upper quadrant pain. She is increasingly fatigued and her partner reports she has been progressively confused for the last few hours, with intermittent disorientation to time and place. There is no headache, no visual disturbance, no vaginal bleeding and she reports no reduced fetal movements but feels generally unwell.

On arrival her BP is 138/88 mmHg, HR 108 bpm, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 98% on air and she appears jaundiced with mild asterixis. Her abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant without rebound; CTG shows a normotypical baseline of 145 bpm with reduced variability. Her bedside capillary glucose is 2.6 mmol/L. Urgent bloods reveal an ALT of 540 U/L, AST 520 U/L, bilirubin 78 micromol/L, INR 1.9, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, platelets 95 x10^9/L, ammonia 92 micromol/L, urate 0.46 mmol/L and creatinine 138 micromol/L. Lactate is 4.2 mmol/L and the blood film shows no schistocytes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/88 mmHg, HR 108 bpm, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 98%, CBG 2.6 mmol/L.
data_table.Examination: Jaundice, mild asterixis, RUQ tenderness, GCS 14, no peripheral oedema, CTG reduced variability.
data_table.Investigations: ALT 540 U/L, AST 520 U/L, bilirubin 78 micromol/L, INR 1.9, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, platelets 95 x10^9/L, ammonia 92 micromol/L, urate 0.46 mmol/L, creatinine 138 micromol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, urine PCR 28 mg/mmol.

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours acute fatty liver of pregnancy over HELLP syndrome?

options.text: Mild hypertension with a urine PCR above 30 mg/mmol
Right upper quadrant pain with raised transaminases above 500 U/L
Platelet count below 100 x10^9/L on this presentation
Maternal hypoglycaemia with raised ammonia and coagulopathy out of proportion to platelet drop
Serum urate above the upper limit of normal in the third trimester

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 with a confirmed MCDA twin pregnancy at 19+5 weeks attends fortnightly surveillance. The 16-week scan was unremarkable. Today's ultrasound: twin 1 (donor) EFW 22nd centile, DVP 1.6 cm, bladder not seen on three sweeps over 30 minutes; twin 2 (recipient) EFW 56th centile, DVP 9.2 cm, distended bladder, normal MCA-PSV. Umbilical artery Dopplers normal both twins, no fetal hydrops, cervix 38 mm.

She has no contractions, no bleeding, no symptoms of pre-eclampsia. The tertiary fetal medicine unit is 2 hours away and offers fetoscopic laser ablation daily. She wants the option that maximises the chance of two healthy survivors.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus appropriate for 24 weeks size
data_table.Investigations: Twin 1: EFW 22nd centile, DVP 1.6 cm, bladder not seen. Twin 2: EFW 56th centile, DVP 9.2 cm, bladder distended, MCA-PSV normal. UA Dopplers normal both twins. Cervix 38 mm closed.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent referral to a tertiary fetal medicine unit for fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses
Reassure and continue routine fortnightly surveillance for 2 more weeks
Amnioreduction of the recipient sac in the local maternity unit
Admit for antenatal corticosteroids and plan delivery this week
Selective fetal reduction of the donor twin by cord occlusion now

subtopic_detail: TTTS - screening and recognition

stem: A 27-year-old G1P0 with an MCDA twin pregnancy is reviewed at 26 weeks. Booking, anatomy scan, and TTTS surveillance to date have been unremarkable. Today the smaller twin has an EFW on the 4th centile with a 28 percent inter-twin weight discordance. The larger twin tracks the 48th centile. Amniotic fluid is normal in both sacs. Umbilical artery Doppler of the smaller twin shows intermittently absent end-diastolic flow that alternates with normal forward flow within a single tracing; the larger twin's UA Doppler is normal. Both ductus venosus a-waves are positive. The cardiotocograph of both twins is reactive. The woman is well with a closed cervix of 34 mm.

data_table.Investigations: Smaller twin EFW 4th centile, discordance 28%, UA Doppler intermittent AEDF (Type III). Larger twin EFW 48th centile, UA Doppler normal. DV a-waves positive both. CTG reactive both. Cervix 34 mm.

lead_in: Which classification and surveillance plan best fits this pattern?

options.text: Type I sIUGR; fortnightly growth scans, aim for planned delivery at 36 weeks
Type II sIUGR; weekly Doppler and CTG surveillance, plan delivery at 32 weeks
Type III sIUGR; twice-weekly Doppler with corticosteroid cover and delivery at 32 to 34 weeks
Discordant growth without sIUGR; reassure the woman and re-scan in 2 weeks
Stage I twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome; refer urgently for fetoscopic laser ablation now

subtopic_detail: Selective IUGR in monochorionic twins

stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 RhD-negative woman with a DCDA twin pregnancy (two viable embryos at 7+1) re-presents at 13+0 with a single episode of pink spotting yesterday, now resolved. She is haemodynamically stable. Ultrasound today: twin A viable, CRL appropriate for 13+0; twin B sac collapsed, embryo CRL 7+5 with no cardiac activity (demised). Antibody screen at booking and today: negative. She has not previously received anti-D in this pregnancy. She is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, closed cervical os, scant brown discharge
data_table.Investigations: TVS: twin A viable, twin B demised (CRL 7+5, no FH). Blood group O Rh-positive.

lead_in: Which combination of management is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure regarding minimal increased risk to the surviving twin from the early loss; administer anti-D 625 IU IM as the bleeding episode is at 13+0; continue routine DCDA twin surveillance
Administer anti-D 250 IU IM as the dose for sensitising events before 20 weeks
Withhold anti-D until 28 weeks routine prophylaxis as the antibody screen is negative
Surgical evacuation of the demised gestational sac to prevent later miscarriage of the surviving twin
Admit for serial coagulation studies given the increased maternal risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation

subtopic_detail: Vanishing twin

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 with a confirmed MCMA twin pregnancy is reviewed at 31+4. Booking confirmed a single placental mass, no inter-twin membrane on serial scans, and entangled cords on colour Doppler. Growth has tracked the 35th to 45th centiles concordantly, Dopplers are normal, and there is no evidence of TTTS. She has been an inpatient since 26 weeks for daily CTG monitoring.

Both twins are presently non-cephalic on today's presentation scan. The cervix is closed at 32 mm on TVS. She received a complete course of antenatal corticosteroids at 26 weeks and an additional rescue course was given two weeks ago. She has received daily inpatient CTG surveillance without abnormal traces, no episodes of bleeding or rupture of membranes, and a recent maternal infection screen is unremarkable. The neonatal unit on site routinely supports infants from 28 weeks. She is keen to proceed with planned delivery once the team agrees timing.

data_table.Examination: Inpatient, comfortable, daily CTG reactive for both twins
data_table.Investigations: Concordant growth, normal Dopplers, no TTTS, both non-cephalic, cervix 32 mm

lead_in: Which delivery plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Planned caesarean between 32+0 and 34+0 weeks after corticosteroids
Planned caesarean at 36+0 to 36+6 after steroids
Planned vaginal birth at 32+0 to 34+0 with continuous CTG
Continue inpatient monitoring and aim for vaginal birth at 37+0
Immediate caesarean today at 31+4 regardless of stability

subtopic_detail: Mode and timing of delivery - MCMA twins

stem:
A 25-year-old G1P0 at 28+3 presents to the birth suite with regular painful contractions every 4 minutes for the past 2 hours. She has had no bleeding, no rupture of membranes, and no fever. Her booking and pregnancy have been uncomplicated. She has well-controlled chronic hypertension on labetalol 200 mg BD with booking BP averaging 130/82 and today 134/86. She has known mild aortic stenosis (peak gradient 22 mmHg, asymptomatic) and is followed by cardiology.

Examination shows a soft tender uterus with palpable tightenings, cephalic presentation, and the cervix is 2 cm dilated and 50 percent effaced on speculum. Fetal heart is reassuring. Fetal fibronectin is not available at this hour. The plan is to give corticosteroids and MgSO4 for neuroprotection and transfer to a tertiary unit.

data_table.Examination: Uterus contracting q4min, cephalic, cervix 2 cm 50% effaced, membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: Fetal heart reassuring, MSU pending, FBC and UEC normal
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg BD

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate tocolytic to commence while corticosteroids and transfer are organised?

options.text: Oral nifedipine immediate-release with continuous maternal BP monitoring and a held dose if systolic falls below 90 mmHg
Intravenous atosiban infusion as oxytocin-receptor antagonist tocolysis, with continuous maternal monitoring and titration to contraction frequency
Oral indometacin 50 mg loading dose then 25 mg six-hourly for up to 48 hours with fetal ductal monitoring on echocardiography
Intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion used primarily as tocolysis with continuous maternal monitoring of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory rate
Intravenous salbutamol infusion as beta-2 agonist tocolysis with continuous maternal cardiac monitoring and held dose if maternal HR exceeds 120 bpm

subtopic_detail: Preterm labour - tocolysis choice

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 at 33+1 presents with painful tightenings every 6 minutes for 4 hours. She had a previous preterm birth at 31 weeks. She has no rupture of membranes or bleeding. Examination shows a cephalic presentation, cervix 1 cm dilated and 30 percent effaced; CTG is reactive. She has no maternal medical comorbidities and is on no regular medication.

Her registrar suggests indometacin tocolysis to allow corticosteroid effect, citing its rapid onset. She has no antepartum haemorrhage and no fever. Maternal observations are normal, urine dipstick is clear and the fetal heart on continuous CTG is reactive with normal variability. Booking scans were unremarkable and a recent fetal anatomy review at 31 weeks was normal. The local maternity unit has nifedipine, indometacin and magnesium sulfate available. The team is balancing tocolytic options to allow corticosteroids to take effect, and the registrar has specifically asked about indometacin given its rapid onset.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 1 cm/30%, cephalic, FH reassuring
data_table.Investigations: CTG reactive, FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: Which is the strongest reason to avoid indometacin in this patient?

options.text: Risk of fetal ductus arteriosus constriction and oligohydramnios at this advanced gestation
Substantially increased risk of maternal pulmonary oedema compared with other tocolytics
Indometacin causes significant maternal hypotension via systemic vasodilation in pregnancy
Indometacin is absolutely contraindicated whenever there is any prior preterm birth
Indometacin significantly reduces lung-maturation efficacy of antenatal corticosteroids in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Indometacin tocolysis - gestational limit

stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 at 31+5 presents with threatened preterm labour. She had a complete course of betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart at 26+0 for an earlier admission with threatened preterm labour that subsequently settled. Today she is contracting every 3 minutes, has a cervix 3 cm dilated and 70 percent effaced on speculum, and a fetal fibronectin from 4 weeks ago was positive. The CTG is reactive. The team plans to start tocolysis, transfer to a tertiary unit, and give magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm/70% effaced, cephalic, contractions q3min
data_table.Investigations: CTG reactive, FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: Regarding antenatal corticosteroids, which is most appropriate now?

options.text: Give a single rescue dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg IM now
Give a full repeat course of betamethasone (two doses 24 h apart)
Do not give further corticosteroids as one course is sufficient lifetime exposure
Give dexamethasone 6 mg IM as a single rescue dose
Withhold steroids until cervix is more than 5 cm dilated

subtopic_detail: Antenatal corticosteroids - rescue dosing

stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 at 29+4 with a singleton pregnancy has progressed in spontaneous preterm labour despite nifedipine tocolysis. She is now 7 cm dilated, contracting every 2 minutes, and birth is expected within the next 2 hours. She has had a complete course of betamethasone 36 hours ago. She has no antepartum haemorrhage, no rupture of membranes, and no features of pre-eclampsia.

The CTG is reactive and maternal observations are normal. Her booking BMI was 23, her booking bloods were unremarkable and she has not received magnesium sulfate at any earlier point in this pregnancy. The unit routinely uses MgSO4 for neonatal neuroprotection in line with RANZCOG and Australian Antenatal Magnesium sulfate Neuroprotection guidance. Birth is now genuinely expected within 1 to 2 hours given her rapid cervical progress.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 7 cm, cephalic, contractions q2min
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, UEC normal (creat 60), CTG reactive

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan for fetal neuroprotection?

options.text: Commence intravenous MgSO4 loading and maintenance now, aim for at least 4 hours before birth
Do not give magnesium sulfate, as it is only indicated in pre-eclampsia for seizure prophylaxis
Give a single intramuscular dose of magnesium sulfate now for fetal neuroprotection
Withhold magnesium sulfate because a complete course of antenatal corticosteroids has been given
Defer magnesium sulfate now as the gestation has progressed beyond 28 weeks

subtopic_detail: MgSO4 neuroprotection - gestational window

stem: A 34-year-old G2P1 at 36+5 presents 3 hours after a gush of clear fluid. She has no contractions, the fetal heart is reassuring, and she is afebrile. Speculum confirms PROM with a pool of clear fluid; the cervix appears favourable. She is GBS positive on a 36-week swab. Her last birth was a spontaneous vaginal birth at term without complication.

data_table.Examination: Pool of clear AF, cervix favourable, no contractions, FH reassuring
data_table.Investigations: GBS positive at 36 weeks, FBC normal, CRP normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Plan induction of labour now with intrapartum benzylpenicillin for GBS
Expectant management at home for 96 hours with daily review
Tocolysis with nifedipine and a course of corticosteroids
Caesarean section now due to PPROM beyond 36 weeks
Expectant management as an inpatient until 39+0 weeks

subtopic_detail: PPROM near term - expectant vs delivery

stem: A 30-year-old G3P0 attends preconception clinic having recently had a third painless mid-trimester loss at 19 weeks. The two prior losses were at 18 and 20 weeks; on each occasion she presented with bulging membranes and minimal contractions, and the cervix was widely dilated on speculum. Anatomy scans had been normal, there was no antepartum bleeding, and she has had no infections or instrumentation between pregnancies. She is keen to conceive again and asks how the next pregnancy will be managed.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no abnormalities
data_table.Investigations: Previous losses at 18, 20, 19 weeks; anatomy scans normal; no infection or instrumentation

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan for her next pregnancy?

options.text: History-indicated cervical cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks of pregnancy
Vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly from 16 weeks without cerclage
Serial cervical length scans from 16 weeks with rescue cerclage if shortening
Pre-conception transabdominal cervical cerclage placement before next pregnancy attempt
Insertion of cervical pessary at 14 to 16 weeks of pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Cervical insufficiency - cerclage

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 at 22+0 with a singleton pregnancy attends for a planned TVS cervical length assessment because of one prior spontaneous preterm birth at 32 weeks. She has no symptoms today: no bleeding, no fluid loss, and no contractions. Anatomy scan was normal at 20+1. TVS today shows a cervix of 18 mm with no funnelling. Fetal fibronectin is not routinely used at her unit at this gestation.

Her previous birth was a spontaneous preterm vaginal birth at 32 weeks with no recognised infection, no antepartum bleeding and no overt cervical instrumentation. She has no other significant medical or obstetric history, takes no medications other than folate and iodine. Her unit follows current RANZCOG guidance recommending vaginal progesterone in women with a singleton pregnancy and short cervix on TVS prior to viability.

data_table.Examination: No contractions, no PV bleed or fluid
data_table.Investigations: TVS cervix 18 mm, no funnelling, FH and AF normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate intervention?

options.text: Commence vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly continued until 36 weeks gestation
Intramuscular 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate weekly until 34 weeks gestation
Rescue cervical cerclage placement now via vaginal approach
Strict bedrest at home until 34 completed weeks gestation
Fetal fibronectin testing now to guide subsequent management

subtopic_detail: Preterm birth prediction - TVS cervix

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 at 29+2 attends pregnancy assessment with intermittent abdominal tightening over 8 hours and pelvic pressure. She has no bleeding, no rupture of membranes, and a reassuring CTG. Examination shows no fluid pooling on speculum and the cervix appears long and closed; TVS measures the cervix at 22 mm. Quantitative fetal fibronectin (qfFN) returns at 12 ng/mL. She has no obstetric history of preterm birth and no infections.

She has no past history of preterm birth, no late miscarriageted uterine anomaly. There is no antepartum bleeding, no offensive vaginal discharge and a urine dipstick is unremarkable. The maternity unit uses quantitative fetal fibronectin combined with TVS cervical length as the basis for triage of suspected preterm labour, with a published unit cut-off of 50 ng/mL above which admission and steroids are considered.

data_table.Examination: No pooling, cervix long/closed on speculum
data_table.Investigations: TVS cervix 22 mm, qfFN 12 ng/mL, CTG reactive, MSU pending

lead_in: Which management approach best reflects current evidence?

options.text: Reassure, discharge home with clear safety-netting advice and outpatient follow-up
Admit, give a course of antenatal corticosteroids and commence tocolysis
Admit and commence prophylactic magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
Repeat quantitative fetal fibronectin in 24 hours and admit until then
Insertion of emergency rescue cervical cerclage now in theatre

subtopic_detail: Fetal fibronectin in threatened preterm labour

stem: A 31-year-old G1P0 at 37+1 with well-controlled gestational diabetes on diet alone is reviewed at her routine antenatal clinic. Fetal growth is on the 50th centile, amniotic fluid is normal, CTG is reactive, and self-monitored capillary glucose has stayed within target. She has no hypertension, no IUGR, and no other complication. She has booked into a private hospital and asks whether elective induction at 37 to 38 weeks would be safer than waiting.

data_table.Examination: Cephalic, FH reassuring
data_table.Investigations: EFW 50th centile, AFI normal, BSL diary within target

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Continue routine antenatal care with planned delivery around 40+0 to 40+6 weeks
Elective induction of labour at 37+0 weeks gestation now
Elective lower segment caesarean section at 38+0 weeks of gestation
Planned induction at 39+0 with cervical ripening regardless of Bishop
Defer delivery until 41+5 weeks with daily CTG from 39 weeks

subtopic_detail: Late preterm / early term decisions

stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 39+3 presents 2 hours after a gush of clear fluid followed by ongoing leakage. Not contracting; speculum confirms a pool of clear amniotic fluid and a closed soft cervix. CTG reactive. GBS swab at 36 weeks was POSITIVE. She has no penicillin allergy. Booking BMI 24, otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy. She asks about waiting at home for spontaneous labour; she has no childcare for her older child and would prefer to wait if it is safe.

data_table.Examination: Pool of clear AF on speculum, soft closed cervix, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: CTG reactive, GBS POSITIVE at 36 weeks

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan in this Australian setting?

options.text: Admit for immediate induction of labour and commence intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin GBS prophylaxis now
Admit for expectant management up to 24 hours with no antibiotics unless fever develops
Wait at home for spontaneous labour for up to 5 days with daily review
Mandatory immediate lower-segment caesarean to prevent ascending infection
Commence oral erythromycin to prolong latency to delivery at term

subtopic_detail: Term PROM management

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 29+0 is on day 9 of expectant PPROM management. She completed corticosteroids 7 days ago and erythromycin is ongoing. She has been afebrile with normal observations until this evening, when she reports increased uterine tenderness and chills. Observations: T 38.4, HR 118, BP 108/64, RR 18, SpO2 98 on RA. Her uterus is tender on palpation.

CTG shows a baseline fetal heart rate of 175 bpm with reduced variability and no decelerations. WCC has risen to 18.6 x10^9/L, neutrophils 16.2 x10^9/L, CRP 92 mg/L (from 18 mg/L two days ago). She has no offensive vaginal discharge but the speculum view shows turbid amniotic fluid pooling. Maternal lactate is 2.1 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Uterine tenderness, turbid AF on speculum, no other localising findings
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.6, neutrophils 16.2, CRP 92 (up from 18), lactate 2.1, MSU pending, CTG: baseline 175, reduced variability

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and expedite delivery now
Continue expectant management with IV antibiotics, aim to reach 32 weeks
Repeat antenatal steroids and reassess clinical status in 12 hours
Add tocolysis to allow safe transfer to a tertiary unit
Amniocentesis for Gram stain and glucose before any decision

subtopic_detail: Chorioamnionitis in PPROM - delivery trigger

stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 with an MCDA twin pregnancy at 27+4 presents with reduced fetal movements over 24 hours. Pregnancy has been uncomplicated; serial scans have shown concordant growth and no TTTS. Today's ultrasound confirms intrauterine demise of twin A with absent cardiac activity and small pericardial effusion. Twin B has a fetal heart rate of 148 bpm with reactive CTG, normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical artery Doppler, and a peak systolic velocity in the middle cerebral artery of 1.8 multiples of the median. Maternal observations and coagulation profile are normal. She has no contractions and the cervix is 35 mm closed on TVS.

data_table.Examination: Soft uterus, no contractions, no PV bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Twin A demised. Twin B: HR 148, reactive CTG, UA Doppler normal, MCA-PSV 1.8 MoM. Maternal coags normal. Cervix 35 mm.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Urgent transfer to fetal medicine for assessment for fetal anaemia
Immediate lower segment caesarean section of the surviving twin at this gestation
Expectant management with weekly outpatient Doppler surveillance of the surviving twin
Commence maternal intravenous heparin to prevent disseminated intravascular coagulation in mother
Selective fetal reduction of the surviving twin by ultrasound-guided cord occlusion

subtopic_detail: Co-twin demise in monochorionic pregnancy

stem: A 29-year-old G2P2 attends her 6-week postnatal review. She delivered vaginally and is exclusively breastfeeding on demand, day and night, no formula or solids. She has had no return of menstruation since delivery, and a urine beta-hCG is negative today. She and her partner do not wish to conceive again for at least 2 years. She has heard friends say 'breastfeeding stops periods so I don't need contraception' and asks whether that is true. She has no UKMEC category 3-4 contraindications.

data_table.Examination: Well, BMI 24, BP 118/74 mmHg. Uterus involuted. Breasts soft, no engorgement, infant feeding well.
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative. No further investigations performed today.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice and recommendation?

options.text: Counsel that LAM provides about 98% efficacy only up to 6 months postpartum and only while she is amenorrhoeic and exclusively/near-exclusively breastfeeding; offer a parallel reliable method (LARC or POP) to avoid the gap when LAM expires
Reassure that breastfeeding alone provides reliable contraception for up to 12 months postpartum
Reassure that any breastfeeding plus amenorrhoea provides reliable contraception regardless of feeding pattern or solids
Counsel that LAM is reliable until 6 months only if one normal menstrual period has occurred to confirm cycles have restarted
Recommend commencing the combined oral contraceptive pill today as the most reliable bridging method

subtopic_detail: Postnatal contraception - lactational amenorrhoea criteria

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P3 woman has just had an emergency caesarean section at 38+5 weeks for fetal distress. Her pre-pregnancy BMI was 36 and her booking weight was 102 kg; she now weighs 108 kg on day 1 postpartum. She has a past history of one provoked deep vein thrombosis 8 years ago after a long-haul flight, was treated with warfarin for 6 months at that time, and has been off anticoagulation since.

Her current pregnancy was uncomplicated apart from gestational diabetes managed with diet. She is a non-smoker, has no thrombophilia testing on record, no family history of unprovoked VTE, and her observations are stable. The estimated blood loss at caesarean was 600 mL with no further bleeding postoperatively. Her platelet count is 198 and her creatinine is 62 micromol/L. She is mobilising with help and is keen to breastfeed.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Wound clean and dry. Calves soft, non-tender, symmetrical. Mobilising slowly with assistance.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 108 g/L, plt 198, creatinine 62 micromol/L, EBL at CS 600 mL. No active bleeding.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate postpartum thromboprophylaxis regimen?

options.text: Mechanical prophylaxis (TEDS plus early mobilisation) alone with no pharmacological prophylaxis
Enoxaparin 20 mg subcutaneously daily for 10 days as postpartum thromboprophylaxis
Enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously daily for 10 days only as postpartum prophylaxis
Enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously daily for 6 weeks as postpartum thromboprophylaxis
Warfarin 5 mg daily for 6 weeks targeting INR 2.0 to 3.0 with bridging LMWH

subtopic_detail: Postpartum VTE thromboprophylaxis - RANZCOG risk-stratified dosing

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P2 woman attends a postnatal review at 5 weeks following an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal birth at 39+4 weeks gestation. She is partially breastfeeding (approximately 60% breast milk, 40% formula because she returns to her finance role in 4 weeks and the workplace lacks lactation facilities) and has had no return of menses since delivery. Her booking BMI was 31, she is a lifelong non-smoker, her blood pressure today is 132/82 mmHg, and her booking and 36-week antenatal BP readings were both normotensive.

She has no personal or family history of VTE or thrombophilia, no migraine with or without aura, no current or prior breast cancer, and no autoimmune disease. She and her partner want effective contraception starting as soon as possible today. She is comfortable returning at any time for a procedure if that is the most appropriate option after counselling.

data_table.Examination: Well, BMI 30, BP 132/82 mmHg. Uterus involuted. Breasts: lactating, no inflammation.
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate contraceptive option to initiate today?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol 30 microg/levonorgestrel 150 microg, starting today
Defer all contraception until 6 weeks postpartum and rely on LAM in the interim
Insertion of a copper intrauterine device at 5 weeks postpartum after speculum examination
Insertion of a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system today at 5 weeks postpartum
Etonogestrel 68 mg subdermal implant inserted today during the consultation

subtopic_detail: Postnatal contraception - timing of method initiation in a partially breastfeeding woman

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P1 woman has just delivered a 4.1 kg infant by spontaneous vaginal birth with a 30-minute active second stage. The delivery was attended by a midwife with an obstetric registrar called for shoulder dystocia which was resolved with McRoberts and suprapubic pressure within 90 seconds. There was a head-to-body interval of 80 seconds. After delivery of the placenta, careful inspection of the perineum demonstrates a tear extending through the perineal skin, perineal muscles, and partial-thickness laceration of the external anal sphincter involving approximately 40% of its thickness; the internal anal sphincter and rectal mucosa appear intact on careful per rectum examination.

The registrar grades the injury as 3a. Maternal observations are stable, the infant is in good condition with Apgars 9 and 9, and the estimated blood loss is 350 mL with no ongoing bleeding. The hospital has a theatre available now and a senior obstetrician on site.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.9 degC.
data_table.Examination: Grade 3a tear: <50% external anal sphincter thickness, IAS and rectal mucosa intact. EBL 350 mL.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L. Group and screen on file.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management approach for repair and after-care?

options.text: Repair on the labour ward bed under local anaesthesia using 2-0 polyglactin (Vicryl) for all layers, no postoperative antibiotics, encourage normal diet, no physiotherapy referral
Repair on the ward without anaesthesia, give one course of oral metronidazole, no laxative and no perineal clinic follow-up

Repair in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics intraoperatively then oral course, lactulose for 10 days, pelvic floor physiotherapy referral, perineal clinic follow-up
Repair in theatre, oral cefalexin only, no stool softener (constipation will protect the repair), no physiotherapy referral, GP review at 6 weeks
Defer repair for 24 hours to allow tissue oedema to settle, then repair in theatre, no antibiotics, lactulose for 3 days, physiotherapy referral

subtopic_detail: Obstetric anal sphincter injury repair - principles of management

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P2 woman attends her general practitioner 5 months after the delivery of her second child. The pregnancy itself was uncomplicated until delivery, when she had a massive postpartum haemorrhage estimated at 3500 mL secondary to uterine atony plus a small lower segment extension during an emergency caesarean section for fetal distress; she required 6 units of packed red cells, 2 units of fresh frozen plasma, 1 unit of cryoprecipitate, intraoperative tranexamic acid, intramyometrial carboprost, a Bakri balloon, and spent 36 hours in the high-dependency unit before stabilising.

Since then she has been unable to establish breastfeeding despite repeated attempts in the first week with a lactation consultant, has had no return of menses at all over the last 5 months, has lost approximately 4 kg of muscle mass with reduced exercise tolerance, sleeps 11 hours daily and is still fatigued during the day, feels persistently cold even in warm rooms, has noticed loss of axillary and pubic hair, has had two episodes of presyncope on standing in the last month, and has reduced libido. On examination today she is thin, pale, has dry skin, fine sparse hair, and a postural blood pressure drop from 108/68 mmHg supine to 86/52 mmHg standing. Her thyroid gland is non-tender and non-enlarged on palpation, and there is no goitre.

data_table.Vital signs: BP supine 108/68 mmHg, standing 86/52 mmHg. HR 58 bpm, T 36.2 degC.
data_table.Examination: Thin, pale, dry skin, fine sparse axillary and pubic hair. Thyroid non-palpable. No goitre.
data_table.Investigations: Pending - GP is determining the most appropriate first-line endocrine workup.

lead_in: Which combination of investigations is most appropriate as the first-line workup to establish her most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Morning 0800 cortisol, TSH plus free T4, LH, FSH, oestradiol, prolactin, IGF-1, and MRI pituitary
TSH and free T4 only, treating empirically with levothyroxine if either is low
Random cortisol and random TSH on the day of consultation only as initial work-up
24-hour urinary free cortisol and an overnight dexamethasone suppression test as the first step
Pelvic ultrasound and anti-Mullerian hormone level to assess her ovarian reserve as first step

subtopic_detail: Sheehan syndrome - investigation strategy after severe postpartum haemorrhage

stem: A 28-year-old G2P2 on day 2 post-vaginal-birth (PPH 1100 mL controlled with uterotonics and tranexamic acid; no transfusion) feels tired but not breathless, ambulates without symptoms, breastfeeds well. Booking Hb 124 g/L. Today: Hb 78 g/L, MCV 76, ferritin 12 mcg/L, transferrin saturation 9%, platelets 240, normal renal function. No active bleeding, no chest pain. She wishes to be discharged tomorrow to care for her toddler. Local protocol follows the National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Module 5 (Obstetrics).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/72 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae. Lungs clear. Cardiac exam unremarkable. Mobilising independently. No active bleeding.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 12 micrograms/L, transferrin sat 9%, plts 240. EBL 1100 mL at delivery.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management of her postpartum iron deficiency anaemia?

options.text: Single dose IV ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg before discharge with review at 4 weeks
Transfuse 2 units of packed red cells before discharge
Oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg three times daily for 3 months
Oral ferrous fumarate 200 mg three times daily with no scheduled follow-up
Erythropoietin-stimulating agent subcutaneously now plus oral iron for 3 months

subtopic_detail: Postpartum iron deficiency anaemia - transfusion vs IV iron vs oral iron thresholds

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P1 woman is reviewed 7 hours after a forceps-assisted vaginal birth at 40+1 with a mediolateral episiotomy. She had an epidural sited in labour and her last top-up was 5 hours ago; sensation in her legs has now fully returned. The estimated blood loss was 450 mL and her perineal tear is a grade 2 episiotomy repair with no extension into the sphincter complex.

She last passed urine spontaneously 9 hours before the start of pushing, which was 11 hours ago in total. She has been encouraged to attempt voiding three times over the last 4 hours but each attempt has produced less than 50 mL despite a sensation of fullness. Bladder ultrasound at the bedside shows 720 mL of urine in the bladder. She has had no haematuria, no flank painin, and her observations are stable. She is keen to mobilise to the shower and start skin-to-skin.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Suprapubic fullness, non-tender. Episiotomy repair intact. Sensation in legs fully returned. Pad: minimal lochia.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside bladder USS: 720 mL. Urinalysis pending.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Encourage further oral fluids now and then re-scan her bladder again in 4 hours
Insert in-out catheter, drain bladder once, then discharge to postnatal ward without further plan
Refer her urgently to urology for cystoscopy under general anaesthesia today in theatre setting
Administer IV furosemide 20 mg and then re-scan her bladder again in 1 hour
Insert indwelling urinary catheter on free drainage for 24-48 hours, then trial of void with bladder scans

subtopic_detail: Postpartum urinary retention - identification and management

stem:
A 31-year-old G1P1 woman was diagnosed with preeclampsia at 36 weeks gestation and delivered at 37+0 by induction of labour with a spontaneous vaginal birth, complicated only by a small first-degree perineal tear that was sutured at the time. Antenatally she received labetalol 200 mg three times daily plus methyldopa 250 mg three times daily for blood pressure control, achieving target BP below 140/90 mmHg from 34 weeks.

She is now day 6 postpartum and is breastfeeding her infant exclusively with good supply. Her blood pressure today on home monitoring has been 158/102 mmHg, 154/96 mmHg and 156/100 mmHg recorded over the last 24 hours despite continuing both of her antenatal antihypertensives at full antenatal dose. She has no headache, no visual disturbance, and no peripheral oedema beyond mild ankle swelling.

Her bloods this morning show a normal full blood count without thrombocytopaenia, normal renal function with creatinine 70 micromol/L, AST and ALT within normal limits, and a urine protein-creatinine ratio elevated at 60 mg/mmol (down from a peak of 180 mg/mmol antenatally).

data_table.Vital signs: BP today average 156/99 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: No focal neurology. No epigastric tenderness. Mild ankle oedema. Breasts soft.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L, plts 220, creatinine 70 micromol/L, ALT 22 U/L, urine PCR 60 mg/mmol.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate adjustment to her antihypertensive regimen?

options.text: Increase methyldopa to 500 mg three times daily and continue current labetalol dose
Wean and stop methyldopa, increase labetalol, add nifedipine controlled-release 30 mg daily if BP elevated
Switch labetalol to atenolol 50 mg daily and continue current methyldopa dose
Commence oral enalapril 5 mg daily and stop labetalol now in this patient
Stop all antihypertensives now because she is more than 5 days postpartum currently

subtopic_detail: Postpartum hypertension - antihypertensive choice in a breastfeeding woman with prior preeclampsia

stem:
A 36-year-old G1P1 woman attends her general practitioner at 10 days postpartum because, despite frequent on-demand feeding and continuous skin-to-skin contact since birth, she has produced very little breast milk and her infant has lost 11% of birth weight on weighed feeds today. The delivery was at 38+5 by elective lower segment caesarean section for breech presentation; the third stage was complicated by a placenta with a retained cotyledon noted on inspection that was manually removed in theatre under spinal anaesthesia, with no postpartum haemorrhage (estimated blood loss 380 mL total).

She had no antenatal complications, normal booking and 36-week bloods including a normal FBC and ferritin, and was discharged on day 4 in stable condition. She noticed no antenatal breast enlargement during pregnancy, which was unusual compared with her friends. On examination her breasts are small, tubular, widely spaced and noticeably asymmetric (left larger than right), with minimal glandular fullness on palpation and no breast engorgement; there are no signs of inflammation, infection, fluctuance, or mastitis.

Her uterus is involuted appropriately to size, her perineum is healed, and her observations are all stable. She is not on any medications, has no past breast surgery, no nipple piercings, and has been seen by an IBCLC lactation consultant twice with optimal latch, optimal positioning, and a normal infant suck assessment confirmed.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Breasts small, asymmetric, widely spaced, minimal glandular tissue, no inflammation. Uterus involuted. Infant: well, tone good, suck normal on assessment.
data_table.Investigations: Pending - GP planning investigations.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to clarify the cause of failure to establish lactation?

options.text: Infant tongue-tie clinical assessment by paediatric ENT for surgical release if confirmed
Maternal full blood count and ferritin level only as initial work-up
Pelvic ultrasound only as the initial single investigation for her presentation today
Serum prolactin and pituitary axis screen (cortisol, TSH and free T4, LH and FSH)
Empirical trial of oral domperidone 10 mg three times daily without further investigation today

subtopic_detail: Failure to lactate - differential and investigation

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P2 woman presents to her general practitioner 4 months postpartum with a 6-week history of palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, anxiety and a 3 kg weight loss despite an increased appetite. She is breastfeeding her infant exclusively. She has no neck pain, no recent viral illnessse, and no past psychiatric history. Her pregnancy was uncomplicated, the delivery was a spontaneous vaginal birth at 39+4, and she had no obstetric or postpartum complications.

Her bloods today show TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L, free T4 32 pmol/L, free T3 9.2 pmol/L, anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies strongly positive at 480 IU/mL, and thyroid receptor (TRAb) antibodies negative. A radioiodine uptake scan would be contraindicated because of breastfeeding but a thyroid ultrasound shows a diffusely heterogeneous gland with reduced vascularity on Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/76 mmHg, HR 108 bpm regular, T 36.9 degC.
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, warm peripheries, no goitre, no eye signs. Breastfeeding well.
data_table.Investigations: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, fT4 32 pmol/L, fT3 9.2 pmol/L, anti-TPO 480 IU/mL (strongly +), TRAb negative. USS thyroid: diffusely heterogeneous, reduced vascularity.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management of her current thyrotoxic phase?

options.text: Carbimazole 30 mg orally daily, titrated to repeat thyroid function tests every 4 weeks
Radioiodine ablation as soon as breastfeeding can be temporarily ceased entirely
Propranolol 10-40 mg three times daily for symptom control, monitoring thyroid function every 6-8 weeks
Levothyroxine 50 microg orally daily and review her thyroid function tests in 8 weeks
Lugol iodine and oral dexamethasone for treatment of thyroid storm now

subtopic_detail: Postpartum thyroiditis - biphasic course and management

stem:
A 29-year-old nulligravid woman presents with 7 months of secondary amenorrhoea, intermittent bilateral galactorrhoea and reduced libido. She has had no recent pregnancy or breastfeeding, no headaches and no visual symptoms. She started risperidone 4 mg daily 9 months ago for chronic schizoaffective disorder, prescribed by her psychiatrist, and is responding well with no recent admissions. She takes no other regular medications and uses no recreational drugs.

BMI 24, BP 116/70. Visual fields are full to confrontation. Bloods: beta-hCG negative, repeat mid-morning serum prolactin 1900 mIU/L (reference <500) on two occasions one week apart, TSH and free T4 normal, U+Es normal. She is keen to conceive in the next 12 months.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/70 mmHg, BMI 24
data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible galactorrhoea, no breast mass, visual fields normal to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative, prolactin 1850 mIU/L (reference <500), TSH 1.4 mIU/L, free T4 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request urgent MRI pituitary with gadolinium before any further investigation
Liaise with the treating psychiatrist about switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic such as aripiprazole, then re-check prolactin
Commence cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly empirically and reassess prolactin in 6 weeks
Macroprolactin screen with polyethylene glycol precipitation as the next test
Stop risperidone abruptly without psychiatric consultation to allow prolactin to normalise

subtopic_detail: Hyperprolactinaemia - first-line investigation

stem:
A 32-year-old woman is reviewed 8 days after IVF oocyte retrieval (21 oocytes). She reports 48 hours of worsening abdominal distension, nausea and reduced oral intake. BP 108/64, HR 108, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air. Abdomen distended, tense ascites palpable to the costal margin, mild generalised tenderness without peritonism. Pelvic ultrasound: ovaries 11 cm right and 10 cm left with multiple cysts; large-volume ascites extending above the umbilicus; small right pleural effusion.

Bloods: haematocrit 0.48 (baseline 0.38), WCC 13.2, sodium 132, potassium 4.6, creatinine 96 micromol/L (baseline 62), albumin 27 g/L, ALT 78 U/L, urine output 25 mL/h for the past 4 hours.

data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen, shifting dullness, mild tenderness, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Hct 0.45 (baseline 0.38), WCC 12.5, Na 137, K 4.2, Cr 72 micromol/L, Alb 32 g/L; USS: ovaries 10 cm R / 9 cm L, moderate ascites pelvic + lower abdo, not above umbilicus

lead_in: Which classification and management plan best fit her ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome?

options.text: Moderate OHSS: discharge home with daily phone review and oral fluids
Severe OHSS: admit for IV crystalloid, VTE prophylaxis with LMWH, strict fluid balance and consider paracentesis
Critical OHSS: transfer to ICU now for invasive ventilation and renal replacement
Severe OHSS: admit but give large-volume normal saline boluses until haematocrit normalises
Severe OHSS: admit but withhold thromboprophylaxis until haemoconcentration resolves

subtopic_detail: OHSS - severity recognition

stem:
A 38-year-old woman and her 40-year-old male partner have been trying to conceive for 18 months. The woman has regular ovulatory cycles, mid-luteal progesterone confirms ovulation, AMH 6 pmol/L (low for age), antral follicle count 6, TSH and prolactin normal, BMI 24, HyCoSy confirmed bilateral tubal patency. The partner has had two normal semen analyses by WHO 2021 criteria 4 weeks apart.

Neither has had pelvic surgery, endometriosis or STI. They are non-smokers and drink within recommended limits. They have not had any prior pregnancies. They ask which ART pathway gives the highest live-birth chance given her age and ovarian reserve.

data_table.Examination: Both partners healthy; female BMI 24
data_table.Investigations: Female: regular ovulatory cycles, normal mid-luteal progesterone, AMH 18 pmol/L, AFC 14, normal TSH/prolactin, bilateral tubal patency. Male: normal semen analysis x2 by WHO 2021

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue timed intercourse for a further 12 months before referral to a fertility specialist
Proceed to in vitro fertilisation given her age and low ovarian reserve
Three cycles of intrauterine insemination with clomifene before considering IVF
Commence clomifene citrate alone with timed intercourse for six cycles
Recommend donor oocyte IVF as her age and reserve preclude autologous IVF success

subtopic_detail: IUI vs IVF - eligibility selection

stem:
A 36-year-old woman and her 38-year-old male partner attend the GP after 8 months of regular unprotected intercourse without conception. She has had regular 28 to 30 day cycles since menarche, no dysmenorrhoea, no abnormal bleeding and no pelvic pain. She has had no pregnancies and her partner has no children from previous relationships. Her past history includes appendicectomy at age 16 without complications.

She has had no pelvic infections, no chlamydia exposure, and her cervical screening is up to date. Her partner has no chronic disease, takes no regular medications, is a non-smoker and works as a teacher. They have intercourse 2 to 3 times per week. BMI 23 (female) and 25 (male). She is on folic acid 0.5 mg daily. Pelvic examination is unremarkable.

They are aware of her age and ask what investigations should be commenced now rather than waiting to the conventional 12-month threshold for younger couples.

data_table.Examination: Female pelvic exam unremarkable; both partners systemically well
data_table.Investigations: None done yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the couple and review in 4 months if there is no conception
Commence parallel investigation: semen analysis, mid-luteal progesterone, ovarian reserve and tubal patency
Order AMH and pelvic ultrasound only and defer semen analysis until a second visit
Refer immediately for IVF without baseline investigations given her age
Diagnostic laparoscopy first to exclude endometriosis as a contributing factor

subtopic_detail: Infertility - couple workup timing and content

stem:
A 34-year-old nulligravid woman is being assessed prior to commencement of IVF for tubal factor infertility (bilateral tubal occlusion confirmed on HyCoSy and laparoscopy). She has regular 28-day cycles with confirmed ovulation, BMI 22, normal TSH and prolactin, and her partner has a normal semen analysis. Her AMH is 4 pmol/L (low for age) and her antral follicle count is 5 (total both ovaries).

Day-3 FSH is 11 IU/L with oestradiol 180 pmol/L. She has had no chemotherapy, no pelvic surgery beyond diagnostic laparoscopy, no autoimmune disease and no family history of premature ovarian insufficiency. She is anxious about the implications of these results and asks what they mean for her IVF cycle planning and her chance of natural conception. She has no menopausal symptoms and her BP today is normal. She is anxious about the implications for her treatment and asks specifically what these numbers mean for her IVF stimulation response.

data_table.Vital signs: BMI 22
data_table.Investigations: AMH 4 pmol/L (low for age), AFC 5 (total), Day-3 FSH 11 IU/L, oestradiol 180 pmol/L; normal TSH and prolactin; bilateral tubal occlusion

lead_in: Which statement most accurately interprets her ovarian reserve markers in the context of planning IVF?

options.text: Low AMH and AFC predict poor ovarian response and low oocyte yield, not per-cycle spontaneous conception
AMH below 5 pmol/L confirms premature ovarian insufficiency, so IVF with her own oocytes is inappropriate
Her elevated day-3 FSH means she will achieve a high oocyte yield on standard stimulation protocols
AMH and AFC accurately predict the absolute number of years remaining until menopause for an individual
An antral follicle count above 4 excludes POSEIDON poor-responder classification regardless of the AMH

subtopic_detail: Ovarian reserve - AMH and AFC interpretation

stem:
A 37-year-old woman presents to her GP after 8 months of unprotected intercourse without conception. Her partner has had a normal semen analysis. Her cycles are 26 to 28 days and she has confirmed ovulation on mid-luteal progesterone. The GP arranges day-3 cycle bloods which return as follows: FSH 9 IU/L, LH 5 IU/L, oestradiol 350 pmol/L (high), AMH 6 pmol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, prolactin within reference range.

AFC is 7 total. She has no abnormal bleeding and no significant dysmenorrhoea. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal-sized uterus, no fibroids, normal-appearing ovaries with the AFC noted, and no endometrioma. She has had no chemotherapy and no pelvic surgery. She asks how to interpret the day-3 FSH given that it appears reassuring. Her BMI is 23 and she is otherwise well, with no symptoms suggesting menopause.

data_table.Investigations: Day-3 FSH 9 IU/L, LH 5 IU/L, oestradiol 350 pmol/L (high), AMH 6 pmol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, prolactin normal, AFC 7

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of these ovarian reserve markers?

options.text: Day-3 FSH within reference range reliably excludes diminished ovarian reserve in this patient
Elevated day-3 oestradiol may falsely suppress FSH; reserve is better assessed by AMH and AFC here
Her LH-to-FSH ratio of less than 1 confirms PCOS as the dominant cause of her subfertility
An AMH of 6 pmol/L with AFC of 7 confirms premature ovarian insufficiency, excluding IVF with own oocytes
Repeating day-3 bloods next cycle without changing strategy will give a definitive answer

subtopic_detail: Day-3 FSH and oestradiol interpretation

stem:
A 25-year-old nulligravid woman has just been diagnosed with PCOS by her GP (Rotterdam criteria: oligomenorrhoea, biochemical hyperandrogenism with elevated free androgen index, polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound with 24 follicles per ovary). Her exclusion bloods (TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP, beta-hCG) were all normal. She has acne, mild hirsutism (Ferriman-Gallwey 9) and recent 5 kg weight gain over 12 months. BMI 29.

Family history: mother with type 2 diabetes diagnosed at 52, paternal uncle with myocardial infarction at age 60. She is not planning pregnancy in the next 2 years. Her GP plans the recommended metabolic screen at diagnosis per the 2023 international PCOS guideline. Blood pressure today is 124/78 mmHg. She has no symptoms of obstructive sleep apnoea, no chest pain and no peripheral oedema, and her cardiovascular examination today is unremarkable. The GP is using the 2023 international evidence-based PCOS guideline as the framework for baseline assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, BMI 29
data_table.Examination: Acne, mild hirsutism (FG 9), no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP normal; beta-hCG negative; free androgen index elevated; TVUS 24 follicles/ovary

lead_in: Which combination of investigations represents the most appropriate metabolic screen at the time of PCOS diagnosis in this woman?

options.text: Fasting lipid panel and a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test plus blood pressure measurement
Fasting glucose and HbA1c alone are sufficient screening in women under 35 with PCOS
Annual fasting insulin level to monitor for insulin resistance and guide treatment
Cardiac MRI with stress testing given her family history of cardiovascular disease at this age
Liver biopsy because PCOS is associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease

subtopic_detail: PCOS - metabolic screening at diagnosis

stem:
A 28-year-old nulligravid woman has been on continuous combined oral contraceptive pill (30 mcg ethinylestradiol + levonorgestrel) plus naproxen as needed for 8 months for clinically suspected endometriosis. Her cyclical pelvic pain has not improved (still requires time off work 2 days each month with pain rated 7/10), her deep dyspareunia persists, and a repeat transvaginal ultrasound now demonstrates a 3 cm right ovarian endometrioma not previously seen.

She has had no abnormal bleeding and no new bowel or bladder symptoms in the last 2 years. She uses condoms with her long-term male partner. Beta-hCG is negative. She has no family history of breast cancer or VTE, no smoking and BMI 23. She is willing to continue medical therapy but wants more effective symptom relief; she remains reluctant to undergo surgery in the short term.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, BMI 23
data_table.Examination: Tenderness right adnexa, no peritonism, normal speculum
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: new 3 cm right ovarian endometrioma; beta-hCG negative; CA-125 not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch to LNG-IUS or trial a 3-6 month GnRH analogue with add-back HRT
Stop hormonal suppression and proceed to abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy
Add tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses to current therapy
Empirical IVF using fresh embryo transfer for presumed endometriosis-related infertility
Continue current therapy and add long-acting oxycodone for breakthrough cyclical pain

subtopic_detail: Endometriosis - escalation after failed first-line

stem:
A 34-year-old G0 woman is referred with 14 months of secondary subfertility and a 9-month history of progressively heavy menstrual bleeding requiring iron supplementation (Hb 108 g/L on presentation, now 118 g/L). Her cycles are regular and ovulatory. Her partner has a normal semen analysis and her tubes are patent on HyCoSy. Transvaginal ultrasound and MRI both demonstrate a single 5 cm submucosal fibroid that is FIGO type 2 (>=50% intramural component, projecting into the endometrial cavity and distorting it) and two further small subserosal fibroids that do not distort the cavity.

Her endometrial biopsy is benign. She has no other gynaecological pathology, no chronic disease, and is actively trying to conceive. She has discussed expectant management and medical options with her clinician and would prefer a definitive intervention that addresses both her heavy bleeding and improves her chance of conception.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L (treated iron deficiency anaemia); TVUS + MRI: 5 cm FIGO type 2 submucosal fibroid distorting cavity, two small subserosal fibroids; endometrial biopsy benign; HyCoSy bilateral patency; normal semen analysis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Hysteroscopic myomectomy as a fertility-sparing intervention addressing both HMB and subfertility
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system insertion as definitive treatment for both subfertility and HMB
Uterine artery embolisation to reduce fibroid volume and HMB while preserving the uterus
Total abdominal hysterectomy as definitive management for both fibroid bulk and HMB
GnRH analogue with add-back HRT as long-term medical therapy for HMB and subfertility

subtopic_detail: Fibroids - fertility-sparing surgical choice

stem:
A 34-year-old woman has been formally diagnosed with premature ovarian insufficiency: 6 months of secondary amenorrhoea, FSH 56 IU/L and 62 IU/L on samples 5 weeks apart with low oestradiol, negative beta-hCG, normal TSH and normal prolactin. She has hot flushes, vaginal dryness with deep dyspareunia and disturbed sleep. Family history: her mother had menopause at 41 and a paternal aunt is on bisphosphonate therapy for osteoporosis.

She has had no chemotherapy, no pelvic radiotherapy and no autoimmune disease known to date. Karyotype is pending and fragile X premutation screen, adrenal antibodies and thyroid antibodies have been ordered. She has no contraindications to oestrogen (no breast cancer, no current VTE, no migraine with aura). BMI 23. BP 118/74. She is in a long-term partnership, not currently planning pregnancy, but is open to consideration of IVF with donor oocytes in the future. A baseline DXA is planned.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, BMI 23
data_table.Investigations: FSH 56 + 62 IU/L (4 weeks apart), low oestradiol, beta-hCG negative, normal TSH/prolactin; karyotype, FMR1, adrenal/thyroid antibodies pending; DXA planned

lead_in: What is the most appropriate hormone management strategy for bone and cardiovascular protection?

options.text: Standard-dose physiological oestradiol with cyclical progestogen or LNG-IUS until the average age of menopause
Bisphosphonate therapy as first-line bone protection without any concurrent hormone therapy
Combined oral contraceptive pill is equivalent to HRT and may be continued lifelong
Defer all hormone therapy and review symptoms again in 6 months
Topical vaginal oestrogen alone as the primary hormone management strategy for this woman

subtopic_detail: POI - bone and cardiovascular protection plan

stem:
A 37-year-old G2P2 woman attends her GP for contraceptive review. She has been on a combined oral contraceptive pill (30 mcg ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel) for the past 4 years. At today's review her blood pressure is 162/96 mmHg, confirmed on a repeat reading 15 minutes later at 158/94 mmHg. Home BP readings over the past 2 weeks have averaged 156/94 mmHg.

She has no headaches, no visual disturbancedema. Urinalysis is negative for protein and blood. She has no history of stroke, transient ischaemic attack, ischaemic heart disease, VTE or migraine with aura. She is a non-smoker, BMI 31, has otherwise normal bloods (renal function, electrolytes, lipids), and no diabetes (HbA1c 5.4%). She has completed her family and would like ongoing reliable contraception. She is reluctant to use barrier methods alone. She has no postnatal depression or mood disorder and her family history is otherwise unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/96, repeat 158/94, home avg 156/94; BMI 31; HR 76
data_table.Examination: Heart sounds dual, no oedema, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: no protein/blood; HbA1c 5.4%, normal lipids, renal function, electrolytes

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate contraceptive recommendation?

options.text: Continue the current combined oral contraceptive pill and re-check blood pressure in 3 months
Switch to a progestogen-only method such as the LNG-IUS, POP, etonogestrel implant or DMPA
Switch to a transdermal combined hormonal patch as this avoids the first-pass hepatic metabolism
Add an antihypertensive and continue the combined oral contraceptive at a lower oestrogen dose
Recommend tubal ligation as the only acceptable contraceptive option for hypertensive women over 35

subtopic_detail: Contraception - hypertension UKMEC application

stem:
A 29-year-old G0 woman with PCOS diagnosed 18 months ago (Rotterdam criteria: oligomenorrhoea, biochemical hyperandrogenism with elevated free androgen index, polycystic ovarian morphology with 26 follicles per ovary) has been trying to conceive for 12 months with intercourse 2 to 3 times per week. Her partner has a normal semen analysis on two occasions. She has bilateral patent tubes on HyCoSy.

AMH 38 pmol/L, AFC 28, normal TSH and prolactin. She has lost 6 kg over 6 months with structured lifestyle intervention (current BMI 28, down from 31), and her cycles remain oligomenorrhoeic (45 to 70 days). HbA1c 5.3% and OGTT normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, BMI 28 (down from 31)
data_table.Examination: Mild hirsutism, no acanthosis nigricans, no virilisation
data_table.Investigations: AMH 38 pmol/L, AFC 28, TSH 1.6, prolactin normal, HbA1c 5.3%, OGTT normal; HyCoSy bilateral patency; partner normal semen analysis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological agent for ovulation induction in this patient?

options.text: Letrozole 2.5 mg daily for 5 days from cycle day 2 to 6, titrated upward if anovulatory
Clomifene citrate 50 mg daily for 5 days from cycle day 2 to 6 with serial follicular tracking
Metformin 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1 g twice daily as sole agent for ovulation induction
Recombinant FSH gonadotrophin injection from cycle day 2 with daily follicular ultrasound monitoring
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling under general anaesthesia as a first-line surgical option for her

subtopic_detail: PCOS - ovulation induction in fertility-seeking woman

stem:
A 32-year-old woman is referred to endocrinology with 14 months of secondary amenorrhoea, bilateral galactorrhoea, reduced libido and a 4-month history of headaches behind her eyes worse on waking. Two months ago she noticed difficulty seeing the side of her vision when driving. On examination today she has bitemporal hemianopia confirmed on confrontation and Humphrey perimetry. Prolactin is 9800 mIU/L (confirmed on a repeat fasting morning sample), TSH and free T4 are normal, beta-hCG negative, renal function normal and she takes no dopamine-blocking medications, antipsychotics, antidepressants or opioids.

MRI pituitary demonstrates a 14 mm pituitary mass with suprasellar extension contacting the optic chiasm with no cavernous sinus invasion. Other anterior pituitary hormones (ACTH/cortisol axis, IGF-1, TSH/T4, LH/FSH) are otherwise within reference range. She is keen to preserve future fertility. She has no symptoms of pituitary apoplexy (no thunderclap headache, no collapse) and her visual loss has been gradual over months rather than days.

data_table.Examination: Bitemporal hemianopia on confrontation and Humphrey; no other focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 9800 mIU/L (repeat fasting morning sample), TSH/T4 normal, beta-hCG negative, renal function normal; pituitary MRI: 14 mm mass with suprasellar extension contacting optic chiasm; other anterior pituitary axes intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly initially with close ophthalmology and endocrine follow-up
Urgent transsphenoidal surgical resection of the pituitary mass within 48 hours
External beam radiotherapy to the pituitary fossa as primary management
Observation with serial MRI and visual fields, deferring treatment until prolactin >20,000 mIU/L
Cyclical combined oral contraceptive pill alone to restore menses and protect bone density

subtopic_detail: Hyperprolactinaemia - macroprolactinoma management

stem:
A 28-year-old G0 woman with PCOS (AMH 48 pmol/L pre-stimulation) presents to the emergency department 9 days after oocyte retrieval (28 oocytes collected, fresh embryo transferred). She reports 3 days of progressive abdominal distension, breathlessness on minimal exertion and reduced urine output. On examination she is tachycardic (HR 112), BP 102/64, RR 24, SpO2 94% on room air, T 36.9.

Abdomen is markedly distended with tense ascites and reduced bowel sounds; she has bilateral basal crackles on chest auscultation. Bloods: haematocrit 0.51, WCC 22 x10^9/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 5.0 mmol/L, creatinine 124 micromol/L (baseline 60), urea 9.5 mmol/L, albumin 26 g/L, ALT 75 U/L, AST 68 U/L. CXR shows small bilateral pleural effusions. Pelvic ultrasound shows ovaries 12 cm bilaterally with large volume ascites extending above the umbilicus. Urine output has been 18 mL/hour over the last 4 hours.

data_table.Examination: Tense ascites, bilateral basal crackles, distended abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Hct 0.51, WCC 22, Na 131, K 5.0, Cr 124 (baseline 60), urea 9.5, Alb 26, ALT 75; CXR bilateral small effusions; USS ovaries 12 cm bilaterally, ascites above umbilicus; urine output 18 mL/hour; D-dimer elevated

lead_in: Which combination of interventions is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Admit; commence IV crystalloid with albumin, prophylactic enoxaparin, fluid balance and urgent paracentesis
Discharge home with oral fluids, simple analgesia and outpatient review in 48 hours
Admit and commence intravenous furosemide infusion to address oliguria and reduce the ovarian volume
Urgent laparotomy with bilateral oophorectomy to remove the hyperstimulated ovaries definitively
Commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and antiviral therapy pending blood culture results

subtopic_detail: Severe OHSS - inpatient management priorities

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P2 woman attends her GP for contraceptive review. She was diagnosed 14 months ago with stage II oestrogen-receptor-positive, progesterone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast. She had wide local excision plus axillary node sampling (1 of 3 nodes positive), adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and commenced tamoxifen 20 mg daily 6 months ago which she plans to continue for at least 5 to 10 years.

She has been amenorrhoeic since chemotherapy but recent bloods show a partial return of menses and an FSH of 18 IU/L with oestradiol 280 pmol/L, suggesting recovery of ovarian function. She uses condoms intermittently with her long-term male partner. She has completed her family. She is anxious to avoid pregnancy because she does not wish to interrupt her endocrine therapy and is aware of the teratogenicity of tamoxifen. She has no other major comorbidity. BMI 24, BP 118/74.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 18 IU/L, E2 280 pmol/L (recovering ovarian function); on tamoxifen 20 mg daily

lead_in: Which contraceptive method is most appropriate for this woman?

options.text: Copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) inserted at the next available family planning visit
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (Mirena) inserted at the next available appointment
Combined oral contraceptive pill at the lowest effective oestrogen dose available
Etonogestrel subdermal contraceptive implant (Implanon NXT) for 3 years
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg IM every 12 weeks

subtopic_detail: Contraception - current breast cancer (UKMEC 4)

stem:
A 31-year-old G1P1 woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (diagnosed 6 years ago) attends for contraceptive review. Her disease has been clinically and serologically stable for 18 months on hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisolone (5 mg daily). She has previously had two episodes of cutaneous lupus and one episode of mild lupus nephritis treated with mycophenolate, now in remission. Her most recent immunology shows positive lupus anticoagulant on two occasions 12 weeks apart, anticardiolipin IgG strongly positive, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I positive (triple positive antiphospholipid profile).

She has no personal history of venous thromboembolism, stroke or ischaemic heart disease and no obstetric morbidity but is high risk for VTE. BP 120/76, BMI 25, non-smoker. She has completed her family, uses condoms inconsistently and would like a more reliable method. She is concerned about both medication interactions with hydroxychloroquine and the impact of contraception on her lupus and VTE risk.

data_table.Examination: No active rash, no active arthritis
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant positive x2 (12 weeks apart), anticardiolipin IgG strongly positive, anti-beta-2-GPI positive; complement and dsDNA stable; renal function normal

lead_in: Which contraceptive method is most appropriate for this woman?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill with the lowest available oestrogen dose to minimise VTE risk
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) inserted at the next available appointment
Combined hormonal contraceptive vaginal ring as it avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg IM every 12 weeks for ongoing contraception
Continue barrier contraception alone (condoms) given the complexity of medication interactions

subtopic_detail: Contraception - SLE with antiphospholipid antibodies

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P2 woman attends for contraceptive review 7 months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery. She has lost 28 kg (BMI now 32, down from 42 pre-operatively). She has not yet resumed menses since surgery and reports breast tenderness, fatigue and intermittent nausea, which she attributes to her vitamin and mineral supplementation. A urine beta-hCG today is negative. Her past medical history includes well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily (BP today 128/78) and previous gestational diabetes (no current diabetes; HbA1c 5.5%).

She uses condoms inconsistently with her long-term male partner. Pre-operatively she was on the combined oral contraceptive pill which was stopped 6 weeks before surgery as part of the VTE risk minimisation protocol. She is fully aware that bariatric surgery is associated with rapid return of fertility and that pregnancy is recommended to be deferred for 12 to 24 months post-operatively. She wishes to use a highly effective method until she is ready for a third pregnancy in 18 months.

data_table.Examination: Surgical scars healed; otherwise unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative; HbA1c 5.5%; no anaemia

lead_in: Which contraceptive method is most appropriate for this woman?

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (Mirena), copper IUD or etonogestrel subdermal implant
Combined oral contraceptive pill at standard dose with continued condom backup
Progestogen-only pill taken daily with a 3-hour mistiming window
Fertility awareness method timed to predicted ovulation each cycle
Recommend immediate pregnancy attempts given strong weight loss and improving metabolic profile

subtopic_detail: Contraception after bariatric surgery

stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents with 2 weeks of thin grey-white vaginal discharge with a fishy odour, worse after intercourse. She has no vulval itch, no dysuria, no abnormal bleeding and no fever. She is in a monogamous relationship of 18 months using a copper IUD, last cervical screening 14 months ago was normal. Speculum: thin homogeneous off-white discharge coating the vaginal walls without inflammation.

Vaginal pH at the lateral wall 5.2; KOH whiff test positive; wet mount shows clue cells, scant lactobacilli, no motile trichomonads, no pseudohyphae. She is not currently pregnant. She had a similar episode 5 months ago which was treated with a 7-day course of oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily; she completed the course, and symptoms resolved for 4 months before recurring.

data_table.Examination: Speculum: thin homogeneous grey-white discharge coating vaginal walls, no inflammation, no strawberry cervix.
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 5.2. KOH whiff test positive. Wet mount: clue cells present, few lactobacilli, no motile trichomonads, no pseudohyphae.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the same 7-day oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily course
Treat with oral metronidazole 400 mg bd for 7 days, then commence intravaginal metronidazole gel twice weekly for 4-6 months as suppressive therapy
Reassure that this is normal discharge and no treatment is needed
Empirically treat both her and her male partner with metronidazole
Remove the copper IUD as it is the underlying cause of recurrent BV

subtopic_detail: Vaginal discharge - microscopy and Amsel recall

stem: A 21-year-old woman at 18 weeks of pregnancy presents with multiple soft non-keratinised fleshy lesions on the vulva and perianal area, first noticed 6 weeks ago and increasing in number. She is otherwise well with an uncomplicated pregnancy on midwifery shared care. She did not receive the HPV vaccine in school. On examination there are approximately 10 papillomatous lesions 2-5 mm distributed over the labia majora and perianal area; no internal vaginal, cervical or intra-anal lesions; cervical screening normal 4 months ago. She is keen to treat them before delivery and prefers home application.

data_table.Examination: Approximately 10 soft non-keratinised papillomatous lesions 2-5 mm on labia majora and perianal area. No cervical, vaginal, urethral or intra-anal lesions.
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative. Cervical screening test 6 months ago: normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment for her anogenital warts?

options.text: Self-applied podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution twice daily for 3 days, then 4 days off, repeated up to 4 cycles
Self-applied imiquimod 5% cream three nights per week for up to 16 weeks
Clinician-applied cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen weekly
Watch and wait until after delivery as warts always regress postpartum
Plan elective caesarean section solely to prevent vertical HPV transmission

subtopic_detail: Anogenital warts - patient-applied therapy choice

stem:
A 23-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder that has worsened over the past 36 hours, with a pleuritic component that is worse on deep inspiration and on lying flat. She also reports four days of lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia and intermenstrual bleeding. She has had two new male partners over the past three months and uses condoms inconsistently.

She is not pregnant (serum beta-hCG < 5 IU/L today). On examination her temperature is 38.1 degrees C, pulse 104 regular, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air. There is right upper quadrant tenderness without Murphy's sign, mild generalised lower abdominal tenderness without peritonism, and bilateral adnexal tenderness with cervical motion tenderness on bimanual examination. Speculum shows mucopurulent cervical discharge with contact bleeding.

Liver function tests show mild transaminitis (ALT 78 U/L, AST 62 U/L) with normal bilirubin and ALP. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows normal gallbladder and biliary tree with no stones, no wall thickening and no pericholecystic fluid. Pelvic ultrasound shows no tubo-ovarian abscess but trace pelvic free fluid. Endocervical NAAT is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 104 bpm, T 38.1 degC.
data_table.Examination: RUQ tender, Murphy's negative. Lower abdominal tenderness without peritonism. CMT, bilateral adnexal tenderness. Mucopurulent cervical discharge.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG < 5 IU/L. ALT 78, AST 62, bilirubin 14, ALP 92. RUQ US: normal GB, no stones. Pelvic US: no TOA, trace free fluid. NAAT: C. trachomatis positive.

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis explaining the right upper quadrant pain?

options.text: Acute viral hepatitis A infection
Acute calculous cholecystitis with ascending cholangitis
Tubo-ovarian abscess with subdiaphragmatic spread
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with haemoperitoneum
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis (gonococcal or chlamydial)

subtopic_detail: PID complication - right upper quadrant pain

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman with chronic HIV-1 infection is reviewed at 36+2 weeks gestation in the antenatal HIV clinic to plan delivery. She has been on tenofovir/emtricitabine/dolutegravir throughout this pregnancy, commenced at 9 weeks gestation, and her adherence has been excellent on pharmacy refill audit. Her booking CD4 count was 540 cells/microL with a baseline HIV viral load of 8400 copies/mL prior to recommencing therapy.

Her most recent HIV viral load taken at 36+0 weeks is < 50 copies/mL (suppressed) and her last three viral loads in the third trimester (at 28, 32 and 36 weeks) have all been < 50 copies/mL. She had a normal vaginal birth with her previous pregnancy four years ago when she was already on suppressive cART. She has no obstetric contraindication to vaginal birth, the fetus is cephalic with appropriate interval growth on the 50th centile, there is no placenta praevia on the 32-week scan, and she has not had any complications this pregnancy.

She is asking about the recommended mode of delivery, whether she requires intrapartum intravenous zidovudine, whether her baby will require post-exposure prophylaxis, and whether she can breastfeed.

data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 36 cm. Cephalic presentation. No oedema.
data_table.Investigations: HIV viral load at 36+0: < 50 copies/mL (suppressed). CD4 540 cells/microL. HBV/HCV negative. GBS swab pending. Growth scan 34 weeks: 50th centile, normal Dopplers.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan for mode of delivery and neonatal prophylaxis?

options.text: Planned vaginal birth, no intrapartum zidovudine required, neonatal zidovudine monotherapy for 2-4 weeks postnatally
