Planned caesarean section at 39+0 weeks, intrapartum intravenous zidovudine, neonatal zidovudine for 6 weeks, no breastfeeding
Planned caesarean section at 38+0 weeks, intrapartum intravenous zidovudine, neonatal triple-drug PEP for 4 weeks, breastfeeding permitted if exclusive
Planned vaginal birth at term, no intrapartum intravenous zidovudine, neonatal zidovudine monotherapy for 4 weeks, no breastfeeding
Planned vaginal birth with intrapartum intravenous zidovudine infusion regardless of viral load, neonatal nevirapine single dose only

subtopic_detail: HIV in pregnancy - mode of delivery decision

stem:
A 26-year-old woman attends the emergency department 28 hours after condomless receptive vaginal intercourse with a male partner she has just learned is living with HIV-1. He told her his combination antiretroviral treatment was 'on and off' over the past six months because he had run out of his prescription, and she does not know his current viral load. She has no symptoms, no genital ulcerationosure, the partner does not inject drugs, and there was no concurrent intercourse with other partners.

She is not pregnant (urine beta-hCG negative today), has no significant past medical history, is on no regular medications other than the etonogestrel implant, has no drug allergies, has normal renal function on baseline pathology (creatinine 64 micromol/L, eGFR > 90), is hepatitis B surface antibody positive (vaccinated as a teenager), HIV antibody/antigen negative on today's baseline 4th-generation test, hepatitis C antibody negative, and syphilis EIA negative. She is not breastfeeding and has no plans for pregnancy in the next month.

data_table.Examination: Well. No mucosal lesions.
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative. Baseline HIV Ag/Ab negative. HBsAb positive (vaccinated). HCV Ab negative. Syphilis EIA negative. Gonorrhoea/chlamydia NAAT sent. Creatinine 64 micromol/L, eGFR > 90.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis regimen and follow-up plan?

options.text: Single-dose tenofovir 300 mg given today, then simply repeat HIV testing again at the 6-week timepoint after exposure
Tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg plus emtricitabine 200 mg daily for 28 days, with no third agent required
Tenofovir alafenamide 25 mg plus emtricitabine 200 mg plus rilpivirine 25 mg daily for 7 days only
Tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine plus dolutegravir 50 mg daily for 28 days, with HIV testing at baseline, 6 weeks and 3 months
Defer PEP until the source partner's plasma viral load is known, then retest her at 4 weeks only

subtopic_detail: Non-occupational HIV post-exposure prophylaxis

stem:
A 29-year-old cisgender woman attends a sexual health service requesting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. Her current male partner of three months has HIV-1 with a viral load that he reports has been detectable on most recent testing because of treatment interruption while changing jobs. They have condomless vaginal sex 2-3 times per week. She has no symptoms of acute HIV illness in the past 6 weeks (no fever, rash, lymphadenopathy or sore throat), is not pregnant (urine beta-hCG negative), is on the etonogestrel implant for contraception, has no history of renal disease, and is hepatitis B surface antibody positive (vaccinated).

She has not injected drugs. Her last STI screen 8 months ago was negative. She has no allergies and no regular medications other than the implant. She is asking whether she is eligible for PrEP, what baseline tests are required, and what monitoring she will need on therapy.

data_table.Examination: Well. No mucosal lesions, no rash, no lymphadenopathy.

She has no significant medical history, is on no regular medications, has no drug allergies, has had a normal menstrual period that finished 8 days ago, and is sexually active with a regular partner from whom she uses no contraception. She is alert, oriented, distressed but cooperative, has minor bruising on her right upper arm and a small abrasion on her left knee, and has not previously had a forensic examination.

There is no immediate life-threatening injury, no head injury, no loss of consciousnesspromise, and she has not consumed alcohol or other substances in the past 24 hours. A specially trained forensic medical examiner is available on call at the local sexual assault service, with chain-of-custody documentation procedures in place, and a social worker can be paged. She is asking what will happen next, what medications she can be offered tonight to reduce pregnancy and infection risk, and whether the examination is mandatory. She has not yet decided whether to formally report to police and is uncertain about disclosing to her family.
